1: Already at the very end of autumn our brother, your son the monk Sisinnius, delivered to me a letter from your Grace; on reading it I rejoiced that you are safe and well, and mindful of me and of all the brothers who serve the Lord in the holy places, in whose relief you make friends for yourself of the unrighteous mammon and prepare eternal tabernacles, so that you can say with David: How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of powers; my soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord. For if the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest for itself where it may lay its young, why should you, who are a high priest of the Lord, and tread the winepresses at the end of the world so as to give to thirsting peoples the wine of the blood of Christ, not freely cry out and say: My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God; blessed are those who dwell in your house. Having heard that you, in the valley of tears, in the place which God has set for the contest so as to give a crown to those who conquer, are arranging ascents in your heart, and going from strength to strength, and imitating the poverty of the Lord, that with him you may become rich, and that he may lay his head upon you, and day by day be received, visited, fed and clothed; and that above all you are fervent in the reading of the holy Scriptures. And since I desired to offer you some little gift of my poor talent, and the exposition I had begun on the twelve prophets was coming to its close, I was unwilling to abandon the work I had undertaken, but what I would have dictated even without you I have consecrated above all to your name; and I am glad that the most obscure book of the prophet Zechariah, and the longest among the twelve, is to be expounded at a time when, because of the haste of him who is to return, the interpretation suffers no delay; but, willing or unwilling, I am compelled to dictate, at least in hours gained and stolen by night, what I am to send you. Origen wrote two volumes on this prophet, reaching from the beginning to the third part of the book. Hippolytus also published commentaries, and Didymus, at my request, dictated five books of exposition, which, with three others on Hosea, he also προσεφώνησεν (dedicated) to me; but their whole ἐξήγησις (exposition) was allegorical, and they barely touched a few points of the history. Therefore, desiring to imitate that householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old, and the bride of the Song of Songs, who says: New with old, my kinsman, I have kept for you, I have mingled the tropology of our writers with the history of the Hebrews, so as to build upon the rock and not upon the sand, and to lay a firm foundation, which Paul the architect wrote that he had laid. It will be for your kindness to look up, not to our learning, which is either none or small, but to the will that leans toward you, so that you may spur us on to the rest and urge us to run in the long field of the Scriptures. But if there are any to whom I previously promised an interpretation both of these and of other books, let them pardon my incredible love for you, and let them consider whatever I have written to you as written to themselves: For love is kind, love is not envious, it does not seek its own. But now it is time that, setting down the words of Zechariah, we spread the sails of interpretation to the Holy Spirit.

In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, saying. LXX: In the eighth month of the second year under Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, saying. That in the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes the seventieth year of the desolation of the temple, which had been foretold by Jeremiah, was completed, Zechariah himself is witness, saying: O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, with which you are angry? Behold, this is the seventieth year; and no one doubts that Cyrus, king of the Persians, who destroyed the empire of the Chaldeans, in the first year of his reign sent back from Babylon into Judea about fifty thousand captives; he also returned the vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had carried off, and ordered the temple to be rebuilt in Jerusalem, and he appointed as leaders of the people that returned Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. So when Cyrus, who reigned thirty years among the Persians, had been killed among the Massagetae by Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae, his son Cambyses succeeded to the kingdom; and when he had completed eight years, he had as successors two brothers, magi; and when these had been killed by the people, Darius son of Hystaspes was made king of the Persians by the decision of the seven families. In the second year of his reign the word of the Lord came to the prophet Haggai, and to Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo. On Haggai we have already spoken; on the title of Zechariah a few things must be said. Since he is the son of Berechiah, the question is asked why he is called the son of Iddo. Nor is it doubted, according to the book of Chronicles, that he is that Iddo who was sent to Jeroboam son of Nebat, under whom the altar was torn down and the king's hand withered, and at his prayers was restored again. Therefore from the first year of King Cyrus to the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes forty years are reckoned, in which only the altar had been built and the foundations of the temple laid, since the neighboring nations round about were hindering the work, and so was Cambyses, king of the Persians, who had sent letters on this matter to the governors of Syria Κοίλης (Hollow), and of Phoenicia and Samaria. Ezra wrote the history of this more fully. But Haggai began to prophesy in the sixth month, on the first day of that month; Zechariah, for his part, in the same year indeed, but not in the same month, for two months later, in the eighth month of the year, he poured out his prophecy. Hence, rightly, according to the order of the twelve prophets, the former is placed tenth and the latter eleventh. And it is a mark of great confidence, nay rather of hope and faith in God, that what had been left undone for so long a time, whether through the king's prohibition or the nations', they should begin to do at the stirring of two men. These things, according to the history, we have set down first in our usual manner. Now we must discuss them briefly according to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy). The eighth month among the Hebrews, which among them is called Marcheshvan, among the Egyptians Athir, and among us November, is the beginning of winter; in it, the heat of summer being spent, all the earth is stripped of its green, and the bodies of mortals are contracted, and there is no solemnity from the Law. For it is written that three times in the year every male must appear before the Lord our God. The first festival is that of unleavened bread, the Phase, which among us is called Pascha in Greek and Latin speech. The second is that of Pentecost, after seven weeks, in which the loaves of proposition are first offered from the new crops. The third, in the seventh month, is that of trumpets, of propitiation and of tabernacles, that is, σκηνοπηγίας, whose last day is called the day of departure and of the end. So the people, placed in captivity and still under the king of the Persians, with the temple not yet built and the ramparts and walls of the city not yet raised, sees prophecy not in a time of gladness, but after gladness. And yet it had the remembrance of the Lord, and because of the remembrance, blessing, and on account of the blessing, testimony. For this reason Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, is sent to it. Zechariah is interpreted remembrance of the Lord; Berechiah, blessing of the Lord; Iddo, his testimony. Let us see, then, what the word of the Lord, which was in the beginning with God the Father, spoke to the people in the prophet Zechariah.

The Lord was angry with your fathers in anger, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Turn to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will turn to you, says the Lord of hosts; be not like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried, saying. LXX: The Lord was angry with your fathers with great wrath, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Turn to me, says the Lord of powers, and I will turn to you, says the Lord of powers; and do not become like your fathers, whom the prophets who were before rebuked, saying. The wrath of the Lord does not signify a disturbance in him who is angry, but the deserts and sins of those against whom the wrath of God rages; for the rest, the Lord never takes vengeance in anger, but rebukes in order to amend. Hence the prophet also prays in the psalms: O Lord, do not reprove me in your fury, nor rebuke me in your wrath, and in another place we read: Rebuke us, O Lord, yet not in your fury, but in mercy. So the Lord was angry with the fathers of those who are now being rebuked, not, as the Seventy translators have it, with great wrath, but simply with wrath. For if he had been angry with great wrath, he would never have called the captives to repentance through Daniel and Ezekiel.

But not all who see are equally enlightened by Christ, but each is enlightened according to that measure by which he is able to receive the force of the light. And just as the eyes of our body are not equally enlightened by the sun, but the higher one ascends into lofty places and beholds its rising by the gazing of a more elevated watchtower, so much the more will he receive both of its splendor and its heat; so also our mind, the more loftily and highly it approaches Christ and presents itself nearer to the splendor of his light, so much the more magnificently and clearly will it be irradiated by his light, as he himself also says through the prophet: "Draw near to me, and I will draw near to you, says the Lord." And again he says: "I am a God drawing near, and not a God from afar."

Indeed, God is good to everyone, but he shows his patient endurance especially to those who sin. And if you want to hear a paradoxical statement—paradoxical because it is not customary, but true for the great piety it reveals—listen. God always seems to be severe to the righteous but good to sinners and quick to clemency. He restores the one who sinned and fell and tells him, "Shall not he who falls arise; or he that turns away, shall he not turn back again?" And "Why did that stupid daughter of Judah turn away with a shameless revolting?" And again, "Return to me, and I will return to you." Elsewhere he assures with an oath the salvation from repentance by much clemency. " 'As I live,' says the Lord, 'I do not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn from his way and live.' " To the righteous he says, "If a man achieves every righteousness and truth and later turns from his way and sins, I will not remember his righteousness, but he will die in his sin." O such strictness toward the righteous! O such abundant forgiveness toward the sinner! He finds so many different means, without himself changing, to keep the righteous in check and forgive the sinner, by usefully dividing his rich goodness.

And although he was angry with them, it is to you that the Lord of hosts speaks, for which Sabaoth is set down in the Hebrew, which the Seventy sometimes translated 'Almighty', sometimes 'of powers'. And he says: Turn to me, and I will turn to you, according to what we read: Draw near to the Lord, and he will draw near to you. To which this is the contrary: You have withdrawn from me, and I have withdrawn from you. Now he commands those who have returned from Babylon to return to the Lord, so that the Lord too may return to them, lest the sons begin to suffer what their fathers once suffered, to whom the prophets of that time likewise spoke. It is to be noted that in a few short verses and brief sentences, in Haggai and Zechariah, says the Lord of hosts is always added, so that they may know that it is God who commands, both against the command of the king and against the enemies raging round about; and that by this confidence they may be roused to the building of the temple.

When God says, "Turn ye unto me, and I will turn unto you," one of these clauses—that which invites our return to God—evidently belongs to our will; while the other, which promises His return to us, belongs to His grace. Here, possibly, the Pelagians think they have a justification for their opinion which they so prominently advance, that God's grace is given according to our merits. In the East, indeed, that is to say, in the province of Palestine, in which is the city of Jerusalem, Pelagius, when examined in person by the bishop, did not venture to affirm this. For it happened that among the objections which were brought up against him, this in particular was objected, that he maintained that the grace of God was given according to our merits,—an opinion which was so diverse from catholic doctrine, and so hostile to the grace of Christ, that unless he had anathematized it, as laid to his charge, he himself must have been anathematized on its account. He pronounced, indeed, the required anathema upon the dogma, but how insincerely his later books plainly show; for in them he maintains absolutely no other opinion than that the grace of God is given according to our merits. Such passages do they collect out of the Scriptures,—like the one which I just now quoted, "Turn ye unto me, and I will turn unto you,"—as if it were owing to the merit of our turning to God that His grace were given us, wherein He Himself even turns unto us. Now the persons who hold this opinion fail to observe that, unless our turning to God were itself God's gift, it would not be said to Him in prayer, "Turn us again, O God of hosts;" and, "Thou, O God, wilt turn and quicken us;" and again, "Turn us, O God of our salvation,"—with other passages of similar import, too numerous to mention here. For, with respect to our coming unto Christ, what else does it mean than our being turned to Him by believing? And yet He says: "No man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father."
On Grace and Free Will, Chapter 10

If we are entirely devoted to God and humbly implore his mercy, through the mercy of God we may deserve to be healed of all our infirmities, rescued from all our sins, set free from the frequent flooding of waters. We ought to believe for certain, dearest brothers, that if our sins cease, the divine mercy will immediately remove the punishments that were due to us. Thus he himself has deigned to promise through the prophet when he said, "Return to me, and I will return to you," and again, "If you groan and return to me, then you shall be saved." Therefore let us turn to a better life while the remedies are still in our power. By our good deeds let us summon to mercy the kind and merciful Lord whom we provoked by our sins. According to his usual practice, he will then deign to keep adversities from us and in his clemency to grant us good fortune.

Thus says the Lord of hosts: Turn from your evil ways, and from your most wicked thoughts; and they did not hear, nor did they attend to me, says the Lord. LXX: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Turn from your most wicked ways, and from your evil devices, and they did not attend so as to hear me, says the Lord. The sentence hangs on what precedes, and what follows must be fitted to what came before. For Zechariah is not speaking to the people, but is showing what the former prophets said to their fathers, to whom they cried, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Turn from your evil ways and from your most wicked thoughts. This is what Isaiah cried, this Hosea and Joel, Amos and Jeremiah: that they should forsake their evil ways and abandon their most wicked thoughts, by which they were sinning both in deed and in mind; and nevertheless they did not hear the Lord warning them through the prophets, nor did they attend, not at all to the prophets who were speaking to them, but to me, says the Lord: for in them it was I who was speaking and being despised. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: He who receives you, he says, receives me.

Your fathers, where are they, and the prophets? Will they live forever? But my words and my ordinances, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not overtake your fathers? And they turned and said: As the Lord of hosts purposed to do to us according to our ways and according to our devices, he has done to us. LXX: Your fathers, where are they, and the prophets? Will they live forever? But receive my words and my ordinances, which I command in my spirit to my servants the prophets, who overtook your fathers. And they answered and said: As the Lord Almighty was prepared to do to us according to our ways and according to our devices, so he has done to us. Where, he says, are your fathers, who did not hear me nor attend to me? Where are your prophets? For it is to be understood Ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (from the shared word): Your fathers, where are they, and your prophets, where are they? that is, the false prophets; for he would never say of the holy prophets: Will they live forever? So, when both those who sinned and refused to return to me, and those who deceived the sinners with false promises, have been taken away by death, my words, which I spoke through my prophets, remain forever; they overtook your fathers and showed that what I said was true. And your fathers, proving upon themselves by the outcome of events the prophecies of my prophets, turned to repentance and said: As the Lord of hosts foretold that he would do to us, according to our works and sins he has repaid us. Let us read Daniel confessing to the Lord, in his own person and in that of the people, that they had refused to hear him, and that whatever they had suffered had befallen them justly.

On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, saying. LXX: On the twenty-fourth, in the eleventh month, which is the month Shebat, in the second year under Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, saying. Some put the twelfth month in place of the eleventh, and, interpreting the twenty-fourth day of that month by arithmetical reckonings, suppose it to be a square, firm and stable number, wishing the things that are written to be certain and stable. But let us say that in the same second year of King Darius, in the third month after the first vision, that is, in the eleventh after the eighth, which among the Hebrews is called Shebat, the word of the Lord came again to Zechariah. That the second number is unclean, and pertains to the union of the flesh, and to the things of the world and of matter, we have often taught. Now the eleventh month, which is called Shebat, and in our language is rendered 'rod', sounds of severity and rebuke, according to that saying of the Apostle: What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod? And of the psalmist, who says: Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me. And it falls in the very bitter season of winter, and is called mechir by the Egyptians, περίτϊος by the Macedonians, and February by the Romans. The twenty-fourth day of the month, too, signifies a conspicuous shadow of night, as the moon wanes into darkness and the blind and continual dread of night increases. Hence, fittingly, those who were still in captivity, and for the greater part of them were in exile among the Medes and Chaldeans and Assyrians, in the second year, and in the most severe cold of the eleventh month, and on the twenty-fourth day of that month, see for the Jewish people the things that follow.

And you will understand the sentence that follows if you compare with it these words in Zechariah:

"8. I saw the night, and behold a man sitting on a bay horse, and he stood in the midst of the shady mountains."

I believe this rider on the bay horse who stands in the midst of the shady mountains to be the same person mentioned in the prophecy before us, which says that the Holy One will come from a thick and shady mountain.

In each passage shady mountains are mentioned, and I believe they refer to the Paradise of God, which He planted eastward in Eden, or perhaps to the Heavenly Jerusalem. For "there are mountains around it, and the Lord is in the midst of his people." And these mountains are said to be shady, because they are full of divine powers and holy spirits, as of trees planted there and far-spreading. But in Zechariah clearly the vision was of a man riding on a bay horse, by which the Incarnation of our Saviour was meant, and the flesh in which He rode: while here "God a Holy One" is named. For to mark that it was from God that He made His approach to men, and that He arrived from diviner regions, it is said, "God came from Thaeman, and the Holy One from a thick and shady mountain."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 15

[Daniel 7:5] "And behold another beast like a bear stood up on one side; and there were three rows in his mouth and in his teeth; and they said to him: 'Arise up and devour flesh in abundance.'" The second beast resembling a bear is the same as that of which we read in the vision of the statue (2:32): "His chest and arms were of silver." In the former case the comparison was based on the hardness of the metal, in this case on the ferocity of the bear. For the Persian kingdom followed a rigorous and frugal manner of life after the manner of the Spartans, and that too to such an extent that they used to use salt and nasturtium-cress in their relish. Let us consult the record of the childhood of Cyrus the Great (i.e., "The Education or Training" of Cyrus). And as for the fact that the bear is said to have "stood up on one side," the Hebrews interpret it by saying that the Persians never perpetrated any cruelty against Israel. Hence they are described in the Prophecy of Zechariah also as white horses (Zechariah 1:7-11). But as for the three rows or ranks that were in his mouth and between his teeth, one authority has interpreted this to mean that allusion was made to the fact that the Persian kingdom was divided up among three princes, just as we read in the sections dealing with Belshazzar and with Darius that there were three princes who were in charge of the one hundred and twenty satraps. But other commentators affirm that these were three kings of the Persians who were subsequent to Cyrus, and yet they fail to mention them by name. But we know that after Cyrus's reign of thirty years his son Cambyses ruled among the Persians, and his brothers the magi, and then Darius, in the second year of whose reign the rebuilding of the Temple was commenced at Jerusalem. The fifth king was Xerxes, the son of Darius; the sixth was Artabanus; the seventh, Artaxerxes who was surnamed Makrokheir, that is Longimanus ("Long-handed"); the eighth, Xerxes; the ninth, Sogdianus; the tenth, Darius surnamed Nothos ("Bastard"); the eleventh, the Artaxerxes called Mnemon, that is, "The Rememberer"; the twelfth, the other Artaxerxes, who himself received the surname of Ochus; the thirteenth, Arses, the son of Ochus; and the fourteenth, Darius the son of Arsamus, who was conquered by Alexander, the king of the Macedonians. How then can we say that these were three kings of the Persians? Of course we could select some who were especially cruel, but we cannot ascertain them on the basis of the historical accounts. Therefore the three rows in the mouth of the Persian kingdom and between its teeth we must take to be the three kingdoms of the Babylonians, the Medes, and the Persians, all of which were reduced to a single realm. And as for the information, "And thus they spake to him: 'Devour flesh in abundance,'" this refers to the time when in the reign of the Ahasuerus whom the Septuagint calls Artaxerxes, the order was given, at the suggestion of Haman the Agagite, that all the Jews be slaughtered on a single day (Esther 3:13). And very properly, instead of saying, "He was devouring them" the account specifies, "Thus they spake unto him..." This shows that the matter was only attempted, and was by no means ever carried out.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER SEVEN

I saw by night, and behold, a man mounting a red horse, and he was standing among the myrtle groves that were in the deep, and behind him horses red, dappled and white. And I said: What are these, my lord? And the angel who was speaking in me said to me: I will show you what these are. And the man who was standing among the myrtle groves answered and said: These are they whom the Lord has sent to walk through the earth. And they answered the angel of the Lord, who was standing among the myrtle groves, and said: We have walked through the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest. And the angel of the Lord answered and said: O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, with which you are angry? This is the seventieth year. And the Lord answered the angel who was speaking in me good words, words of consolation. LXX: I saw in the night, and behold, a man mounting a red horse, and he was standing between two shady mountains, and behind him horses red, and dappled, and white. And I said: What are these, lord? And the angel who was speaking in me said to me: I will show you what these are. And the man who was standing between the mountains answered and said to me: These are they whom the Lord has sent to go round the earth. And they answered the angel of the Lord, who was standing between the mountains, and said: We have gone round all the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest. And the angel of the Lord answered and said: O Lord Almighty, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, with which you are angry? This is the seventieth year. And the Lord answered the angel who was speaking in me good words and consoling speeches. Let us first discuss the history: I saw, he says, by night, not by day, like Moses, who saw God face to face, and Isaiah, who said: I saw the Lord upon a throne high and lifted up, before the people was led into captivity, before Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed; but now, with the people still set in the evils of servitude, he discerns in darkness the things he sees on their behalf. And behold, a man mounting a red horse. This the Hebrews think is the angel Michael, who is the avenger of the iniquities and sins of Israel. And as to his having stood among the myrtle groves that were in the deep, they want the myrtles to be understood as the prophets and saints who were living in the midst of the captive people and were in the deep; and the man, that is, Michael, was followed by horses red and dappled and white, the order, as they suppose, being changed, so that the white signify the Medes and Persians, because under them the captivity was released and the temple restored; the dappled, the Macedonians, some of whom were friends, others persecutors — the last vision of Daniel speaks most fully on this —; and the red, the kingdom of the Romans, bloody and murderous, which slew the people and overthrew the temple. Others, however, keeping the order as it is written, interpret the man who mounted the red horse, and the red, dappled and white horses, as four kingdoms. The first and second, the bloody ones, are the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the first of whom led the ten tribes captive under Shalmaneser, the second Judah and Benjamin, when the city of Jerusalem had been burned and the temple overthrown. The third and fourth, the dappled and white, they think signify the Medes and Persians, some of whom were merciful, like Cyrus, and Darius son of Hystaspes, and Ahasuerus, whom the Greeks call Artaxerxes, under whom the story of Esther is fulfilled, and others cruel, like Cambyses and the rest.

But the teachers of the churches understand the night in which the vision is seen as the obscurity of a mystical vision. For God made darkness his hiding place. And according to the Seventy translators it is said of him: The abyss like a garment is his clothing. Now the man who was mounting the red horse is the Lord and Savior, who, taking it up for the dispensation of our flesh, hears in Isaiah: Why are your garments red? He who is now shown as red to the captive people is described in the Apocalypse of John as sitting in white garments and on a white horse. And as to his being said to stand between two shady mountains — although 'two' is not found in the Hebrew — they take them as the New and the Old Testament, which is said to be covered with very dense foliage, and grove, and shady woods, because it is wrapped in many obscurities. And the myrtle groves that were in the deep, among which he is described as standing, they understand as the angelic powers, which ministered to him even when he was set in the flesh. Or else, removing what is not written, 'two', we can take the mountains absolutely and without number as very many saints, and the apostles and apostolic men, who are recorded as having traveled through the whole world, red, and dappled, and white; of whom some are crowned with martyrdom and are called red; others, for their works and teaching and the variety of their signs, are named dappled; others have received the rewards of virginity and of uncorrupted doctrines, and of the pure heart, which sees God.

It is quite clear that all the things shown to the prophet were tokens of certain realities, just as Joseph saw sheaves, sun, moon and stars, each of which carried a clue to some coming event, and the Pharaoh saw ears of corn and oxen, some fat and some skinny, and by these as well other events were signified from what was shown. In exactly the same way the prophet also sees these things by divine revelation, and each of the things shown him contained some sign or indication of a reality. Likewise blessed Peter also saw a cloth let down from heaven, full of various living creatures clean and unclean, and the vision contained a clue to some other things.

It is clear that those who were seen are invisible powers, "sent for service," according to the divine apostle, "for the sake of those who are due to inherit salvation." Their natures are not seen, however, being incorporeal: he who is Lord of them and of everyone else renders them discernible according to need in each case. The divine Scripture clearly teaches us this, giving a glimpse of their different forms: Daniel saw them in one fashion, Ezekiel in another fashion, and Isaiah and Micah in different forms. Not that they have many forms, being naturally incorporeal and spiritual: the Lord of all when need arises gives them a form for discernment. This he did also in the case of Zechariah: he reveals to him the angel who is a leader of the people; St. Michael was this angel.

So when the prophet saw a man mounting a red horse, and behind him red, dappled and white horses, and did not know what he had seen, and desired to know the meaning of his vision, and said: What are these, my lord? the angel who was speaking in him promises that he will tell; and while he keeps silent, the man who was standing among the myrtle groves relates it. These are the kingdoms which the Lord commanded to walk through the earth and to subject it to their power.

Then the prophet questions the same man and angel who was standing among the myrtle groves, and says: What are these, my lord? And the angel who was speaking in him, namely the prophetic sense, promises that he will show what he sees. And when he has promised, it is not he himself who answered, but another who was standing among the myrtle groves, and he says: These are they whom the Lord has sent to walk through the earth. For the apostles were sent by the Lord to fill the whole world with the preaching of the Gospel; and after they had fulfilled the work, they returned to the angel of great counsel who was standing among them (they who said with the Apostle: We are the good odor of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing) and among the peoples of both callings. And they said to him: We have walked through the earth, we have fulfilled the work enjoined on us, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest, which before was deserted by God; now it is his dwelling, it rests from wars, from the battles of the vices and from sins, because it has received the inheritance of the Lord as he returned to the Father and said: My peace I give you, my peace I leave you.

You see that God speaks not in the ears but in the heart; just as Zechariah too says: "And the angel who spoke within me said to me." There the angel is understood to be our Lord, who announces the will of the Father, who in Isaiah is called the "angel of great counsel."

Likewise, who will tell with what bodies angels appear to people, in such fashion as not to be visible but to be tangible? And again how, not through tangible corporeality but by spiritual power, angels produce certain visions, not to the eyes of the body but to those of the spirit or the mind, or can utter speech, not of the ear from without, but within the soul of humans, being themselves placed there, as is written in the book of the prophets: "And the angel that spoke in me said to me" (for what the prophet says is not "that spoke to me," but "in me").… They appear also in sleep and speak through dreams (for we read in the Gospel: "Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying"). These methods of communication tend to show that the angels have intangible bodies, and make it a very difficult question how the patriarchs could wash the feet of angels, and how Jacob could wrestle with an angel in contact so unmistakable. Asking these questions and answering them with such guesses as we can is not a useless exercise for the mind, if the discussion is kept within bounds and if those who take part avoid the error of thinking they know what they do not know. For what need is there of affirming or denying or making nice distinctions about these and similar matters, when ignorance of them imputes no blame?

"And the devil came with them." What are you saying? "With the angels?" He who rebelled, who dishonored himself? Do not worry, my dear; this is an image, a figure. It is like another passage in the [First] Book of Kings, where it is said, "And there came forth an evil spirit, and the Lord said, 'Who will deceive Ahab?' " And the spirit responded: "I will deceive him," and he indicates it in such a way. The Scripture often takes on an anthropomorphic character.… The angels came, according to the text, and the devil came with them having compassed the earth and walked around in the subcelestial regions. What do we understand by that? That the earth is filled with demons and angels, and that both are under the power of God; and that the angels present themselves before God, from whom they receive orders; and that the devil can do nothing to please himself, if he has not received permission for it from above. For if he has totally rejected the bridle and is no longer in service to God, he is not in the least held back by fear as by a bit which restrains him from using his own power. But note this: whereas the angels present themselves as servants who render an account to him of their doings, as one can see in Zechariah, the devil has nothing to say to him. Consequently the expression "he came with them" means nothing else but that he too is dependent on God.… What does the expression therefore signify? It signifies that he is with them in the world. In the same way as deceitful people and good people are mixed, so are the angels and the demons.

In short, the angels who presided over the kingdoms and nations come not to another, but to the man himself and angel of the Lord who was standing among the myrtle groves, and say: We have walked through the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest. And the sense is: All the kingdoms under us are safe and pacified, and are not oppressed by any distress.

And if you reckon the period of the seven and sixty-two weeks in another way a third time, they will comprise 483 years, up to Augustus and Herod, the first king of foreign stock, in whose reign the Birth of our Saviour Jesus Christ is recorded to have occurred, if you begin to reckon from Darius and the completion of the Temple. For the prophet Zechariah shews that the seventy years of the Desolation of Jerusalem were completed in the second year of Darius, when he says: "On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month (this is the Sabbath), in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Barachiah." And then he adds, "And the Angel of the Lord answered, and said, O Almighty Lord, how long wilt thou not pity Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, which thou hast despised these seventy years past?"

This, then, was the very time that Daniel, inspired by the divine spirit, marked when he said, "I Daniel understood in the books the number of the years, what was the word of the Lord to Jeremiah the prophet, for the fulfilment of the desolation of Jerusalem seventy years, and I turned my face to the Lord my God, to present my prayer and petition." Then after his prayer the Angel prophesied to him of the seventy weeks, and told him at what point to begin to reckon the time, saying, "And thou shalt know and understand from the going forth of the word of answering and from the building of Jerusalem until Christ the governor." The first answer allowing Jerusalem to be rebuilt was of course that of Cyrus, but it did not take effect, because the neighbours interfered. But when Darius gave his order afterwards, and the building of the Temple was also completed in his reign, from that date began to be fulfilled the prophecy of Daniel, which said, "From the going forth of the word of answering and from the building of Jerusalem," and that which said, "I Daniel understood in the books the number of the years, which was the word of the Lord to Jeremiah the prophet, for the fulfilment of the desolation of Jerusalem seventy years." The completion of the period of seventy years is therefore shewn to have been reached in the second year of Darius, so that we must anyway reckon the seventy weeks from the sixty-sixth Olympiad, and from the second year of Darius, in which the building was completed. And if you reckon the succeeding period from that date up to King Herod and the Roman Emperor Augustus, in whose times our Saviour was born on earth, you will find it amounts to 483 years, which are the seven and sixty-two weeks of the prophecy of Daniel. From the sixty-sixth Olympiad to the 186th Olympiad there are 121 Olympiads, or 484 years, an Olympiad consisting of four years, during which time Augustus the Roman Emperor, in the fifteenth year of his reign, gained the kingdom of Egypt and of the whole world, under whom Herod was the first foreigner to ascend the Jewish throne, and our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ was born, the time of His birth synchronizing with the fulfilment of the seven and sixty-two weeks of Daniel's prophecy.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 2

[Daniel 5:2] "Being now drunken, he therefore gave order that the golden and silver vessels be brought in which his father, Nebuchadnezzar, had taken away from the temple which was in Jerusalem, in order that the king might drink from them..." The Hebrews hand down some such story as this: that up until the seventieth year, on which Jeremiah had said (Jeremiah 25:11) that the captivity of the Jewish people would be released (a matter of which Zechariah also speaks [Zechariah 1:12] in the first part of his book), Belshazzar had esteemed God's promise to be of none effect; therefore he turned the failure of the promise into an occasion of joy and arranged a great banquet, scoffing somewhat at the expectation of the Jews and at the vessels of the Temple of God. Punishment, however, immediately ensued. And as to the fact that the author calls Nebuchadnezzar the father of Belshazzar, he does not make any mistake in the eyes of those who are acquainted with the Holy Scripture's manner of speaking, for in the Scripture all progenitors and ancestors are called fathers. This factor also should be borne in mind, that he was not sober when he did these things, but rather when he was intoxicated and forgetful of the punishment which had come upon his progenitor, Nebuchadnezzar.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FIVE

From this answer the angel who interceded for Israel, taking the occasion to pray for the people, also says to the Lord: Since the whole world is quiet and at peace, why, O Lord, will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, especially since, according to your promises, the time of the captivity has been fulfilled?

And as to the plea, full of mercy, that, with the seventieth year at hand, God should have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, they refer it to this understanding: that until true peace comes, and the sabbath rest, and the number of seven decades, that is, the seventieth year, is fulfilled, neither does Jerusalem, which is interpreted vision of peace and is the Church, receive full liberty, nor do the cities of Judah, the souls that confess the Lord.

And the Lord answered the angel who was speaking in the prophet good words, words of consolation: good concerning the promise of things to come, consoling concerning the need of things present. These things we have given according to the letter, lest we should seem to hide from our own people what we have learned from teachers of a foreign tongue.

In short, the Lord answered good words and words of consolation, which now we see in part and prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, may the things that are in part be done away, and, set free from the Babylon of this world, may we cry out: When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became as those consoled.

Jerusalem and Zion, the vision of peace and the watchtower, which looks not on the wars of this world, nor on things lowly and earthly, but on peace and concord and the heights of heaven, can be understood as the Church. Angry with her because of vices and sins and charity growing colder every day, the Lord will hand her over to persecutions, so that, as in a smelting furnace, pure gold and silver may appear. But the adversaries to whom she has been handed over, striving to blot her out, fill Jerusalem with the blood of the slain from gate to gate.

And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I am jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with a great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry with the wealthy nations; for I was angry a little, but they helped toward evil. Therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem in mercies, and my house shall be built in it, says the Lord of hosts; and the plumb line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem. LXX: And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I am jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with a great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry with the nations that have been set on top, because I indeed was angry a little, but they have set themselves on top unto evils. Therefore thus says the Lord: I will turn to Jerusalem in mercy, and my house shall be restored in it, says the Lord Almighty; and the measure shall be stretched out over Jerusalem. These are still good words, words of consolation, which the prophet is now commanded to cry out: that the Lord has been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with a great jealousy. But he who is jealous shows that he loves her for whom he is jealous, by no means saying through Jeremiah: As a woman despises her husband, so the house of Israel has despised me. To her the Lord used to speak through Ezekiel: Being angry, I will no longer be angry with you, and my jealousy has departed from you.

He, then, who was jealous for Jerusalem and Zion, which are, moreover, one and the same city, is now angry with the wealthy nations, which he named above as the red, white and speckled horses: because he himself handed them over to be chastened, but they raged against those handed over; he wished them corrected as a son by a tutor, they tried to kill and punish them as an enemy. Like this is that passage in Isaiah: I gave them into your hands, but you showed them no mercy. On the old man you made the yoke very heavy, and you said: I shall be mistress forever. Now jealousy is taken ἀνθρωποπάθως (in human fashion), in the same way as anger. By this passage the heretics who disparage the Old Testament are refuted, since God, when he is angry, desires not to destroy those with whom he is angry, but to amend them.

Because, therefore, he says, I am jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with a great jealousy, which the adversaries have pressed down more than I wished, therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem not in one mercy but in many mercies, and my house, that is, the temple, shall be built in it under Zerubbabel and Joshua son of Jehozadak; and the plumb line of the masons shall be stretched out over Jerusalem.

Hence the Lord, promising peace and mercy, says that he will build her again, and that the plumb line, or the cord, is to be stretched out in her according to the measures and ranks of each one. What the cord is, is shown in the following passage, where the prophet says: I lifted up my eyes and saw: and behold, a man, and in his hand a measurers' cord. And the temple of the Lord which the adversaries destroyed can also be understood as the venerable body of the Lord, of which he himself said: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. Destroyed in the passion, it was raised in the resurrection, and it was the seedbed and the beginning of all temples, of which the Apostle too speaks: You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you.

Cry out yet, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet my cities shall overflow with good things; and the Lord shall yet comfort Zion, and shall yet choose Jerusalem. LXX: And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out yet, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Yet the cities shall be poured out in good things, and the Lord shall yet have mercy on Zion, and shall yet choose Jerusalem. The angel who had said to the prophet above: Cry out; thus says the Lord of hosts, now too urges him to cry out, not with the straining of the voice but of the mind; and this is what he commands him to cry out: Yet my cities shall overflow with good things; those which you now see laid waste by the Babylonian fire shall again abound in all things, and with present good things the Lord shall console their past misery, and shall choose Jerusalem, which a little before he had cast off. But if we refer it to the Church, to which he promises true and everlasting good things, those good things must be believed to be the ones of which we read it written: May you see the good things of Jerusalem, and in another place: If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land, and that saying: You shall trust in the Lord, and he shall lift you up above the good things of the earth. These a wise man, to whom the Lord had revealed the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom, promises himself in the hope of things to come, and says: I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. With these good things, now that peace has been restored after the fires of the most savage persecution which the churches of the Lord endured both from the Gentiles and from the Arian heretics, we see the churches of the Lord overflow, and Zion consoled, and Jerusalem chosen, which he had formerly cast away. This very thing we can also understand both of the temple of the Lord and of each one of the believers. Some refer the consoled Zion and the chosen Jerusalem, and the other things that are proclaimed in this manner by all the prophets, to the heavenly Jerusalem, which, destroyed through a fall, is to be built up through virtues. All of which we shall more rightly interpret of the Church.

These four kingdoms which overthrew Judea Zechariah writes that he saw in four horns, the angel saying to him: These are the horns which have scattered Judah and Israel and Jerusalem. And again: I lifted up, he says, my eyes and saw; and behold, four chariots coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze; in the first chariot, red horses; and in the second chariot, black horses; and in the third chariot, white horses; and in the fourth chariot, dappled, strong horses. And when the prophet had said to the angel who spoke in him: What are these, my lord? The angel answered: These are the four winds of heaven, which go forth to stand before the ruler of all the earth; and the sense is: These are they who go forth from the face of the Lord, to fulfill his will.

And I lifted up my eyes and saw. And behold, four horns; and I said to the angel who spoke in me: What are these? And he said to me: These are the horns that have winnowed Judah, and Israel and Jerusalem. And the Lord showed me four smiths, and I said: What are these coming to do? He spoke, saying: These are the horns that have winnowed Judah man by man, and none of them lifted up his head, and these came to terrify them, to cast down the horns of the nations which have lifted up the horn over the land of Judah, to scatter it. LXX: And I lifted up my eyes and saw. And behold, four horns, and I said to the angel who spoke in me: What are these, Lord? And he said to me: These are the horns that have scattered Judah, and Israel, and Jerusalem. And the Lord showed me four smiths, and I said: What are these coming to do? And he said: These are the horns that have scattered Judah, and have broken Israel, and none of them lifted up his head, and these have gone out to sharpen them in their hands. The four horns are nations that have lifted up the horn over the land of the Lord, to scatter it. That the four horns which winnowed and scattered Judah, and Israel, and Jerusalem are four nations, the Babylonians, the Medes and Persians, and the Macedonians and the Romans, both the Lord now explains when questioned by the prophet, and Daniel unfolds most fully, who in the vision of the image that had a golden head, and a silver breast, and a bronze belly, and legs and feet of iron and of clay, interpreted these four nations. And again in another vision, by four beasts, a lioness and a bear, and a leopard, and another horrible beast whose name he did not set down, he showed the same nations under another figure. That the Medes and Persians were one kingdom after the victory of Cyrus no one will doubt who has read both secular and sacred literature. And most rightly he has put horns for kingdoms, since holy Scripture has this custom, that it always signifies a kingdom by horns, as in that verse: And he exalted the horn of his Christ. And in another place: And he has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant. And the same prophet Daniel testifies to ten horns that are to reign at the last. At the time, then, when this vision was seen, the kingdom of the Babylonians had already passed away, that of the Persians and Medes was at hand, and that of the Greeks and Macedonians, and of the Romans, was yet to come. What the Babylonians, what the Medes and Persians, what the Greeks, that is, the Macedonians, did to Judah and Israel and Jerusalem, a learned man knows, above all under Antiochus, surnamed Ἐπιφανεῖ (Epiphanes), under whom the history of the Maccabees is woven. After the coming of the Lord and Savior as well, when Jerusalem was besieged, what the Israelites suffered both the Gospel foretells and Josephus, the native writer of the Jewish history, teaches most fully.

But that the prophet says he lifted up his eyes is to be fitted to the spiritual sense: I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help shall come, and: Lift up your eyes, and see the regions, for they are already white for harvest, and what we read in Isaiah: The Holy One said: Lift up your eyes, and see who has shown all these things. There is need, therefore, of the lifting up of the eyes and of spiritual understanding, that we may see the opposing powers which have lifted up their horn against us, and of which the Apostle speaks: Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of this world, of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. These four adversaries, who were always fighting against the saints, Christ crushed at his coming. And of these the psalmist says over again: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon. We can also take the four horns, which reigned against the people of God, as the four πάθη (passions), which learned men, not rendering them word for word κακοζήλως (with misplaced zeal) as passions, translate as perturbations: distress and gladness of mind, two present, and two future, fear and desire, of which the illustrious poet also gives indication:

Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.

These horns winnowed and scattered Judah almost man by man, so that none of them, pressed down by the heavy weight of evils, lifted up his head. The four smiths too, or craftsmen, whom the Greeks call τέκτονας, the prophet does not behold by himself, but the Lord shows them to him, and explains who the smiths and craftsmen are, whom we understand as angels obedient to the Lord's power, so that what the nations had destroyed, these may build. Now this, for which we translated from the Hebrew: These came to terrify them, namely the kingdoms, the Seventy translated: These came to sharpen them, in their hands. But sharpening them is to be taken for terrifying them. Or else they terrify, so that all may submit their necks under the yoke of Christ, and not, as someone has interpreted: when they have been sharpened, let them become worse. For if the angels come for this, to make the wicked worse, they are not to be called smiths, that is, destroyers of evils and builders of good things; but they too are to be taken as wicked and as destroyers. And this is to be noted, that these four horns of the nations lifted up one horn against the people of God; for they did not reign together and oppress Israel at the same time, but succeeded one another: the Medes and Persians the Babylonians, the kingdom of the Macedonians the kingdom of the Persians, the empire of the Romans the kingdom of the Macedonians. These things we have said following the order of the history.

Against these, four smiths and, so to speak, physicians and good craftsmen are not seen by the prophet, for he could not yet see them by himself without God's showing them, but they are shown to him by the Lord: namely the four virtues, prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, of which Tully disputes most fully in the books On Duties, writing also a book of its own on the four virtues. Those, then, who destroy vices and build virtues, and all the saints who, possessing these remedies, are ever restoring the Church, are to be called smiths. Hence the Apostle too said: As a wise architect I have laid the foundation. And the Lord in his anger says that he will take away from Jerusalem the architect and the wise man. And the Lord himself, the Son of God Almighty and of the Creator of all things, is called the son of a smith. We have read in someone's commentaries that the four smiths are understood as the four evangelists, who restore to its former seat the oppressed Israel, that is, the mind that sees God, and Judah, who confesses the Lord, and Jerusalem, the vision of peace; and those whom the nations of the vices had scattered from the Church, they have drawn back to salvation through the preaching of the gospel.
2: And I lifted up my eyes, and saw; and behold, a man, and in his hand a measurers' cord. And I said: Where are you going? And he said to me: To measure Jerusalem, and to see how great is its breadth, and how great its length. LXX: And I lifted up my eyes, and saw; and behold, a man, and in his hand a geometer's cord. And I said to him: Where are you going? And he said to me: To measure out Jerusalem, and to see how great is its breadth, and how great its length. He who before, with eyes lifted up, had seen sad things in the four horns, now again lifts up his eyes to see the man of whom it is written: Behold a man, the Rising is his name, of whom we also read above: And behold a man mounting upon a red horse, and he was standing among the myrtles that were in the deep, or, among the shady mountains. And of whom the Father speaks: He has built my city, whose craftsman and founder is God. He is also seen by Ezekiel, holding a cord in his hand, and a reed for the measure of a man's cubit, to measure Jerusalem, whose description, that is, its breadth and length, the same prophet pursues in mystical speech. Some think this was fulfilled in part under Zerubbabel, and Joshua, and Ezra, and Nehemiah and the other leaders or kings who ruled the people of Israel up to the coming of the Lord and Savior. But others, and above all the Jews, interpret it of the kingdom of a thousand years, bodily men seeking bodily things. Most of our writers, however, refer it to the heavenly Jerusalem, and say that it is to be built up again, having been left desolate by the fall of sinful souls. Let heretics suspect this. But let us interpret Mount Zion, and the mother of the firstborn and of the saints, as the Church, which was built in the passion and resurrection of the Lord, and is built every day by him who knows the measures and the merits of each one. What we have said of the Church can also be taken of the souls of believers, which are built every day by the Lord, and behold his peace, which was left to the apostles.

And behold, the angel who spoke in me was going out, and another angel was going out to meet him, and he said to him: Run, speak to this boy, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall, because of the multitude of men and cattle in its midst. And I will be to it, says the Lord, a wall of fire round about, and I will be in glory in its midst. LXX: And behold, the angel who spoke in me was standing, and another angel was going out to meet him, and he said to him, saying: Run and speak to that youth, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited fruitful from the multitude of men and cattle in its midst. And I will be to it, says the Lord, a wall of fire round about, and I will be for glory in its midst. The angel who spoke in the prophet, and was standing, or, as is read in the Hebrew, was going out, for that is what iasa means, the Hebrews think to be Michael. And the other angel, who was going out and coming to meet him, they suppose to be Gabriel, who speaks to Michael so that he may tell the prophet how great an abundance of all things, and multitude of men and cattle, and strength of walls Jerusalem shall have, which at present seems destroyed down to embers and ashes.

But because in certain passages of Scripture we have learned that some things are done through the cherubim, and other things through the seraphim, whether they do these things by themselves, or whether they are done through the hosts subject to them, which, as is said, receive the names of the greater ones because they come from the greater ones, we do not wish to affirm what we do not prove by clear testimonies. This, however, we know most certainly, that to carry out service from above, some spirits send others, as the prophet Zechariah testifies, who says: Behold, the angel who was speaking in me went forth; and behold, another angel went forth to meet him, and he said to him: Run, and speak to this young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls. For when an angel says to an angel "Run and speak," there is no doubt that one sends another. Those who are sent are lesser, those who send are greater.

But we, according to the spiritual sense, interpret all these things of the Church, which is inhabited without a wall, or, as the Seventy translated, κατάκαρπος, that is, with an abundance of all fruits, and has a multitude of men and cattle, and the Lord is fire round about her, and he himself dwells in glory in her midst. This is the city of which we read elsewhere: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God, and again: Great is the Lord and exceedingly to be praised, in the city of our God, in his holy mountain. Whoever dwells in her can say: But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, and: The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture, there he has set me. By the water of refreshment he has brought me up.

All these things the Jews think will come carnally under the ἠλειμμένῳ (anointed one), whom they promise themselves with the vainest hope: that Jerusalem will have such great blessedness that, because of the multitude of men and of all cattle, it cannot have a wall; but the defense of the Lord himself will be its wall, and it will enjoy the glory of him who dwells in its midst.

And Jerusalem, he says, shall be inhabited without a wall because of the multitude of men and cattle, or, with an abundance of all fruits. Some interpret men and cattle as two peoples, of the Jews and of the Gentiles: that those who were versed in the law and came to the faith of Christ are called men, while we, who after idolatry were as it were in the desert of the law and the solitude of the prophets, and have received his passion, ought to be called cattle. But others want all rational men, learned in the knowledge of the Scriptures, to be understood as men, and as cattle all the simple among the believers, and that of these it is said: Men and cattle you will save, O Lord.

These cattle and these living creatures hear the voice of the good shepherd, and know it, and follow him, because he is both the shepherd, who also rules us, and the door, because through him we enter into the Church and to the Father, and a wall of fire round about, so that he may warm those who believe and dwell in the midst, who before had grown lukewarm from the coldness of charity, and that they may be fervent in spirit. But the wolves and the most savage beasts — of which it is written: Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you, and whose fruit is hay, wood, stubble, and they bring forth thistles and thorns —, let him consume with his fire; and he who is fire to the adversaries, let him be glory in the midst of the believers. That the Lord is the wall of Jerusalem we read in another place too: Mountains round about it, and the Lord round about his people.

O, O, flee from the land of the north, says the Lord; for I have scattered you into the four winds of heaven, says the Lord. O Zion, arise, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. For thus says the Lord of hosts: After glory he has sent me to the nations that despoiled you; for he who touches you touches the pupil of his eye. For behold, I lift up my hand over them, and they shall be spoil for those who served them, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me. LXX: O, O, flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for from the four winds of heaven I will gather you, says the Lord. In Zion be saved, you who inhabit the daughter of Babylon. For thus says the Lord Almighty: After glory he has sent me to the nations that despoiled you, for he who touches you, as it were touches the pupil of his eye. Behold, I will bring my hand upon them, and they shall be spoil for those who had served them, and you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me. The regions of the world, which the Greeks call κλίματα, are understood according to the situation of Jerusalem and of the temple. The Assyrians, therefore, and the Babylonians, who laid waste the people of God, dwell in the land of the north. In short, in Jeremiah the pot which according to Ezekiel is full of flesh — and by it the city of Jerusalem is understood —, is kindled from the face of the north. Since, therefore, the angel who had come to meet the angel who prophesied in Zechariah had commanded him to speak to the boy — for in comparison with the dignity of angels all human nature is called boyhood, because it is not angels who advance into us, but we who advance into angels —, and to say to him: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall, and the rest. Now the same word of the Lord is addressed to those who dwell in the north, that they may be gathered from the four winds into which they had been scattered over the whole world, and that those who dwelt in Babylon may return to Zion. Or else thus: You who have been scattered into the four regions of heaven, flee from the land of the north; and O Zion, you who now dwell in Babylon, flee and return to your former seat. But that O is said a third time, in the vocative case, is an exhortation to flight, so that they may know that they have been warned to flee not once, but more often. It must also be said another way: the north wind is a very harsh wind, which makes very hard the hearts of those who dwell in its land, and from which evils are kindled upon all who dwell on the earth, and toward which, according to this very prophet Zechariah, the black horses go out, to take their stand in its region. He too who in Isaiah had said in his boasting: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, I will sit on a lofty mountain, above the high mountains in the north, vaunts that he holds his kingdom in the coldest place of the earth. We read also in another place: Behold, smoke comes from the north; and of those who had departed far from the holy city it is said: Behold, these come from afar, from the north and the sea. And through Jeremiah the Holy Spirit speaks, calling those who are in captivity to return to Jerusalem: Go and read these my words toward the north, and you shall say: Return to me, dwelling of Israel, says the Lord. It is commanded, therefore, to us who have dwelt in the north and have lost the warmth of the Lord's fervor, who have been scattered over the world, and of whom the Gospel proclaims that the Lord sends his angels into the four winds and gathers us, and who are caught up in the vices and confusion of this world, that we flee to Zion, the Church of the Lord, and, leaving lowly things behind, take our stand on her watchtower and on the sublimity of her doctrines.

"Say no evil thing, my brothers, against Him that was crucified, and treat not scornfully the stripes wherewith all may be healed, even as we are healed. For it will be well if, persuaded by the Scriptures, you are circumcised from hard-heartedness: not that circumcision which you have from the tenets that are put into you; for that was given for a sign, and not for a work of righteousness, as the Scriptures compel you [to admit]. Assent, therefore, and pour no ridicule on the Son of God; obey not the Pharisaic teachers, and scoff not at the King of Israel, as the rulers of your synagogues teach you to do after your prayers: for if he that touches those who are not pleasing to God, is as one that touches the apple of God's eye, how much more so is he that touches His beloved! And that this is He, has been sufficiently demonstrated."

[Passage quoted, Zech. ii. 8.]

IN these words the Almighty Lord Himself says that He has been sent, and teaches who it was that sent Him, saying, "And ye shall know that the Almighty Lord has sent me." Here, then, you have clearly two Persons using one Name, the Almighty Lord that sent, and Him that is sent having the same Name as the Sender. And whom else could you suppose Him that is sent to be, but Him that we have so often called God the Word, Who states that He is sent by the Father, and says clearly, "After his glory he has sent me," shewing that though pre-existing in the glory of the Father He was sent afterwards unto the nations that spoiled you? For the Word of God was sent unto the nations, who before were hostile to the people of God, and subjected them to Himself, making a spoil of them by His disciples, who belonged to the Jewish nation, which the Gentiles had long spoiled enslaving it to their own idolatry. This, then, He says that the nations will suffer, as He ordained. For as they perverted the people of God from their ancestral religion, and made them a spoil for their own daemons, so some day shall they be made spoils from their fathers' idolatry to them who of old have served them, and be brought under the yoke of the Jewish religion. And the Lord says that this will be done by Himself, as He will be sent by His Father to accomplish it. It might also be said that certain invisible spiritual powers are meant by the nations which spoiled and enslaved the souls of men, which the Word of God here says He loves as the apple of His eye. And the proof of His great love to the human race is that He did not draw back, though He was the Word of God and in the glory of the Father, but agreed to live with men and govern them.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 16

[Passage quoted, Zech. ii. 8.]

IF, then, the Lord that sent (Him) is Lord Almighty, and He that says He was sent is so also, surely there are Two; And He that was sent as Almighty Lord of the nations says clearly, "He sent me."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 25

He was sent, therefore, after the glory of the divine majesty, to the nations that despoiled the people of God, so that those who had formerly plundered them might be spoil for those who served them, and the whole crowd of those who once served might know that the Lord Almighty has sent him.

But what follows: Thus says the Lord of hosts, after glory he has sent me, and the rest, introduces the voice of the Savior speaking, who, being almighty God, says that he was sent by the almighty Father, not according to that by which he is almighty, but according to that by which he was sent after glory. Who, though he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, the death of the cross. Nor is it a wonder that Christ is called almighty, in whose person we read in the Apocalypse of John: Thus says the faithful witness, the beginning of the creation of God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Lord God Almighty. That too which we read in Psalm 23 (24): Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the king of glory shall enter, and which again is said by other angels who did not know the mystery of the flesh assumed: Who is this king of glory? The Lord of powers, he is the king of glory, is referred to Christ. For where we read the Lord of powers, in the Hebrew Sabaoth is written, which is rendered almighty by the LXX translators. From this we understand that wherever the Lord of powers is said of Christ, he must be understood as almighty. Nor is it a wonder if Christ is called almighty: To whom has been given all power in heaven and on earth, and who says: All things that are the Father's are mine. But if all things, that is, God from God, Lord from Lord, light from light, then also almighty from almighty; for it cannot be that those whose nature is one should have a different glory.

But as for what he says: He who touches you touches the pupil of his eye, take the touching as harassment and injury, according to what we read: Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no evil to my prophets. For whoever touches the saints of the Lord is as one who desires to harm the pupil of his eye, and strives to deprive him of the clear light, of which he speaks in the Gospel: You are the light of the world.

Another example to prove the same point may be found in a passage of Zechariah where the "Almighty" sends the "Almighty." This can only mean that God the Father sends God the Son. The text runs, "So says the Lord Almighty: 'After the glory he has sent me to the nations that have robbed you; for he that touches you touches the apple of my eye. For behold, I lift up my head upon them, and they shall be a prey to those who served them; and you shall know that the Lord almighty sent me.' " In this case, the Lord almighty says that he is sent by the Lord almighty. How can anyone doubt that it is Christ who is speaking and, in fact, speaking to the lost sheep of the house of Israel? Remember what is said in the Gospel: "I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." The comparison of these lost sheep to the apple of God's eye is explained by the perfection of God's love. And, of course, it was to this flock of sheep that the apostles belonged. "After the glory" of his resurrection—a glory alluded to in the words "Jesus had not yet been glorified"3—it was in the person of these apostles that Jesus was sent to the Gentiles. And this was to be the fulfillment of what the psalmist had prophesied: "You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people; you will make me head of the Gentiles."

Suppose for the sake of the argument that what we said was true only of all the most powerful and noble. Were the vices that were common to noble and ignoble alike less serious? I mean the hatred and abuse of all holy men, for surely it is a sort of sacrilege to hate those who worship God. Just as the man who injures our slaves thereby harms us, and the man who flogs another's sons tortures the father's affection by his children's suffering, so anyone who injures a servant of God violates the divine majesty, as the Lord said to his apostle: "He that receiveth you, receiveth me, and he that despiseth you, despiseth me.'' Our most gracious and loving Lord shared his honor and disgrace alike with his servants, to the end that no one who injured a servant of God should think that the man alone was hurt by his action, since injury to God would undoubtedly be mingled with the harm inflicted on his followers. Of this God gave us proof, according to his most indulgent love, in these words: "For he that toucheth you toucheth the pupil of my eye.'' To express the tenderness of his love he used the most tender part of the body, that we might clearly understand that God is injured by a contempt of his saints as slight as the touch required to injure the eyesight. So the people of Africa injured and hated the servants of God and God himself in them.
On the Government of God, Book 8, Chapter 3

And God lifts up his hand to strike the hostile nations, and to lead his people back either into Jerusalem or into the Church. By the hostile nations, according to tropology, understand the opposing powers, which every day subject sinners to their power and compel them to serve them.

And if it be admitted to be a noble privilege to be and to be reckoned the people of God, and if this one thing is the noblest of the divine promises, that God should say of those who are worthy of Him, "I will be their God, and they shall be my people," Israel was naturally proud in days of old of being the only people of God, but now the Lord has come to sojourn with us and promises graciously to extend this privilege to the Gentiles, saying:

"Lo, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of you, and many nations shall flee unto the Lord, and they shall be to him a people."

On which I may aptly quote : "And I will say to a people that were not my people, Ye are my people. And they shall say, Thou art the Lord our God."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

[Passage quoted, Zech. ii. 10, 11.]

AND this prophecy is like the former one, telling of the coming of the Christ to men, and the call of the Gentiles to salvation through Him.

"For I the Lord myself will come," He says, "and at My coming no longer Israel of old, nor one single nation of the earth alone, but many nations shall take refuge in the greater and high Lord, the God of Me Myself and of the Universe, to Whom fleeing the nations shall reap the great harvest of being called and actually becoming the people of God, and of dwelling in the midst of her that is called the daughter of Zion."

So it is common in Holy Scripture to call the Church of God on earth, as being as it were a daughter of the heavenly Zion. And this good news is told in the oracle which says:

"Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Zion, because I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee." For we believe that God the Word dwells in the midst of the Church. As indeed He promised when He said, " Lo, I am with you all the days, until the end of the world''—and, "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." And when, He says:

"I the Lord Myself, do come and dwell in the midst of you; thou shalt receive a greater knowledge of God, for I the Lord will refer the cause of My being sent to men to My Father who sent Me. Thou shalt know that the Lord Almighty has sent Me unto you."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 26

[Passage quoted, Zech. ii. 10.]

As it is now my object to unfold from the prophets the second cause of our Lord's living our life on earth, the prophecy before us appears to state it so clearly that it hardly needs any elaboration. You will notice that He gives the cause of His coming, where He says, "And many nations shall flee unto the Lord in that day, and they shall be to me for a people." And the Word announces this to the daughter of Sion, calling the Church of God by this name, through her seeming to be the daughter of the heavenly Jerusalem, she that is the mother of the Saints, according to the holy apostle. Or the Church of God might be called the daughter of Sion for another reason as one separated from the former congregation of the Jews by the apostles and evangelists, who also were the children of a mother divorced for her own impiety, and a widow because she had driven away her Husband, Who rebuked her by the prophets and said, "Hast thou not called me as a husband, and father, and leader of thy virginity?" And accusing their mother's ways also to them that were born of her He says: "Where is the bill of thy mother's divorcement, by which I rejected her?" And again: "Judge the cause of your mother, judge it, because she is not my wife, and I am not her husband."

So, then, this prophecy rightly announces the presence of the Lord to those who had rejected their mother (calling them) the daughter of the Lord. And it is the Church of the Gentiles that is reckoned by the apostles of our Saviour to have taken the place of her that before was daughter.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 17

So prophesied Zechariah after the Return from Babylon, in the reign of Darius, King of Persia, when Jerusalem was but just arisen from the desolation which it suffered under the Babylonians. And the whole period from Darius the Persian, in whose time Zechariah prophesied, even to Augustus, Emperor of Rome, amounts to the seven and sixty-two weeks of years in Daniel, which are equivalent to 483 years, as I have shewn in my recent investigations.
