For the Lord rebukes in order to amend; and in the twenty, which is made up of two decades, harsh and sad things are announced; in the ten, that is, one decade, better and prosperous things; for Israel is instructed through all scourges and punishments.

As to the suggestion you made in your letter that we should examine together the nature of an oath extorted by force, I beg of you, do not let our discussion turn crystal-clear matters into murky ones. If a servant of God were threatened with certain death, so that he should swear to do something forbidden and wicked, he still ought rather to die than to swear, so as not to commit a crime in fulfilling his oath. But in this case, … it was only the persistent shouting of the people that was forcing the man not to any crime but to what could be lawfully done, if it were done. And … the only thing to fear was that a few violent men, mingled with a crowd of mostly good ones, might seize the occasion to start a riot, under pretence of virtuous indignation, and might break out into some accursed disturbance to satisfy their passion for robbery. And when even this fear was unfounded, who would think that perjury could be committed even to avoid certain death, much less loss or some kind of physical injury? That individual called Regulus had never heard what the holy Scriptures say about the wrongfulness of a false oath. He had learned nothing about the sickle of Zechariah, and obviously he had not sworn to the Carthaginians by the sacraments of Christ but by the filthiness of demons. Yet he did not so fear certain torture and a horrible sort of death as to take his oath under compulsion, but he went to meet them to avoid perjuring himself, because he had sworn on oath of his own free will.

It comes in opportunely today even from the Old Testament to show you the heinousness of perjury. "There was," it says, "a flying sickle, ten cubits in breadth." The "flying" betokens the swift advent of the vengeance which pursues oaths; that it is many cubits in length and breadth, signifies the force and magnitude of the woes; that it comes flying "from heaven," is to show that the vengeance comes from the judgment-seat on high: that it is in the form of a "sickle," denotes the inevitableness of the doom: for just as the sickle, where it comes and has hooked the neck, is not drawn back with nothing but itself, but with the head reaped off, even so the vengeance which comes upon the swearers is severe, and will not desist until it have completed its work.

But if we swear and escape, let us not be confident; this is but to our woe. For what think ye? How many, since Ananias and Sapphira, have dared the same with them? How is it then, say you, that they have not met with the same fate? Not because it was allowed in them, but because they are reserved for a greater punishment. For those who often sin and are not punished, have greater reason to fear and dread than if they were punished. For the vengeance is increased for them by their present impunity and the long-suffering of God.

I have read that the twenty cubits of length and the ten of breadth refer to the age of the Lord Savior, that is, they make the number thirty, because the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, and by him the world is to be judged.

And at the same time let us warn those who think theft and perjury small crimes, that the curse which is described in the scroll and the sickle is brought into the house of the thief and of the perjurer, and remains in it, and consumes all its timbers and stones. But if in these things which are thought lesser — theft, I mean, and perjury — there is so great a threat of punishments, what shall we say of fornication, adultery, homicide, sacrilege, and all the crimes which are numbered by the Apostle among the works of the flesh?

For "now," saith he, "the axe is laid unto the root of the trees." There is nothing more terrible than this turn of his discourse. For it is no longer "a flying sickle," nor "the taking down of a hedge," nor "the treading under foot of the vineyard;" but an axe exceeding sharp, and what is worse, it is even at the doors. For inasmuch as they continually disbelieved the prophets, and used to say, "Where is the day of the Lord?" and "let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel come, that we may know it," by reason that it was many years before what they said came to pass; to lead them off from this encouragement also, he sets the terrors close to them. And this he declared by saying "now," and by his putting it to "the root." "For the space between is nothing now," saith he, "but it is laid to the very root." And he said not, "to the branches," nor "to the fruits," but "to the root." Signifying, that if they were negligent, they would have incurable horrors to endure, and not have so much as a hope of remedy. It being no servant who is now come, as those before Him were, but the very Lord of all, bringing on them His fierce and most effectual vengeance. Yet, although he hath terrified them again, he suffers them not to fall into despair; but as before he said not "He hath raised up," but "He is able to raise up children to Abraham" (at once both alarming and comforting them); even so here also he did not say that "it hath touched the root," but "it is laid to the root, and is now hard by it, and shows signs of no delay." However, even though He hath brought it so near, He makes its cutting depend upon you. For if ye change and become better men, this axe will depart without doing anything; but if ye continue in the same ways, He will tear up the tree by the roots.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 3:7.4

The angel who was speaking in the prophet, having gone out from him and speaking as it were face to face, bids him lift up his eyes and see the sins of the people of Israel heaped up into a full measure, and the offences of all filled up; and that this is their eye, which in Hebrew is called enam, and is written with ain, iod, nun, mem. Or their iniquity, which, if it were written with the letter uau, would rightly be read onam, as the LXX rendered; and this error has often crept into the common edition, that because the letters uau and iod are of the same shape but differ in size, one is read for the other. This jar or measure is their eye in the whole earth, that is, the showing of sins, so that those whose vices lay hidden, scattered, might be heaped up into one and laid open to the eyes of all, and Israel might go forth from its place, and it might be shown to all the nations what Israel had been in its own land.

And the angel who was speaking in me went out, and said to me: Lift up your eyes, and see what this is that goes forth. And I said: What is it? And he said: This is a jar going forth; and he said: This is their eye in the whole earth. And behold, a talent of lead was being carried, and behold, a woman was sitting in the midst of the jar. And he said: This is impiety, and he cast her into the midst of the jar, and put a lump of lead into its mouth. LXX: And the angel who was speaking in me went out, and said to me: Look up with your eyes and see what it is that goes forth; and I said: What is it? And he said: This is the measure that goes forth. And he said: This is their iniquity in all the earth. And behold, a talent of lead was lifted up; and behold, a woman was sitting in the midst of the measure, and he said: This is iniquity, and he cast her into the midst of the measure, and cast a stone of lead into its mouth. A jar, or a measure, was going forth and being carried in the air. And so that we should not be in doubt by what word it is properly named, the angel himself who had shown the jar, or measure, gives it a name; and he says, according to the Seventy: This is their iniquity in the whole earth; according to the Hebrews: This is the eye, that is, the showing of all sins. And behold, a woman was sitting in the midst of the jar, or measure, which among the Hebrews is called epha, and is often rendered by the LXX οἴφι; and this woman herself was called impiety. While he was seeing these things, behold, a talent of lead, that is, a lump like a stone, was being carried, either by its own impulse, or by the Lord's command, or it was carried by another whose name is passed over in silence. And this angel who was speaking in the prophet, and going out from him was showing him everything, seized the woman who was called impiety, and threw her headlong into the midst of the jar, she who before was being carried freely and, sitting upon the jar, was visible to all. And lest she should perhaps raise her head again, and rejoice in her iniquity and impiety, he puts the talent of lead, like a very heavy stone, into the mouth of the jar, to press down impiety in the midst and shut her in, so that she cannot in any way break out. These things we have drawn as certain shadows and outlines of the picture to come, so that we may fill in the rest with its proper colors.

"They went down into the deep like a stone." Why did "they go down into the deep like a stone"? Because they were not such "stones as those from which sons of Abraham could be raised up," but such as loved the deep and cherished the liquid element — that is, who seized the bitter and fleeting pleasure of present things. Whence it is said of them: "They were sunk like lead in the mightiest water." Sinners are heavy. Finally, iniquity too is shown "to sit upon a talent of lead," as the prophet Zechariah says: "I saw," he says, "a woman sitting upon a talent of lead, and I said: what is this? And he answered: iniquity." Thence it is, therefore, that the wicked "were sunk into the deep, like lead in the mightiest water."

For virtue is a light and buoyant thing, and all who live in her way "fly like clouds," as Isaiah says, "and as doves with their young ones"; but sin is a heavy affair, "sitting," as another of the prophets says, "upon a talent of lead." If, however, this reading of the history appears to any forced and inapplicable, and the miracle at the Red Sea does not present itself to him as written for our profit, let him listen to the Apostle: "Now all these things happened unto them for types, and they are written for our admonition."

The deserts of each one of us are suspended in the balance, which a little weight either of good works or of degenerate conduct sways this way or that; if the evil preponderate, woe is me! if the good, pardon is at hand. For no man is free from sin; but where good preponderates, the evil flies up, is overshadowed, and covered. Wherefore in the Day of judgement our works will either succour us, or will sink us into the deep, weighed down as with a millstone. For iniquity is heavy, supported as by a talent of lead; avarice is intolerable, and all pride is foul dishonesty. Wherefore exhort the people of God to trust rather in the Lord, to abound in the riches of simplicity, wherein they may walk without snare and without hindrance.

And upon this measure and jar of all offences sat impiety in the midst, which by another name we can call idolatry, and the denial of God. Hence it is said by the Savior to the Jews: Fill up the measure of your fathers. This impiety, which sat upon the sins of Israel and gloried in its wickedness, is afterwards sent into the midst of Babylon, and is crushed by the evil of captivity. Or, according to Theodotion, she casts herself and hides in the midst of the jar, and draws over herself the very heavy weight of lead, so that she has her mouth stopped and can no longer boast herself. Or else she is crushed by the angel of God, so that she who before rejoiced in wickedness may fall silent in eternal silence. But whither, and by whom, she is carried shut in, the following reading teaches.

And behold, a talent of lead was being carried. For talent of lead we read in what follows stone of lead. A talent is called chachar; a stone, aben. It is, then, the stone of lead which is also the talent of lead, which we, expressing it more plainly, have translated as a lump or ball of lead, by which is signified the very heavy weight of sins.

If we choose to take the two women as the peoples of the heretics and of the Jews — both of whom go out from the face of the Lord, and are borne by an unsteady spirit, and have the wings of the kite, the heron and the hoopoe, since, after the manner of the partridge, they are forever gathering riches, and not with judgment, and hasten to snatch from the Church, and delight in contentions and quarrels, and drag to destruction whomever they have deceived, and wallow in the mire of lusts and in everlasting filth —, these women lift up the most heavy weight of impiety, and build their house in confusion, and serve the Babylonian king, so that the peoples of the heretics and of the Jews may dwell there, where the idolaters abide, serving wood and stones.

And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, two women coming out, and the spirit was in their wings, and they had wings like the wings of a kite, and they lifted up the jar between earth and heaven. And I said to the angel who spoke in me: Where are these carrying the jar? And he said to me: That a house may be built for it in the land of Shinar, and that it may be established, and set there upon its base. LXX: And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, two women coming out, and the spirit was in their wings, and they had wings as are the wings of a hoopoe. And they lifted up the measure between earth and heaven. And I said to the angel who spoke in me: Where are these carrying the measure? And he said to me: To build a house for it in the land of Babylon, and to prepare it, and to set it there upon its seat. The Jews take the two women coming out to be the kingdom of the Medes and that of the Macedonians, each of which afflicted the Babylonian people, and there their impiety set up its seat. But this they invent with cunning, so that what was said of themselves may not be understood of themselves. For the two women who come out, no doubt from the land of Judea, are to be understood as the ten tribes and the two, of which the one were taken captive by the Assyrians, the other by the Chaldeans. And in their wings was the spirit, that is, the power of the devil, of which it is written in Ecclesiastes: If the spirit of him who has power rises up against you, do not leave your place. And in the Gospel we read of the unclean spirit which, when it has been cast out of its house, goes about through desert and dry places and returns to its former house with seven other spirits more wicked than itself. By this spirit, then, these women were snatched along as by wind and blast and borne in swift flight, and they had wings; in the Hebrew asida, which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated heron, the LXX alone hoopoe. The Hebrews think the asida is the kite, a most rapacious bird, forever lying in wait for the birds of the farmyard; but of the heron, those who have written on the nature of birds declare that there are three kinds: one white, another starred, the third black, which is both the fiercest and bloodthirsty, and quarrelsome, and so impatient in mating that blood bursts from their eyes. The hoopoe, again, whose name we drew from the likeness of the Greek name (for they too call it epopa, because it settles on human dung), they say is a most filthy bird, forever lingering in tombs, forever in human dung; in short, it is even said to make its nest of it, and to feed its young on the little worms of rotting dung. Whichever of the three birds you choose to understand by asida, it suits these women, Judah and Israel, who because of their stinking sins were handed over to the power of demons and were led by them into captivity. And they took up the jar, or measure, in which impiety was held shut in, with a lump of lead laid on top so that it could not get out, and the most heavy weight of all sins, through the air between earth and heaven.

The prophet, understanding this, does not ask who these women are, for that was plain to the prophetic spirit, nor what they carry, about which he had been instructed above, but where they carry it. In short, there follows: I said to the angel who spoke in me: Where are these carrying the jar? He answered: That a house may be built for it in the land of Shinar. For which the Seventy translated, in the land of Babylon. For Shinar is a plain of the Chaldeans, in which those who had moved their feet from the east, and could not stand in the service of God, built the tower of pride; whence the city itself also was called Babylon, that is, confusion, because there the tongues of all were confounded and mingled. Impiety, therefore, is carried by these women into Babylon, so that there its house may be built, and it may be established, and set upon its base, and rest in an everlasting abode. For truly in Babylon is the seat of impiety, both according to the history and according to the mystical senses.
6: According to allegory, let us take in the present place too whatever we said about the four horns and the four smiths. I have read in a certain person's volume that the four chariots, in which are red, and black, and white, and spotted and strong horses, are to be understood as the four Gospels, and the horses as the apostles, possessing different graces through the diversity of the colors: of whom some are red with martyrdom, others dark and black, knowing the mysteries of Christ, of whom it is said in the psalm: Darkness was under his feet, and: He made darkness his hiding place. Others white, with the grace of virginity; others spotted and strong, having the grace of healings and of various powers.

These four kingdoms which overthrew Judea Zechariah writes that he saw in four horns, the angel saying to him: These are the horns which have scattered Judah and Israel and Jerusalem. And again: I lifted up, he says, my eyes and saw; and behold, four chariots coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze; in the first chariot, red horses; and in the second chariot, black horses; and in the third chariot, white horses; and in the fourth chariot, dappled, strong horses. And when the prophet had said to the angel who spoke in him: What are these, my lord? The angel answered: These are the four winds of heaven, which go forth to stand before the ruler of all the earth; and the sense is: These are they who go forth from the face of the Lord, to fulfill his will.

And I turned, and lifted up my eyes and saw. And behold, four chariots coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains, mountains of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses, and in the second chariot black horses, and in the third chariot white horses, and in the fourth chariot spotted and strong horses. And I answered, and said to the angel who spoke in me: What are these, my lord? And the angel answered, and said to me: These are the four winds of heaven, which go out to stand before the Ruler of all the earth. The one in which were the black horses went out into the land of the north, and the white went out after them, and the spotted went out toward the land of the south. But those which were the most robust went out, and sought to go and run to and fro through all the earth. And he said: Go, walk through the earth; and they walked through the earth. And he called me, and spoke to me, saying: Behold, those who go out into the land of the north have made my spirit rest in the land of the north. LXX: And I turned, and lifted up my eyes, and saw. And behold, four chariots coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses, and in the second chariot black horses, and in the third chariot white horses, and in the fourth chariot spotted, starling-colored horses. And I answered, and said to the angel who spoke in me: What are these, lord? And the angel who spoke in me answered and said: These are the four winds of heaven, which go out to stand by the Lord of all the earth. The one in which were the black horses went out over the land of the north, and the white went out after them, and the spotted went out into the land of the south, and the starling-colored went out, and they looked to go around the earth. And he said: Go and go around the earth; and they went around the earth, and he cried out; and he spoke to me, saying: Behold, those who have gone out over the land of the north have made my fury rest in the land of the north. I passed, he says, to another vision, and lifted the eyes of my heart higher, toward heaven, and saw: four chariots came out from between two mountains which were of bronze, that is, unconquerable and most strong, and such as could be consumed by no age. For those he had called above mountains of myrtles, or shady and wooded ones, he now calls mountains of bronze.

In the first chariot were red horses, bloody and bloodthirsty, and terrible with the cruelty of Babylon. In the second chariot, black horses, the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, which, seated in a two-horse chariot and going out through the edict of King Ahasuerus, bore before it, with sad tidings, the death of all the Jews. In the third chariot, white horses, the Macedonians, under whose king Antiochus we read of the victory of the Maccabees. In the fourth chariot, spotted, strong horses. For we know that of the kings of the Romans some were merciful toward the Jewish nation, such as Gaius Caesar, Augustus and Claudius; others persecutors and terrible, such as Gaius Caligula, Nero, Vespasian and Hadrian. For strong, which Aquila translated κρατεροὺς (strong), the Seventy ψαροὺς (dappled), in the Hebrew is written amasim. And certain copies wrongly have πυῤῥοὺς, confusing the differences of the colors and of the kingdoms, since πυῤῥοὶ, that is, red, are called not amasim but adamim.

So when the prophet asks what the things he saw meant to signify, the angel who spoke in him answers, and relates that they are the four winds of heaven, that is, the four quarters of the world, which the Greeks call κλίματα, which stand by and obey the will of the Lord. For these four kingdoms of which we have spoken did nothing apart from the will of the Lord.

These chariots, four in number, or cars, were sent into the four winds of heaven, that is, to the hinges of the world, and the whole circle of the lands, to fulfil the will of the Lord; to whom it is afterward said by the angel: Go, and walk through the earth, and sow the Gospel in all the ends of the earth.

The one in which were the black horses, he says, went out into the land of the north. How finely the first chariot, in which were the red horses, is passed over, and what the second and the third and the fourth did is described! For already at the time when the prophet was relating these things, the kingdom of Babylon had passed away, and the power of the Medes held all Asia; under their king Darius, in his second year, in the eleventh month, which is called Shebat, on the twenty-fourth day of the month, he beholds all that we have expounded above. The one, then, in which were the black horses went out into the land of the north, so that the might of the Medes might overthrow the kingdom of the Chaldeans. And this is to be noted, that the κλίματα, that is, the quarters of the globe and of the world, are named in the holy Scriptures according to the situation of Jerusalem and of the temple. The white also went out after them: the kings of the Macedonians, following the footsteps of the Medes and Persians, to subjugate the Chaldeans and Babylon to their own rule. But the fourth, that is, the starling-colored and spotted, for which in the Hebrew is read borodim, and which by another name are called amasim, that is, strong and robust, went out toward the southern quarter, and traversed the whole earth with swift onset. And the angel who spoke in the prophet cries out to the empire of the Romans: Go, walk through the earth, and go around the circle of the lands, and lay all kingdoms beneath your feet.

And turning to the prophet he testifies with a clear voice: Behold, those who go out into the land of the north have made my spirit rest in the land to which they set out. In a passage that is indeed most difficult, it was handed down to me by the Hebrews that Alexander and all the Macedonians, that is, the white horses which went out after the Medes and Persians, who had themselves also gone into the land of the north, made the prophetic spirit rest in the land of the north, because against the Medes they fulfilled the will of God, and in a short time the empire of the Medes and Persians was destroyed by the Macedonians. For great is the consolation of those who are oppressed, if they know that their enemies will soon perish. These things, as we were able, or rather as we received them, we have handed on to those devoted to our language, following the truth of the history; not hunting out with tenacious memory, after the fashion of the Egyptian exposition, the chariots of Pharaoh and the Babylonian cars; for what must be considered is not where something is written, but for what reason it is written.

This too, which follows: Behold, those who go out into the land of the north have made my spirit rest in the land of the north, he explained in such a way as to say that the spirit of the Lord, or of the angel, rested when, in the land of the north, the most harsh kingdoms of the devil were overthrown by the apostolic preaching; and that these are the kingdoms which the devil, showing them to the Lord and Savior on a high mountain, boasted had been handed over to himself.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Take from the exiles, from Heldai and from Tobijah, and from Jedaiah, and you shall come on that day, and enter the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who came from Babylon. And you shall take silver and gold, and make crowns, and set them on the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and you shall speak to him, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts, saying: Behold a man, the Rising is his name, and beneath him it shall rise, and he shall build a temple to the Lord. And he himself shall raise a temple to the Lord, and he himself shall bear glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne, and he shall be a priest upon his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between the two of them. And the crowns shall be for Helem and for Tobijah and for Jedaiah and for Hen son of Zephaniah, a memorial in the temple of the Lord. And those who are far off shall come and build in the temple of the Lord, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. And this shall be, if with hearing you hear the voice of the Lord your God. LXX: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Take the things that are from the captivity, from the rulers, and from its useful men, and from those who have known it; and you shall go in on that day into the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who came from Babylon, and you shall take silver and gold, and make crowns, and place them upon the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and you shall say to him: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Behold a man, the Rising is his name, and beneath him it shall rise, and he shall build the house of the Lord, and he himself shall receive power and shall sit, and shall rule upon his throne. And there shall be a priest at his right hand, and the counsel of peace shall be between the two; but the crown shall be for those who wait, and for its useful men, and for those who have known it, and for the favor of the son of Zephaniah, and for a psalm in the house of the Lord; and those who are far from them shall come and build in the house of the Lord. And you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you, and it shall be, if with hearing you hear the voice of the Lord your God. I resolved once for all to bring forth to Latin ears the secrets of Hebrew learning and the hidden teaching of the masters of the synagogue, only so much of it, at any rate, as agrees with the holy Scriptures. For this reason I must, in the most obscure places, draw the lines of the history, and so set forth openly what I have received from churchmen, leaving it to the reader's judgment which he ought rather to follow. And first the order of the reading must be rendered, so that what is said may become clear according to the letter. Take, he says, from Heldai and from Tobijah, and from Jedaiah, who came from the Babylonian captivity, and you shall take from them the gifts that are offered, silver and gold, and you shall enter the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah; and there you shall make crowns, set off by the variety of gold and silver, not one crown but two or more; for ataroth, that is, στέμματα, signifies not the singular but either the dual or the plural number.

But upon us lies the necessity of saying, according to the LXX translators, what our forefathers said. Take from the captivity, and from the rulers, and from its useful men, and from those who have known it, gold and silver, and having gone into the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who himself too came from Babylon, make in it crowns of gold and of silver, which you shall place upon the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. The captivity of the Jews, that is, of the people that confesses the Lord, is vices and sins, which he who has begun to do repentance and to long for the former Jerusalem, that is, the Church of Christ, abandons and leaves behind in Babylon; and it is offered by the rulers of the captives, and by its useful men, that is, of the captivity, who themselves too were handed over for their own profit to an angel of Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit might be saved; and by those who know that it, namely the captivity, is to be turned to good account after the punishments. And the gold and silver is offered by those who confess the Lord both in understanding and in speech, and from it, that is, from the gold and silver, crowns are made in the house of Josiah, who is interpreted saved, and is the son of the visitation of the Lord, that is, ἐπισκοπῆς κυρίου. For he is visited by the Lord who before had been grievously sick. And rightly is he called Josiah, saved, because he too returned from Babylon.

And when you have made the crowns, you shall set one of them on the head of Joshua (Iesus, the same name as Jesus) son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and you shall speak to him: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Behold a man whose name is the Rising, which in Hebrew is called sema, written not with the letter sin but with sade. He is called the Rising, that is, ἀνατολὴ, or ἀναφύη, or βλάστημα, that is, shoot, for this reason: because he shall suddenly spring up of himself, and shall sprout from his own root in the likeness of a shoot; and this man shall build the temple of the Lord.

And the crowns, or the crown, are set upon Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, because, as we advance and return to better things, the Lord is crowned through each of our virtues; or rather, as we are crowned through the virtues of repentance, the Savior receives a crown in each one, according to what Paul also says: For the rest, there is laid up for me a crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me; and not to me only, but also to all who love the coming of our Lord Savior Jesus Christ. Whence the father of the Lord Savior also took his name from the crown of justice. For Jehozadak is interpreted Lord of justice, because he renders to each according to his works. Of this crown James too speaks in his epistle: Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proved he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.

And in the days of Joshua, son of Jehozadak, why did an angel say to the adversary who was opposing him, "The Lord rebuke you, O Satan"? And why are the Jews called "sons of Satan" for transgressing the laws, if he [the adversary] perseveres in the command he received and they transgressed the commandment? And why would he be called utterly a liar, he who remains faithful to the rule? Because that evil comes not from him but from the very one who made him so. And why should he be sent into the "outer darkness"?

Nor was there night in Peter when he confessed, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," when the heavenly Father revealed it to him, but there was night in him too at the moment of his denial. And in the present instance, moreover, when Judas received the morsel [and] went out immediately, night was present in him at the same time he went out, for the man whose name is "Sunrise" was not present with him because he left "the Sun of justice" behind when he went out. And Judas, who was filled with darkness, pursued Jesus; but the darkness and the one who had taken it up did not apprehend the light that was pursued. Wherefore also, when he said as word of justification, "I have sinned because I betrayed just blood" and "went and hanged himself," Satan, who was in him, led him to the noose and hung him, at which time the devil also touched his soul. For Judas was not such that the Lord could say to the devil on his behalf what he said on Job's behalf, "But touch not his soul."
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 32:315-17

But in all battles He triumphed over the devil, and all the unseen enemies and foes led by him, and made us who were slaves His own people, and built of us, as of living stones, the house of God, and the state of holiness, so that He exactly agrees with the oracle, which says:

"Behold a man, whose name is the Branch. And he shall spring up from below, and shall build the house of the Lord. And he shall receive virtue, and shall sit and rule upon his throne."

Note, therefore, with care, in what manner in speaking mystically of the Jesus of days of old, who bears the image of the true, he says: "Behold a man, whose name is the Branch." And a little later, it is said to Jesus himself then present, as if concerning some one else who was the Branch: "Hear, Jesus, the High Priest, thou and thy neighbour, for the men are diviners. Behold, I bring my servant the Branch."

If, then, the speech related to some one yet to come, who was more truly called the Branch than he that bore the name then, he must have been only an image of him that was yet to come, as he is not only called Jesus in figure, but the Branch as well, if this was said to him when present: "Behold a man, whose name is the Branch." He was, therefore, naturally because he was the image thought worthy of the name of the Saviour, as well as of the Branch: for the name of Jesus translated into Greek means "Salvation of God." For in Hebrew "Isoua" is "salvation," and the son of Nave is called by the Hebrews Joshua, Joshua being "Salvation of Jab," that is, Salvation of God. It follows that wherever the Salvation of God is named in the Greek versions, you are to understand that nothing but Jesus is meant.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 17

Therefore God helps the city, producing in it early morning by his own rising and coming. "Behold a man," it is said, "the Orient is his name." For those upon whom the spiritual light will rise, when the darkness that comes from ignorance and wickedness is destroyed, early morning will be at hand. Since, then, light has come into the world in order that he who walks about in it may not stumble, his help is able to cause the early morning. Or perhaps, since the resurrection was in the dim morning twilight, God will help the city in the morning early, who on the third day, early on the morning of the resurrection gained the victory through death.

The inscription, "for the octave," therefore, that we not look to the present time, but that we look toward the "octave." For whenever this transitory and fleeting time ceases, in which one thing comes to be and another is dissolved, and the necessity of coming to be has passed away, and that which is dissolved no longer exists … the hebdomad too, which measures time, will by all means halt. Then that "octave," which is the next age, will succeed it. The whole of the latter becomes one day, as one of the prophets says when he calls the life, which is anticipated "the Great Day." For this reason the perceptible sun does not enlighten that day, but "the true light," the "sun of righteousness," who is designated "rising" by the prophecy because he is never veiled by the settings.
ON THE INSCRIPTIONS OF THE PSALMS 2:5.53

And beneath him shall rise the multitude of believers, and he shall build the house of the Lord, the Church, and he himself shall receive the power and beauty and progress and glory of each one, and shall sit and rule on his throne, on the throne of David, of which it is also written in the Gospel: And there shall be a priest at his right hand, or, according to the Hebrew, upon his throne, because he himself is both king and high priest, and shall sit on the royal as well as on the priestly throne, and there shall be a peaceful counsel between the two, so that neither shall the royal eminence depress the priestly dignity, nor the dignity of the priesthood the royal eminence, but both shall agree in the glory of the one Lord Jesus. I have read in a certain person's book that what is said: And a peaceful counsel shall be between the two, refers to the Father and to the Son, because he came to do not his own will but the Father's, and the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father.

And the prophet is commanded, after he has placed the crown, or the crowns, upon the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, to speak to him and say: Thus says the Lord: Behold a man, the Rising is his name, and beneath him it shall rise, and the rest. We do not divide Jesus, nor can we make two persons in one person, but he who is called Jesus because he saved the world is himself also called the Rising, because in his days justice has risen. And it is sung in the psalm: Truth has risen from the earth, because, begotten from a virgin's womb at the consummation of the ages, he said: I am the truth, and he came at the last hour, according to the epistle of John, who says: Little children, it is now the last hour, in which he hired for a denarius the people of the nations, who were standing and doing nothing, and sent them to the vineyard. Otherwise, if he becomes different according to the diversity of names, the shepherd will be one, the ram another, the lamb another, the door another, the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense another. He, therefore, who has been crowned with our virtues shall rise and shall be called the Rising. To him the Father said: You are my Son, today I have begotten you.

And there shall be peace between those two, that is, between him who is of the royal tribe and him who descends from the Levitical stock, so that priesthood and kingdom alike may rule the people of God; and the crowns themselves which you have made of gold and silver, after they have been set on the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak and on the head of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, you shall consecrate in the temple with the names of those by whom they were offered, that is, of Helem, and Tobijah, and Jedaiah, and Hen. The second and third names are the same as above. The first has been changed; for in place of Heldai he has now put Helem; a fourth, which he had not mentioned above, has been added, that is, Hen; of these we shall speak in what follows.

And when he has raised it, he himself also shall bear glory, that is, the second crown, which in Hebrew is hod, and is written by one ἐπιδοξότης, by another εὐπρέπεια, by another ἀρετὴ, by another δόξα; which mean either renown, or beauty, or virtue, or glory. And they think Zerubbabel is signified, who, rising suddenly from a lowly man and a captive to be leader of the Jewish people, built the temple of the Lord, and sat upon his throne, and ruled with the power of a prince; but the high priest too, he says, Joshua son of Jehozadak, shall sit on the priestly throne, and with minds and counsels joined they shall govern the people of God.

And those who said in Babylon: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion; on the willows in the midst of it we hung up our instruments, once they have returned to Jerusalem, let them take up psalm and timbrel, and sing in the Church of the Lord; and let those who through greater sins had been far from Judea come, with a most true confession too, and through each of their advances build the house of the Lord; and then let all with one mind know that the Lord Almighty has sent the prophet to them. And all that has been promised shall come to pass, if they are willing to hear the Lord, and, having done repentance, remain in good works.

Heldai is interpreted the entreaty of the Lord, which in Greek is said more expressively λιτάνευσις κυρίου. Tobijah, good of the Lord. Jedaiah, known of the Lord. In place of Heldai he has now put in the first place Helem, which means dream; and in the fourth place he has added Hen, that is, grace. The crowns of these four men shall be with the son of Zephaniah, whom we read above was Josiah, who is the guardian and warden of the temple of the Lord, and there they shall rest in an everlasting abode. The Hebrews relate that Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael, coming from the captivity, brought gold and silver as gifts for the temple, and the crowns of the high priest and of the leader; and that Hen, whom he had not mentioned above, that is, grace, means Daniel, who came with a gift; and that Helem was put in place of Heldai for this reason, so that from the interpretation of the name, which means dream, it might be shown that Daniel, set in captivity, and the three young men knew the mysteries of the king's dream. For Daniel, taking the three young men with him, prayed to the Lord and obtained the interpretation of the dream. This is how the circumcision tries to expound these things according to the history.

And the crown, that is, the emblem of victory, once Christ has been crowned, is promised also to those who wait for him, and understand the profit of their former captivity, and know all the mysteries of God, so that they may be for the favor of the son of Zephaniah, that is, of the visitation of the Lord.

And when the crowns, he says, have been laid up in the temple of the Lord, and consecrated for an everlasting memorial, nations from the whole circle of the lands and set far off shall come, and shall build in my temple, each according to his strength. And then, by the outcome of events and the prosperity of all, you shall know that the Lord has sent me, and that at his command I foretold all things. And all these things shall come to pass if you obey the precepts of the Lord and do his commandments.
7: And it came to pass in the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, on the fourth of the ninth month, which is Chislev. And Sharezer and Regem-melech, and the men who were with him, sent to the house of God, to entreat the face of the Lord, to speak to the priests of the house of the Lord of hosts and to the prophets, saying: Must I weep in the fifth month, or ought I to sanctify myself, as I have done now for many years? And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: Speak to all the people of the land and to the priests, saying: When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and the seventh through these seventy years, did you fast a fast to me? And when you ate and drank? Did you not eat for yourselves and drink for your own selves? Are these not the words which the Lord spoke by the hand of the former prophets, when Jerusalem was still inhabited and was wealthy, she and her cities round about her, and it was inhabited toward the south and in the plains? LXX: And it came to pass in the fourth year under King Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev. And Sharezer and Arabesser the king, and his men, sent to Bethel to entreat the Lord, saying to the priests of the house of the Lord Almighty and to the prophets, saying: Sanctification has come in here in the fifth month, as they have done now for many years; and the word of the Lord of powers came to me, saying: Say to all the people of the land and to the priests, saying: If you fast and mourn in the fifths and in the sevenths, and behold, seventy years, did you fast a fast to me? and if you eat or drink, is it not you who eat, and you who drink? Are not these the words which the Lord spoke by the hands of the prophets who were before, when Jerusalem was inhabited and was abundant, and her cities round about, and the hill country and the plains were inhabited? In the fourth year of King Darius, in the ninth month, which is called Chislev, and on the fourth day of the same month, Sharezer and Regem-melech and the others who were with them, who the Hebrews maintain were Persians, generals of King Darius who feared God, sent to the house of the Lord, that is, to the temple which had already been restored by Zerubbabel and by Joshua, so that, since they had already heard that the temple had been built, they might ask of the priests of the house of the Lord and of the prophets whether they ought to weep and fast according to the former custom, or to change mourning into gladness. And the sense of those inquiring is this: In the fifth month, which among the Romans is called July, Jerusalem was overthrown by Nebuchadnezzar; for which reason, because of the desolation of the temple, we have fasted and mourned until now, and have consoled our grief with weeping and fasts. Now, since it is said that the temple has been built, and we see that the cause of sadness by no means remains, answer, we beg you, whether we ought to do this, or to exchange grief for joy? And at the same time it must be considered that weeping and fasting are called sanctification. Hence in Joel too the priests are commanded to sanctify a fast and to proclaim a healing. For abstinence and fasting heal the wounds of the offender, and sanctify all whom they have healed.

What is written in the Seventy, Sharezer and Arabesser the king sent from Bethel, none of our writers has been able to expound; for what has been badly translated from the Hebrew cannot be explained by any reasoning. For who is this Sharezer, or Arabesser the king? Or king of what province? Or into which Bethel, or from which, did he send? Or of what Bethel could Arabesser be king, a place that had long before been left desolate together with Judea, and at that time was by no means called Bethel, that is, house of God, but Beth-aven, that is, house of an idol?

This too which follows, Sanctification has come in here in the fifth month, as they had done now through many years, they try to expound thus: that the sanctification which came in is the vessels of the temple, which had been carried off by Nebuchadnezzar, restored at that time. As for the fast of the fifth and the seventh, they tried to refer it to the days of the week. But since the fast of the tenth follows, they were compelled to refer it to months, and as to what this fast of the fifth, seventh and tenth month itself is, they were entirely silent. Hence let us be content with the former explanation, and let us not incline to the false attempts of the commentators, which came from an error of translation.

After the generals of the Persians had made their inquiry through those whom they had sent, and the embassy of the inquirers to the priests and prophets had been carried out, the word of the Lord came to the prophet, commanding him to speak to the common people and to the priests, telling them what they ought to answer the envoys. When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month, that of the captivity of Jerusalem, and in the seventh month, when Gedaliah was slain by Ishmael, through the seventy years of the desolation of the temple and of the overthrow of Jerusalem, was it of any profit to me that you fasted? And on the other hand, whenever you eat and drink, is it not for yourselves that you both eat and drink? For God is not appeased by these things, but by good works, and if we do his commandments, because food does not commend us to God. Neither, if we do not eat, shall we lack; nor, if we eat, shall we abound.

Even when they were exiles in Babylon and their captors were trying to force them to sing a sacred hymn, they neither yielded nor obeyed, even though they were captives and slaves to the masters who had conquered them.…And they could not observe the fast. The prophet made this clear when he said, " 'Did you keep a fast for me for seventy years?' said the Lord." Nor could they offer sacrifice or pour libations. Listen to the three boys when they said, "We have no prince, prophet or leader, no place to offer firstfruits in your sight and find mercy." The prophet did not say, "We have no priest," because there were priests among the captives. But to make you understand that the whole matter was a question of the place and that the whole code of laws was bound up with that place, he said, "We have no place."

After all, if the loving Lord said to the hardhearted Jews through the prophet, "Behold those seventy years: surely it was not for me that you kept that fast? And if you eat and drink, is it not for yourselves that you eat and drink? This is what the Lord, mighty ruler, says: 'Deliver just judgments, show mercy and pity each of you to your neighbor, do not oppress widow or orphan, sojourner or poor person, and let none of you plot evil against your brother in your heart.' " In other words, if those people sitting in darkness and caught up in the shadow of error gained no benefit merely from fasting without performing those other good works or expelling from their heart evil intended against their neighbor, what sort of an excuse can we offer of whom more is required—not simply commanded to abstain from that, but even obliged to love our enemies and be kind to them? And why do I say "be kind"? Also to pray for them and beseech the Lord and implore his providence in their behalf. After all, this most of all will be a recommendation for us on that fearful day, and our best insurance against our sins, if we are disposed in this way toward our enemies. I mean, even if the commandment is exceedingly rigorous, provided you keep in mind the prize laid up for those who do right, it will seem nothing at all, even though it is in fact very rigorous. Why is that? Scripture says, "If you do this, you will be like my Father in heaven." To make the point clearer to us it added, "Because he makes his sun rise on the evil and the good"; that is, it is saying, you are imitating God as far as human beings can. I mean, just as he makes the sun rise not only on the just but also on those who do evil, and provides rain and seasonal storms not only to the good but also to the evil, so you too, if you love not only those who love you but also those badly disposed to you, are imitating your Lord as far as you can.

By righteousness, I say, and by continence and by the rest of the virtues, God is worshiped. For Zechariah also tells us, saying, "If you eat or drink, is it not you that eat or drink?" declaring thereby that meat and drink do not pertain to God but to humankind: for neither is God fleshly, so as to be pleased with flesh; nor is he careful for these pleasures, so as to rejoice in our food. God rejoices in our faith alone, in our innocence alone, in our truth alone, in our virtues alone. And these dwell not in our belly but in our soul; and these are acquired for us by divine awe and heavenly fear, not by earthly food. And such the apostle fitly rebuked as "obeying the superstitions of angels, puffed up by their fleshly mind; not holding Christ the head, from whom all the body, joined together by links, and inwoven and grown together by mutual members in the bond of charity, increase to God" but observing those things: "Touch not, taste not, handle not; which indeed seem to have a form of religion, in that the body is not spared." Yet there is no advantage at all of righteousness, while we are recalled by a voluntary slavery to those elements to which by baptism we have died.

Are not these my words, while Jerusalem and the cities of Judah were still standing, which I spoke to you by the hands of my prophets, when Jerusalem still stood, and the cities of Judah abounded in all things, and both the hill country and the plain overflowed with crops and enjoyed a most secure peace? Now these were the words of the Lord, as the Scripture that follows testifies: that he wills true judgment and mercy toward one's neighbors, and that one not wrong the widow and the orphan and the stranger and the poor, and not devise evil in one's heart. These things, he says, they would not do, and with deaf ears they despised my commands; for which reason great indignation came upon Jerusalem; and as they would not hear me, so I too did not hear them; and now they ask with such scrupulousness when they ought to fast and mourn, although I said before through Isaiah: This is not the fast I have chosen, says the Lord, nor that a man should humble his soul; but loose every bond of iniquity, undo the obligations of violent contracts, give your bread to the hungry from your heart. If you see the naked, cover him; and the poor and the roofless clothe within your tent. Then your early light shall break forth, and your healings shall quickly arise.

[You] should have fasted then, when drunkenness was doing those terrible things to you, when your gluttony was giving birth to your ungodliness—not now. Now your fasting is untimely and an abomination. Who said so? Isaiah himself when he called out in a loud voice: " 'I did not choose this fast,' says the Lord." Why? "You quarrel and squabble when you fast and strike those subject to you with your fists." But if your fasting was an abomination when you were striking your fellow slaves, does it become acceptable now that you have slain your master? How could that be right?

And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts, saying: Judge true judgment, and show mercy and compassion, every man with his brother. And do not wrong the widow and the orphan and the stranger and the poor; and let no man devise evil against his brother in his heart. And they would not attend, and they turned a withdrawing shoulder; and they made their ears heavy, that they might not hear; and they made their heart adamant lest they hear the law and the words which the Lord of hosts sent in his spirit by the hand of the former prophets, and great indignation came from the Lord of hosts. And it came to pass as he spoke, and they did not hear: so they shall cry, and I will not hear, says the Lord of hosts. And I scattered them through all the kingdoms which they do not know; and the land was left desolate by them, because there was none passing through and returning; and they made the desirable land into a desert. LXX: And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty, saying: Judge just judgment, and let each one show mercy and compassion toward his brother; and do not oppress the widow and the orphan and the poor; and do not, each of you, remember the malice of his brother in your hearts. And they would not attend, and they gave a scornful back; and they made their ears heavy, so as not to hear; and they made their heart disobedient, so as not to hear my law and my words, which the Lord Almighty sent in his spirit by the hands of the former prophets. And great wrath came from the Lord Almighty, and it shall be as I said, and they did not hear him. So they shall cry, and I will not hear them, says the Lord Almighty; and I will cast them out among all the nations which they did not know; and the land was made desolate after them, of anyone passing through and returning, and they made the chosen land into a wilderness. These things I wanted rather, these I sought, and because you did not do them you were handed over to captivity; not the fast of desolation and death of the fifth and the seventh month. Judge just judgment, lest you hear in the psalms: How long will you judge iniquity, and accept the persons of sinners? Judge for the orphan and the widow; justify the humble and the poor, lest Isaiah too say to you: Who justify the wicked for gifts, and take away from the just what is just; and lest, because of you, Habakkuk, in the person of those who are oppressed, cast reproach upon God: Judgment has been given against me, and the judge takes; therefore the law is scattered, and judgment does not come through to the end, because the wicked oppresses the just. And let us not think that this is a new commandment of God; long ago he had enjoined these things through Moses: So shall you judge the great as the small; you shall not accept a person, and you shall not pity the poor in judgment, since the judgment is God's. Show also mercies and compassions, every man with his brother. After truth of judgment let clemency follow toward all, and most of all toward brothers, whom we perceive to be either of the same blood as we or of one faith with us.

For this reason, beloved, I am inserting certain headings and notes as to how you ought to understand and receive these matters, so through the goodness of God you can accept and observe them better. In order that the things that I have said may be kept more closely in your hearts, I am briefly repeating what I mentioned. Therefore, in these matters, as I already said above, we judge others dangerously when it is doubtful whether they are acting with a good or bad intention in fasting, keeping vigils, bestowing alms, abstaining or not abstaining from wine and meat, and other similar matters. These things can be done for the sake of God or for human praise, and because we do not know with what motive they are done, we should not judge at all. In matters of this kind the Lord said, "Do not judge, that you may not be judged," but in a matter of open sin it is said, "Reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and teaching." Moreover, there is what we already mentioned: "Render just judgment." Now if we are willing to consider these words carefully, as we believe, brothers, and with God's help to observe them with great solicitude, we are freed from not a little sin. For by the indiscreet judgment, the majority of the human race is proven to be prompt and ready to criticize, although they are not so willing to be judged by others as they are to judge them. Because of this fact sacred Scripture admonishes us, saying, "Before investigating, find fault; examine first, then criticize." Every person first wants to be questioned, and then, if he is guilty, he patiently endures reproof. Now since we all want this to happen to us from others, it is just that we strive to fulfill the same thing toward them. Let us first inquire with patience and solicitude. Then, when we have learned something quite certainly, we should be willing to give reproof if it is evil and to defend it if it is good, because of what is written, "All that you wish men to do to you, even so do you also to them in like manner; for this is the law and the prophets." And so let us turn to the Lord and implore his help, so that he himself may deign in his goodness to grant us true discretion and perfect charity: to whom is glory and might together with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

And Zechariah also, among the twelve prophets, pointing out to the people the will of God, says: "These things does the Lord Omnipotent declare: Execute true judgment, and show mercy and compassion each one to his brother. And oppress not the widow, and the orphan, and the proselyte, and the poor; and let none imagine evil against your brother in his heart." And again, he says: "These are the words which ye shall utter. Speak ye the truth every man to his neighbour, and execute peaceful judgment in your gates, and let none of you imagine evil in his heart against his brother, and ye shall not love false swearing: for all these things I hate, saith the Lord Almighty." Moreover, David also says in like manner: "What man is there who desireth life, and would fain see good days? Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips that they speak no guile. Shun evil, and do good: seek peace, and pursue it." From all these it is evident that God did not seek sacrifices and holocausts from them, but faith, and obedience, and righteousness, because of their salvation.

And therefore this question must at once be determined, whether the discipline of patience is enjoined by the Creator? When by Zechariah he commanded, "Let none of you imagine evil against his brother," he did not expressly include his "neighbor;" but then in another passage he says, "Let none of you imagine evil in your hearts against his neighbor." He who counseled that an injury should be forgotten was still more likely to counsel the patient endurance of it.

The widow too, and the orphan, concerning whom we have been commanded: Be a father to orphans, and in place of a husband to their mother; judging the orphan and justifying the widow. And do not wrong the stranger and the poor, because sojourning abroad makes the one lowly, and need the other. And let no man devise evil against his brother in his heart, or, as it is said by the Seventy: And let each one not remember the malice of his brother in their hearts. By brother and neighbor we ought to understand either the whole race of men, because we are begotten of one parent, or those who are of the household of the faith, according to the parable of the Gospel, which wants the neighbor to be understood not as a blood relative but as all men. And that anger ought to be ended before the sun goes down, and the memory of all the evils we have suffered from others be blotted out, we read both in many places and most of all in Jeremiah, who speaks in the person of God: And do not, each one, remember in your hearts the malice of his neighbor.

We can also refer these things to those who, sinning in the Church, have been cast out of the land of confession, because they would not hear the Lord, and turned a withdrawing shoulder to him, and made their ears heavy, and made their heart adamant. And the indignation of the Lord came upon them, and they were scattered through all the kingdoms of the vices, and their land was made desolate, whether soul or body, not having God as its inhabitant, nor the spirit returning into it. And the land once desirable, which was the lodging of the Trinity, was turned into a desert and a dwelling of dragons. Let us pass quickly over what is plain, so that there may be room for discussion in what is obscure; for we are not writing long and florid treatises, in which a speech that seeks applause plays, but commentaries, whose office is to pass over what is evident and to discuss what is obscure.

Though I had commanded these things, they would not attend, and turned a withdrawing shoulder, or a scornful back, rejecting my commands by the bearing of their body. For when, with wrinkled brow and contracted nostril, we scorn those who admonish us, we are accustomed to turn our back; according to what is written: They turned their backs to me, and not their faces. And they made their ears heavy, he says, lest they hear, like the ears of the deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of the charmers, and of the sorcerer who charms wisely. For they made their ears heavy so as not to hear, and they set their heart so as not to yield to the law of God. Hence Isaiah speaks to them threateningly: The heart of this people has grown fat, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes, lest perhaps they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.

And because they had, nay rather made, their heart adamant, esteeming hardness of heart by their own will, so as not to hear the words of the Lord which he sent in his spirit, that is, in the Holy Spirit, by the hand of the former prophets, Isaiah, Hosea and the rest, who had clean hands, and who, it is plain, were before the captivity: therefore, for great sins, great indignation came about, and the words of the Lord were fulfilled, who repays like for like, so that, as they walked perversely toward him, he too should go perversely against them, and not hear the words of those crying out, because they too had despised the words of the Lord with a deaf ear.

Moreover, what is said according to the Hebrew, And they made their heart adamant, shows hardness of heart, and a heart of stone, in that they would not receive the words of God. For adamant, a very strong stone, which in Hebrew is called samir, is so hard that it breaks all metals and is itself broken by none. Hence it is called untamable by the Greeks. With this adamant the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, so that he would not let the people of God go.

Since this is the case and since we keep none of the Lord's commands, why do we complain of God, who has far more right to complain of us? Why should we grieve that he does not hear us, when we ourselves do not hear him? What right have we to whisper that God does not look upon the earth, when we ourselves do not look up to the heavens? What reason have we to be vexed that our prayers are despised by the Lord, whose commands we despise?

Suppose that we were equal to our Lord; what chance is there for just complaint when each side receives the same treatment it gives? And this entirely overlooks a point easily proved, that we are very far from receiving what we give, since God really treats us much more kindly than we do him. For the moment, however, let us act on the assumption that I proposed. The Lord himself spoke thus: "I cried unto you and ye did not hear me: you too shall cry unto me and I shall not hear you." What is more fair and just than this? We have not hearkened, therefore he does not hear us. We have not been mindful of him, therefore he does not consider us. What mortal master, I ask, is content to treat his underlings according to this rule, that he will scorn them only in proportion to their contempt of him? And yet we do not stop with such injurious scorn of God as mortal masters receive from their slaves, since the greatest contempt a slave can show is in not doing what he has been ordered. We, however, bend all our efforts and energy not only to neglecting our orders, but even to acting directly contrary to them. For God commands us all to love one another, but we rend each other in mutual hatred. God enjoins us all to give our goods to the poor, but we plunder other men's goods instead. God orders every Christian to keep his eyes pure; how many men are there who do not wallow in the filth of fornication?
On the Government of God, Book 3, Chapter 9

For which reason he also scattered them through all the kingdoms which they do not know, those of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, of the Medes and Persians, and of the other nations which lay subject to these empires and in whose lands they were sown abroad. And all Judea was deserted, because it had no inhabitant, and there was none in it passing through and returning. And the land which was a honeycomb above all lands, and for the greatness of its abundance flowed with milk and honey, they turned into a wilderness.
8: And the word of the Lord of hosts came, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have been jealous for Zion with a great jealousy, and with great indignation I have been jealous for her. Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have returned to Zion, and I will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; and Jerusalem shall be called the city of truth, and the mountain of the Lord of hosts, the sanctified mountain. LXX: And the word of the Lord Almighty came, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with a great jealousy, and with very great fury I have been jealous for her. Thus says the Lord Almighty: I will return to Zion, and I will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; and Jerusalem shall be called the true city, and the mountain of the Lord Almighty, the holy mountain. That the Lord took Jerusalem, that is, the Israelite people, in the wilderness as a wife, and, as she lay in the blood of idolatry, covered her with his cloak and cherished her with a husband's love, we learn more fully in Ezekiel; and she afterward, eating fine flour and honey and oil, adorned with the most beautiful garments, and having from her husband's bounty every ornament of gems, committed fornication with the Assyrians and Chaldeans; and she heard from the Lord: As a wife despises her husband, so the house of Israel has despised me. But handed over to captivity and mocked by her lovers, and stripped of her former beauty, after she had spread her feet to every passer-by and was defiled to the crown of her head, mindful of her former happiness she says again and again: I will return to my former husband, for it was better with me then than now. And he, receiving her and having her again in marriage, he who had said to her before: I will not be angry with you, and my jealousy has departed from you, now says: I have been jealous for Zion with a great jealousy, and with great indignation I have been jealous for her. As much as I was indignant before, because she was disfigured by many lovers and stained my bed, for which reason I also handed her over to her lovers, not at all as an adulteress under a husband, but as a harlot and a vile slave, prostituted in brothels, so much the more have I now returned to her, because she has done repentance and has built my temple, in which I will dwell in the midst of her. And she shall be called the city of truth, she who before was called the city of falsehood, of which it is also written in Isaiah: Truth slept in her, but now murderers. And the mountain of the Lord Almighty shall also be called the sanctified mountain, on which, the temple being restored, victims are sacrificed and the order of the ceremonies is kept. These things according to the history. But no one doubts that Zion and Jerusalem, watchtower and vision of peace, can be taken as the souls of the faithful, whom, when they have sinned, the Lord in anger hands over to captivity, so that those who had not perceived God through good and prosperous things may perceive him through evil and adverse ones. And when they have done repentance, the Lord will return to Zion, and dwells in the midst of Jerusalem, which we understand to be one and the same city; and in those in whom the falsehoods of sins and vices formerly reigned, Christ, the truth, will afterward abide. And the mountain of the Lord of hosts shall be called the holy mountain, of which it is said: Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion, and: Great is the Lord and exceedingly to be praised, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain. Of which Isaiah and Micah cry aloud: In the last of days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains and lifted high above the hills; and all peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall prosper; and they shall say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob. Of this mountain and of this city the apostle Paul also — if indeed, in receiving the epistle, the Latin tongue does not reject the authority of the Greeks —, discoursing in a sacred speech, says: You have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and many thousands of angels, and the Church of the firstborn, who are written in the heavens.

Thus says the Lord of hosts. Old men and old women shall yet dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, and a man's staff in his hand for the multitude of days. And the streets of the city shall be filled with infants and girls, playing in its streets. LXX: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Old men and old women shall yet sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each one holding his rod in his hand, for the multitude of days; and the streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls, playing in its streets. So great, he says, once I have returned to Zion and am dwelling in the midst of Jerusalem, will be the prosperity of all things and the rest and tranquillity from wars, that, with no enemy remaining, old age in both sexes will reach the furthest span of life and support its trembling limbs with a guiding staff. The streets of the city too shall be filled with boys and girls playing. Now this is wont to happen when there is security and deep peace in the cities, so that playful youth celebrates the joy of the cities with games and dances.

But if we refer it to the Church, of which it is said: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God, and: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle; God in the midst of her shall not be moved, who can doubt that the streets of the Church are the virtues, in which wisdom acts confidently and is proclaimed on the tops of the walls? Hence the psalmist too cries out to the Lord: Your commandment is exceedingly broad. Seeking the Lord and Savior in these streets, the bride says in the Song of Songs: I will rise and go about the city, in the market and in its streets, until I find him whom my soul has loved. So there shall dwell, or sit, old men and old women, of whom it is written — if, however, anyone is pleased to receive the book —: Honorable old age is not that of long time, nor is it reckoned by the number of years. But grey hairs are men's prudence, and a spotless life is old age; of such the Lord also speaks to Moses: Appoint with you seventy elders, whom you yourself know to be elders; for which reason, too, before Abraham no one was called an old man, of whom we read it written: Abraham, failing, died, nourished in a good old age, an old man and full of days. For grey hairs are the glory of old men, of which it is said: A man's grey hairs are his wisdom. These, for the multitude of their days, shall hold rods and staffs in their hands, and shall say to their disciples: What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness and meekness? For he who brings forth wisdom from his lips strikes the senseless man with a rod. And on the contrary: He who spares his staff hates his son, but he who loves him corrects him diligently. And not only old men but old women too shall sit in the streets of Jerusalem, whom Paul describes with apostolic mouth: Honor, he says, widows who are truly widows, and in another place: Let a widow be chosen not less than sixty years of age, who has been the wife of one husband, having testimony in good works; if she has brought up children, if she has received guests, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has ministered to those placed in tribulations, if she has pursued every good work.

This is that wine with which, when youths and maidens are intoxicated, they at once thirst for virginity. They are filled with the spirit of chastity, and the prophecy of Zechariah comes to pass, at least if we follow the Hebrew literally, for he prophesied concerning virgins: "And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof. For what is his goodness, and what is his beauty, but the corn of the elect, and wine that gives birth to virgins?" They are virgins of whom it is written in the forty-fifth psalm: "She is led to the king, with her virgin companions, her escort, in her train. With joy and gladness they are led along as they enter the palace of the king."

Old men and old women of this sort shall sit in the streets of Jerusalem, and shall hold staffs in their hands, and the streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing. These are the boys and girls, the old men and the young, whom the psalmist exhorts to sing to the Lord, saying: Young men and maidens, old men with the younger, let them praise the name of the Lord. And John, the evangelist and apostle: I write, he says, to you, children, because your sins are forgiven you for the name of the Savior. I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. And of these Solomon speaks in Proverbs: To give shrewdness to the innocent; and to the younger boy sense and understanding. And again: Hear, children, the instruction of a father, and attend, that you may know understanding. Of these boys, little maidens and girls, Psalm 44 (45) also speaks: There shall be brought, he says, to the king virgins after her, according to what is written: The daughters of Judah exulted and rejoiced in all your judgments, O Lord. And when they hear from the Apostle: Rejoice, again I say rejoice, they will show the gladness of the mind by the gesture of the body, and, leaping in the dance, they will say with David: I will dance and play in the sight of the Lord.

Thus says the Lord of hosts: If it shall seem difficult in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, shall it be difficult in my eyes? says the Lord of hosts. LXX: Thus says the Lord Almighty: If it shall be impossible before the remnant of this people in those days, shall it also be impossible before me? says the Lord Almighty. At each of the words and sentences in which prosperity is promised to Israel, and which, because of the greatness of the things, seem almost incredible, the prophet sets forth: Thus says the Lord Almighty; saying this in other words: Do not think that the things I pledge are mine, and do not disbelieve them as though they came from a man; the promises I unfold are God's. He had said above that old women and old men would sit in the streets and, for the length of their time, would hold staffs in their hands; that the streets would be thronged with a multitude of people; that boys and girls would lead dances as on feast days; and that Jerusalem was to be built up and restored to the state of its former happiness. This seemed incredible to the remnant of the people, who had come from the captivity, as they saw the city utterly abandoned, and the ruins of the walls and the burnt houses displaying the hands of Babylon. Therefore he joins to it: If to you who are the remnant of the captive people what I pledge seems either difficult or impossible, that in those days in which Jerusalem is to be built there should be such happiness, will it be either difficult or impossible in the sight of the Lord, who by my mouth promises that these things shall be? For the things that are impossible with men are possible with God. We have seen these things fulfilled in the churches of Christ in the time of persecution, when the ferocity of the persecutors was roused to such madness that they even destroyed our meeting places and handed the divine books over to the flames, and all the islands, mines and prisons were filled with chained flocks of confessors and martyrs. Who at that time would have believed that churches would be built again by those very men who had destroyed them before?
