But by the ass's colt, on which no man had ever sat (for so it is found recorded in the other evangelists), we are to understand the Gentile nations which had not received the law of the Lord; by the ass, on the other hand (for both animals were brought to the Lord), that people of His which came of the nation of Israel, and was already so far subdued as to recognize its Master's crib.

Again, although John tells us nothing as to the way in which the Lord despatched His disciples to fetch these animals to Him, nevertheless he inserts a brief allusion to this colt, and cites also the word of the prophet which Matthew makes use of. In the case also of this testimony from the prophet, the terms in which it is reproduced by the evangelists, although they exhibit certain differences, do not fail to express a sense identical in intention. Some difficulty, however, may be felt in the fact that Matthew adduces this passage in a form which represents the prophet to have made mention of the ass; whereas this is not the case, either with the quotation as introduced by John, or with the version given in the ecclesiastical codices of the translation in common use. An explanation of this variation seems to me to be found in the fact that Matthew is understood to have written his Gospel in the Hebrew language. Moreover, it is manifest that the translation which bears the name of the Septuagint differs in some particulars from the text which is found in the Hebrew by those who know that tongue, and by the several scholars who have given us renderings of the same Hebrew books. And if an explanation is asked for this discrepancy, or for the circumstance that the weighty authority of the Septuagint translation diverges in many passages from the rendering of the truth which is discovered in the Hebrew codices, I am of opinion that no more probable account of the matter will suggest itself, than the supposition that the Seventy composed their version under the influence of the very Spirit by whose inspiration the things which they were engaged in translating had been originally spoken. This is an idea which receives confirmation also from the marvellous consent which is asserted to have characterized them. Consequently, when these translators, while not departing from the real mind of God from which these sayings proceeded, and to the expression of which the words ought to be subservient, gave a different form to some matters in their reproduction of the text, they had no intention of exemplifying anything else than the very thing which we now admiringly contemplate in that kind of harmonious diversity which marks the four evangelists, and in the light of which it is made clear that there is no failure from strict truth, although one historian may give an account of some theme in a manner different indeed from another, and yet not so different as to involve an actual departure from the sense intended by the person with whom he is bound to be in concord and agreement. To understand this is of advantage to character, with a view at once to guard against what is false, and to pronounce correctly upon it; and it is of no less consequence to faith itself, in the way of precluding the supposition that, as it were with consecrated sounds, truth has a kind of defence provided for it which might imply God's handing over to us not only the thing itself, but likewise the very words which are required for its enunciation; whereas the fact rather is, that the theme itself which is to be expressed is so decidedly deemed of superior importance to the words in which it has to be expressed, that we would be under no obligation to ask about them at all, if it were possible for us to know the truth without the terms, as God knows it, and as His angels also know it in Him.
The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 2, Chapter 66

Now since many historical facts have already been mentioned, let us briefly relate some of the allegorical ones at the end. If you see opposing power attacking God's people, you will realize who it is that is sitting upon the ass. If you further consider how people are destroyed by demons, you will understand what the ass is. Indeed, in the Gospel you will recognize Jesus sending his disciples to an ass which was tied and its colt, so that the disciples might loose and bring her for the Lord himself to sit upon her. Perhaps this ass, that is, the church, first carried Balaam and now Christ. She had been loosed by the disciples and released from the bonds that tied for this very purpose, that the Son of God might sit upon her and with her enter the holy and heavenly city of Jerusalem. Then was fulfilled the Scripture which says, "Rejoice, O daughter of Zion, exclaim, O daughter Jerusalem! See, your king comes to you, meek and riding on a beast of burden," that is, an ass (doubtless he is speaking of believers among the Jews) "or young colt" (these apparently are those of the Gentiles who believe in Christ our Lord).

Rejoice greatly O daughter of Sion, shout O daughter of Jerusalem; behold thy King cometh unto thee; he is just and having salvation; lowly and riding upon an ass—even a young colt. This passage he uttered with reference to Zerubabel, in a strain of hyperbole as regards him, for it had properly its accomplishment in the Lord Christ, whom Zerubabel as it were, personified.

For peace and tranquillity of the soul is above all glory of any house; for peace passeth all understanding. This is that peace above all peace which shall be granted after the third shaking of the heaven, the sea, the earth and the dry land, when He shall destroy all Principalities and Powers. For heaven and earth shall pass away, and all the fashion of this world; and every man shall rise up against his brother with the sword, that is, with the word piercing the marrow of the soul, that whatever opposes itself, the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem may be cut off, as Zechariah says. And thus there will be peace over all, the passions of the body offering no resistance, and the unbelieving mind no obstacle, that Christ may be all in all, offering in subjection to the Father the hearts of all men.

And I will destroy, he says, the chariot from Ephraim. It is still spoken in the person of God the Father, that the four-horse chariot, or the chariot, should perish from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem. And meanwhile according to the letter he says this: There shall be no battles, all things having been set at peace by the coming and birth of Christ. Moreover, according to a higher understanding, Ephraim, which is interpreted καρποφορία, that is, fruitfulness and abundance of crops, is referred to the multitude of heresies; of which it is written in Psalm 77 (78): The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle. Of these chariots and cars we read: Some in chariots and some on horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God; they are bound and have fallen, but we have risen and are set upright. The horse that is destroyed from Jerusalem is the one of which we read: A horse is a deceitful thing for safety. And in Jeremiah those who gave themselves up to luxury and lust hear: They have become to me horses mad after females; each one neighed after his neighbor's wife. Hence they are called back to repentance, as the psalmist says: Do not become like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding. And when God has destroyed the chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, those who have been set free from such horses and chariots shall be transferred into the service of the Lord, and shall become Cherubim, and of them it shall be said: The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of those who rejoice, and: To my cavalry among the chariots of Pharaoh I have likened you, my nearest one, and: You shall mount your horses, and your riding is salvation. The bow of war shall be scattered, so that the fiery darts may not be shot that could strike the hearts of the pleasure-loving. And he shall speak peace to the nations, of which it is written: He shall be the expectation of the nations, and again: In him the nations shall hope, and: His power from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the world. This is not to be weakened by allegory, but to be believed as truly fulfilled, according to what we read: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession. In Psalm 71 (72) also it is said, under the person of Solomon and of the true peaceful one: And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.

Be glad, therefore, O Jerusalem, since of such a kind is a king appointed for you by God, and he has come to you, capable of saving his own on account of the divine influence accruing to him and justly inflicting total punishment on the adversaries. While he is riding a lowly animal for the reason that he has just arrived back from captivity, he assumes great power through divine grace, and so from Ephraim and from Jerusalem he will remove all the chariots of the adversaries, every war horse and every battle bow—that is to say, he will drive off all enemies so that there will be no longer any adversary against the country of Judah. He will also wipe out a great multitude of the adversaries and completely deprive them of peace, crushed and destroyed in a war waged by him.

The sun was darkened because of the Sun of justice. The rocks were rent because of "the spiritual rock." Tombs were opened, and the dead arose, because of him who was "free among the dead." He "sent forth his prisoners out of the pit, wherein there is no water." Do not be ashamed, then, of the Crucified, but say with confidence, "He bears our sins and carries our sorrows, and by his bruises we are healed." Let us not be ungrateful to our Benefactor. Again, "For the wickedness of my people was he led to death; and I shall give the ungodly for his burial, and the rich for his death." And Paul says clearly "that Christ died for our sins, according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day, according to the Scriptures."

With this proviso, however, that they interpret the earlier testimony otherwise than we have explained it, and say: O Christ, whom we hope will come, and who are to reign in all the ends of the earth, by the blood of your testament, in which, according to Ezekiel, you found Jerusalem spattered with her own blood, and by which you entered into a covenant with Abraham in the dividing of the calf and the ram and the goat, you have released your people Israel from the captivity and the furnace of the Chaldeans, in whom there was no mercy. Therefore you too, O Israelites, who were prisoners and hoped in the Lord, return to most strongly fortified Jerusalem, for today you have the Lord promising you that for the brief injury of captivity you shall receive all things doubled, as we read that Job also received them.

You also, by the blood of your testament, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water; turn to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope; today also, announcing, I will render double to you. LXX: And you, by the blood of the testament, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit that has no water; you shall sit in the stronghold, prisoners of the congregation, and for one day of your sojourning I will render double to you. After the word of the prophet, or rather God the Father Almighty himself, had announced to Zion and Jerusalem that their king was coming to them, meek and mounted upon a she-ass, a beast of burden, and upon the foal of an ass, and that his power would be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth, he makes an apostrophe to Christ himself, of whom the prophecy speaks, and says: You also, by the blood of your testament, or covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water. This is understood as follows: By the blood of your passion you have, in your clemency, set free those who were held bound in the prison of hell, in which there is no mercy. In short, after the Lord rose again, those who were held by the bonds of Adam's sins, or, as some would have it, of ingrained error, and of death, rose with him and appeared in the holy city. Of this blood of the testament he himself also spoke to the disciples, pointing to his future passion: Take and drink of this, all of you; for this is the cup of the new testament in my blood. In prefiguration of this pit which has no waters, Joseph was sent into one by his brothers, and Daniel and Jeremiah by the Chaldeans and by the people of the Jews. Benaiah too, in the time of snow and cold, went down into a pit to kill a lion there. Jeremiah, however, is plunged not into the water of the pit but into the mud and mire of the pit, which could suffocate a thirsty man rather than refresh him. Hence it is also written in the psalm: I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance. In this pit of hell there abode also that rich man once clothed in purple, whose boastful tongue was burned by the fires of punishment, and who was so far from having any refreshment of waters that he begged for the refreshment of the tip of the poor man's finger dipped in water.

It was fitting that the herald of his resurrection is reported to have been sitting, so that by sitting he might prefigure him who, having triumphed over the author of death, would ascend to his seat in the everlasting kingdom. Concerning this he said a little later, as he appeared to his disciples, "All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me"; and the evangelist Mark says, "The Lord, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at God's right hand." [The angel] was sitting upon the stone with which the tomb was closed, but which had been rolled away, to teach that [Christ] had cast down and triumphed over the closed places of the lower world by his power, so that he might lift up to the light and the rest of paradise all of his own whom he found there, according to the prophet's [statement], "You also because of the blood of your covenant, have led your prisoners back from the pit, in which there is no water."

But who will deliver us from these plagues? Certainly there is one alone who came to deliver us, namely Christ, who made ten condescensions against the ten plagues. The first was down to our flesh. The second was down to our mortality. The third, to our neediness, for he suffered hunger, thirst, and cold. The fourth was to our poverty, for "he was made destitute," having no place to which he might turn. The fifth, to our temptation, when he permitted himself to be tempted; and in this he bore our weakness. The Apostle: "We do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tempted in all things." The sixth, to the weariness of body and our toil. The seventh, to our anxiety; whence: "Jesus began to be fearful and distressed and said: My soul is sorrowful even unto death." The eighth was to the cross, and this was wondrous. The ninth was to death. The tenth was to the prison of hell.

These are the ten condescensions by which God condescended to man. But why did he descend to the prison of hell? Certainly, so that in the blood of the covenant he might lead the captives out of prison, those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. Christ, through the blood of the new covenant, freed us and led us from death to life, and from darkness to light.

Since it was fitting for Christ to die in order to deliver us from death, so it was fitting for Him to descend into hell in order to deliver us also from going down into hell. Hence it is written (Hosea 13:14): "O death, I will be thy death; O hell, I will be thy bite." Secondly, because it was fitting when the devil was overthrown by the Passion that Christ should deliver the captives detained in hell, according to Zechariah 9:11: "Thou also by the blood of Thy Testament hast sent forth Thy prisoners out of the pit."
Question 52. Christ's descent into hell, Article 1

And again the word is directed to those very ones who were prisoners and who were to be set free by the mercy of Christ: Turn to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope. And the sense is: You who are now prisoners and are held in a harsh and terrible hell, you who hope for the loosing of your bonds at the coming of Christ, turn to the stronghold, or, you shall sit in the stronghold, of which it is written: The fear of the Lord is the bulwark of the holy one, so that you may say: Be to me a God, a protector, and a fortified place, that you may save me; and so that the prophet may also say of you: Behold, a strong city, and our salvation shall set a wall and an outer wall. But this stronghold, to which God exhorts the prisoners of hope, or the hoping prisoners of the Church, we ought to take as nothing other than the dwelling of paradise, into which the thief was the first to enter with the Lord; and for this reason they are called forth to the stronghold through Zechariah, because already then, and from that time, the Lord was promising that for a brief tribulation they would receive eternal rewards. Or, as is read in the LXX: For one day of your sojourning, I will render double to you. For in comparison with eternity, all that we suffer in the world must be called one day, a day not of dwelling but of sojourning, because we are strangers and sojourners, as all our fathers were. For what is at present momentary and light in our tribulation works in us, beyond measure, in sublimity, a weight of eternal glory, while we look not at the things that are seen, but at those that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but those that are not seen are eternal.

For I have stretched Judah for myself, as a bow I have filled Ephraim; and I will raise up your sons, O Zion, over your sons, O Greece, and I will set you as the sword of the mighty. LXX: For I have bent you, O Judah, for myself, as a bow I have filled Ephraim; and I will raise up your sons, O Zion, over the sons of the Greeks, and I will handle you as the sword of a warrior. The Jews refer this to the times of the Maccabees, who conquered the Macedonians and, after a space of three and a half years, cleansed the temple that had been defiled by idolatry. And what follows: As a bow I have filled Ephraim, they think signifies those who had come, under Hezekiah, from the ten tribes that are called Israel, over whom Josiah too is recorded to have reigned.

According to tropology this place can be explained thus: Judah is stretched as a bow when the Lord and Savior is sent by the Father into this world, he who is himself both the bow and the archer and the arrow. The bow, as in the present place. The archer, as in Psalm 44 (45): Your arrows are sharp, most mighty; and when someone has been wounded by them, he says: I am wounded with love. And the arrow is he himself who speaks through Isaiah: He has set me as a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he has hidden me. The chosen arrow is the Word of God; the quiver in which the arrow is hidden is the dispensation of the flesh he assumed. With this Ephraim is filled, so that, when he has been armed and made ready for war, he too, together with the nations, may be wounded by the arrows of the Lord; Ephraim, from whose tribe Jeroboam first split the people, whom the prophet Hosea shows more fully to be taken in the person of heretics; and what we said above: The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle. For when the Lord raises up the sons of Zion, that is, the sons of the Church, both the masters of contrary doctrines and every assertion of the philosophers and the arguments of the Gentiles will be destroyed, because the Lord himself is the sword of the mighty, of whom it is said: Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty. In your comeliness and your beauty, set forth, proceed prosperously and reign, because of truth and meekness and justice; and your right hand shall lead you wonderfully. With this sword the Ethiopians are wounded, of whom it is written: And you, O Ethiopians, shall be wounded by my sword; and after they have been wounded by the sword of Christ, they will lay aside their dark color and, exulting, will say: The splendor of the Lord our God shall be upon us; which David too promises himself after his repentance: You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow. This is the sword of which the Apostle writes: The word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword, and reaching even to the division of soul and spirit.

And the Lord God shall be seen over them, and his javelin shall go forth like lightning; and the Lord God shall sound the trumpet, and shall go in the whirlwind of the south. The Lord of hosts shall protect them. LXX: And the Lord God shall appear over them; and his arrow shall go forth like lightning; and the Lord God Almighty shall sound with the trumpet, and shall go in the commotion of his terror. The Lord Almighty shall protect them. This place too they refer to the times of the Maccabees: that when these fought against Antiochus and conquered, the fight and the victory were the Lord's, who went forth mighty to battle, and his power appeared like lightning, and, when the adversaries had been conquered and scattered as by a whirlwind, he protected the people of the Jews. We, however, shall refer everything to the understanding of the Savior, of whom it was said above: I have stretched Judah for myself as a bow. When he has been stretched, and the heretics and the Gentiles have been slain by the sons of Zion, the glory of the Lord will appear, and his javelin will go forth like lightning; of which lightning we read in Habakkuk too: In the light of your arrows they shall go, in the splendor of your flashing spear. This lightning and splendor is called by another name the trumpet and its blast, so that, when the holy cry has sounded, he who before had deaf ears may say: The instruction of the Lord has opened my ears, and has given me an ear to hear. And what follows: And he shall go in the whirlwind of the south, or, he shall go in the commotion of his threatening. He threatens and says that he will inflict punishments for this reason, that he may have mercy on those who repent. In short, he adds and says: The Lord Almighty shall protect them, those whom he had first terrified by his threatening. Let us read the history of the Ninevites.

And they shall devour and subdue with sling stones, and drinking they shall be made drunk as with wine, and they shall be filled like bowls, and like the horns of the altar.

And the Lord their God shall save them in that day as the flock of his people, because holy stones shall be lifted up over his land. LXX: And they shall consume them, and overwhelm them with sling stones, and they shall drink their blood like wine, and they shall fill the altar like bowls. And the Lord shall save them in that day as sheep, his people, because holy stones shall roll upon his land. For what we have rendered shall be lifted up, and what is written in the Hebrew as methnosasoth, can be interpreted as wandering, or fleeing. When the sons of Zion have been protected, and the Lord has sounded the trumpet and gone in the whirlwind against their adversaries, so great will be the ruin of the Greeks that they will be crushed, I will not say by swords, but by the casting of stones and the whirling of slings, so that they will be a prey and a meal for their enemies. Then, drinking, they shall be made drunk as with wine. It is not those who have been slain who will be drunk with their own blood, but those who have conquered will fight with desperation, as though drunk, and will please the Lord like the horns of the altar and its libation. For this is what is understood by the bowls, with which libations are poured out upon the altar. The Lord will also save them as sheep and the flock of his people; for they will not fight against the Macedonians as an armed army, trained in the art of war, but will come like a flock ready for death, and, with the Lord's help, will overcome. And the holy stones that have been oppressed — and he calls them stones because of the hardness of their tribulations and their fortitude of mind — will be lifted up from their lowliness, and will be glorious in his land. Otherwise: his holy stones, of priestly stock, fleeing in different directions, will, by his gift, obtain the victory.

Let us speak also according to anagogy, or rather let us explain a prophecy wrapped in many obscurities. The sons of Zion, protected by their Lord, will devour their adversaries, whom we understand as the sons of Greece. And they will subdue them with sling stones, with the threatenings of the Scriptures, making their adversaries subject and humble; for nothing strikes so hard as an example from the holy Scriptures, and a testimony sent forth by the whirl of the mouth. But what is said in the LXX: And they shall drink their blood like wine, we do not read so in the Hebrew, but: Drinking they shall be made drunk as with wine, so that they may hear that word of the Song of Songs: Drink, friends, and be drunk. And so their drunkenness will please like the sacrifice of the altar, and like the horns, or corners, of the altar.

The Lord will also save them as the flock of his people, because holy stones shall roll upon his land, stones that will be so light and so striving upward that they will not wait for the hands of the builders, but will themselves hasten to be laid upon the foundation of Christ and to be held together by the cornerstone; of whom the apostle Peter also speaks: As living stones be built up into a spiritual house, and a holy priesthood, offering spiritual victims, pleasing to God. These are the stones that will cry out if the people of the Jews keep silent, and they will roll upon the earth as long as they are in the body, because the earthly habitation weighs down the mind that is anxious about many things; and, set in the flesh, the holy man says: Who will give me wings like a dove? As far as lies in him, he strives and rolls and is raised toward the heights, but he is held back by the frailty of the flesh. And the earth upon which the stones roll is that of which we read: Sing to the Lord, all the earth, and: Let all the earth worship you, and sing psalms to you.

This we have said in a general way: but let us speak also in particular of the inner man. The wheel stands upon the earth with only some small trace of contact, and it not only stands, but as it were runs on: it does not stand still, but touches and passes by: finally, when it is rolled, it always mounts up to higher things. So too the holy man, because he is in the body, has the necessity of thinking some things about earthly matters; and when he has come to food and clothing and the rest of such things, having food and clothing, with these he is content, touching the earth, and he hastens to higher things. In him who runs and hastens to higher things, in him is your word. We read also in the prophet: "Holy stones are rolled upon the earth." See what he said: Holy stones are rolled upon the earth. For because they are wheels, therefore they are rolled upon the earth and hasten to higher things.

Now concerning the several sorts of food, the Lord says to you, "You shall eat the good things of the earth," and "All sorts of flesh shall you eat, as the green herb," but "You shall pour out the blood." For "not those things that go into the mouth, but those that come out of it, defile a man." "I mean blasphemies, evil speaking, and if there be any other thing like that. But "do you eat the fat of the land with righteousness." For "if anything be pleasant, it is his; and if there be anything good, it is his: wheat for the young men, and wine to cheer the maids." For "who shall eat or who shall drink without him?" Wise Ezra does also admonish you and says, "Go your way, and eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and do not be sorrowful."

For what is his goodness, and what is his beauty, but the grain of the elect, and wine that makes virgins spring forth? LXX: For if there is anything best of his, and if anything good from him, grain for young men and wine of good odor for virgins. Therefore, they say, the Maccabees, fleeing hither and thither, will overcome with the Lord's help, so that, when the Macedonians have been cast out of the land of Israel, the temple may be cleansed, the precepts of the law may be kept, and the learning of the Scriptures may again make virgins spring forth, that is, peoples believing in one God, who before had been defiled by the worship of idolatry. By the grain of the elect, that is, baurim, they would have us understand not young men, as the Seventy translated, but chosen and learned men, who are found worthy to eat the grain, that is, the law of God. For wine, which in Hebrew is called thiros, Aquila translated οἰνίαν (vintage), which itself also can be referred to the abundance of the vintage. So the Jews think. But we understand the grain of the elect, or of the young men, and the wine that makes virgins spring forth, or the wine of good odor for virgins, as the Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel: Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears greater fruit. From this wheat is made that bread which came down from heaven and which strengthens the heart of man. This bread is eaten by those who are strong in Christ, and to whom John the Evangelist speaks: I write to you, young men, because the word of God abides in you, and you are strong, and you have conquered the evil one. He who is the grain of the elect, or of the young men, is himself also the wine that gladdens the heart of man, and it is drunk by those virgins who are holy both in body and in spirit, so that, made drunk and rejoicing, they may follow the Church; and that it may be said of them: Virgins shall be brought to the king after her, her companions shall be brought to you; they shall be brought with gladness and exultation. For how shall they not have gladness, who, made drunk by the cup of the Savior, are begotten into virgins, and dare to say: Bring me into the little chamber of wine, strengthen me with ointments? This wine is of good odor, whence it is said in the same song: You shall give me to drink of the perfumer's wine, of the streams of your pomegranates. With this wine are made drunk those who follow the Lamb of God wherever he goes, clothed in white garments; because they have not defiled themselves with women, for they remained virgins.
10: Ask of the Lord rain in the late season, and the Lord will make snows and will give them showers of rain, to each one grass in the field. For the idols have spoken what is useless, and the diviners have seen a lie, and the dreamers have spoken in vain, they comforted vainly; therefore they have been led away like a flock, they shall be afflicted, because they have no shepherd. LXX: Ask rain of the Lord in due season, early and late. The Lord has made phantasies, and he will give them winter rain, to each one grass in the field, for those who spoke have spoken troubles; and the diviners false visions, and they have spoken false dreams, they comforted vainly; therefore they have been dried up like sheep, and they have been afflicted because there was none to heal. This happiness which was promised for the time of the Maccabees, when the holy stones were lifted up over the land and the Israelite state grew greater, so much that the peoples again fed on the grain of the law, and your virgins were made drunk with the wine of the Holy Spirit, is promised in part. But since it is now the last time of the prophets, and the world is declining toward its end, and all the things that have been foretold await their fulfilment, ask of the Lord that he give you the late rain, that the Christ who has been promised may come and grant you dews and snows, for which azizim is written in the Hebrew. And I do not know what the LXX meant in translating phantasies, unless perhaps they wished to describe the greatness of the grace and the wonder of the gifts by the name of phantasy. So the Lord, who is to make the snows and is to water the dryness of the whole earth with the rains of the Gospel preaching, will himself give showers to those who believe, and all things will be filled with abundance, so that, after the nations have believed in Christ, they may understand that the things they worshipped before are vain.

But according to the spiritual understanding we can say that the Lord exhorts those who believe in Christ to ask for the late rain at the consummation of the world, when the fullness of grace is to be given, and grass will grow up for each one in his own field, so that they may be able to say: The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture, there he has set me, beside the waters of refreshment he has brought me up.

Or else Israel itself, which was once deceived and held fast by the errors of idolatry, may understand that it worshipped idols in vain, and listened to the lies of diviners, and acquiesced in dreams, which Scripture commands us not to believe. And for this reason they were led like a flock into captivity, and afflicted, without God as their shepherd, because they did not have knowledge of the law. This whole place is obscure and doubtful, and the reader ought to pardon us if, in things that are ambiguous, we too walk with a hesitant step.

For all the idols, and the diviners and the dreamers, have spoken in vain, and comforted vainly. These things he says of the heretics, who under the Christian name understand neither what they are saying nor what they are affirming, and who give heed to erring spirits and to teachers of demons who speak lies in hypocrisy, and have their conscience seared, so that, being by no means believers, they are led away by the consolations of those who promise vain things; and for this reason they have been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, and led away into the captivity of the king of Babylon, and they shall be afflicted, because they do not have Christ as their shepherd, whom they promise themselves under a false name.

Observe, you who are our beloved sons, how merciful yet righteous the Lord our God is, how gracious and kind to humankind. And yet most certainly "he will not acquit the guilty," though he welcomes returning sinners and revives them, leaving no room for suspicion to such as wish to judge sternly and to reject offenders entirely, and to refuse to grant them exhortations which might bring them to repentance. In contradiction to such, God by Isaiah says to the bishops, "Comfort you, comfort you my people, you priests; speak comfortably to Jerusalem." It therefore behooves you, upon hearing those words of his, to encourage those who have offended, and lead them to repentance, and afford them hope, and not vainly to suppose that you shall be partakers of their offenses on account of such your love to them. Receive the penitent with alacrity and rejoice over them, and with mercy and bowels of compassion judge the sinners. For if a person was walking by the side of a river and ready to stumble, and you should push him and thrust him into the river instead of offering him your hand for his assistance, you would be guilty of the murder of your brother.… You ought rather to lend your helping hand as he was ready to fall, lest he perish without remedy, that both the people may take warning and the offender may not utterly perish. It is your duty, O bishop, neither to overlook the sins of the people nor to reject those who are penitent, that you may not unskillfully destroy the Lord's flock or dishonor his new name which is stamped upon his people, and you yourself be reproached as those ancient pastors were, of whom God speaks thus to Jeremiah: "Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard; they have polluted my heritage." And in another passage, "My anger is waxed hot against the shepherds, and against the lambs shall I have indignation."

My fury is angered against the shepherds, and I will visit upon the he-goats; for the Lord of hosts has visited his flock, the house of Judah, and has made them like the horse of his glory in war. From him the corner, from him the peg, from him the bow of battle, from him shall go forth every exactor together; and they shall be like mighty men treading down the mire of the streets in battle, and they shall fight, because the Lord is with them. LXX: My fury is stirred up against the shepherds, and I will visit upon the lambs; and the Lord God Almighty will visit his flock, the house of Judah, and will make them like his comely horse in battle; and from him he looked, and from him he set, and from him the bow in fury, there shall go forth everyone who goes forth together, and they shall be like warriors treading down the mire of the streets in battle, and they shall be made ready, because the Lord is with them. In this place too the Jews have a twofold exposition. For some think that all of it is to be fulfilled at the coming of the Christ; others, that it has already been fulfilled under the Maccabees. And this is their explanation of the things the Lord promises: the Lord was angered against the shepherds, both the princes and the priests, and he visited upon the he-goats, that is, the people, according to that which is written: My people has become a lost flock, the shepherds have cast them out, so that the disciples were punished for the fault of their masters; not by the injustice of a judge who repays the sins of the fathers upon the sons, but because, when those men sinned, the people applauded along with them. And then indeed the Lord visited his he-goats, or his fattest lambs, and, according to the Seventy, caused them to be dried up with drought. But afterwards the Lord Almighty visited his flock, the house of Judah; for he raised up Judas Maccabeus, and the others descended from him, against the generals of Antiochus, and made them like the horse of his glory in battle, that is, those who were begotten of his stock; for they oppressed the Macedonians for a long time.

Our writers, however, refer these things to the times of persecution, because for the fault of the priests the people too is often handed over to its adversaries; and yet the Lord Almighty afterwards visits his flock, the house of Judah, which confesses God both in word and in mind, and makes them like the horse of his glory in war, of which the saints say: Mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation.

It was their duty to have known the meaning of what had been spoken of old, as being before decreed by God concerning them. For among others are words like these, "My wrath is kindled against the shepherds, and I will visit the lambs." For the wicked shepherds perished miserably: while the calling of those who were obedient to salvation was a kind of visitation; for a remnant of Israel was saved.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

And what follows: From him the corner, from him the peg, from him the bow of battle, from him shall go forth every exactor together, they understand μεταφορικῶς (metaphorically), so that they interpret the corner as the royal power, because it holds the walls together. And from him, he says, the peg, that is, the priesthood. Read Isaiah, in whom Eliakim is fastened in the temple of God like a peg. From him the bow of battle: men strong for war; from him also every exactor together, which in the Hebrew is written noges, and Aquila translated εἰσπράσσων (exactor), so that not only were there strong and good men, but others among them were unworthy of their lineage. For Judas Maccabeus, and all who were princes among the people from his line, were both the corner, because they held the people together with royal power, and the peg, for they themselves were priests, and the bow of battle, because they proved most valiant men, so that they not only marshalled the army and the battle line, but were the first to leap forward into battle. Concerning what follows: From him shall go forth every exactor together, for which the LXX translated: From him shall go forth everyone who leads out together, we can also say this: there will be no rank in the army that is not arranged at his discretion. And they shall be most valiant men, treading down the Macedonians like the mire of the streets in battle; and they shall be most valiant, and shall fight, because the Lord is with them.

He himself will also be the bow of the Lord's fury, of which he says: I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and again: My arrows shall consume them. Of this bow, and of these arrows, we read in Psalm 7: He has bent his bow and made it ready, and on it he has made ready the instruments of death; he has made his arrows for the burning.

And the riders on horses shall be confounded.

And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph; and I will bring them back, because I will have mercy on them; and they shall be as they were when I had not cast them off, for I am the Lord their God, and I will hear them. And they shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim, and their heart shall rejoice as from wine; and their sons shall see and shall rejoice; and their heart shall exult in the Lord. LXX: And the riders on horses shall be confounded, and I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph, and I will make them dwell, because I have loved them. And they shall be as when I had not cast them away, for I am the Lord their God, and I will hear them; and they shall be like the warriors of Ephraim, and their heart shall rejoice as in wine, and their sons shall see and shall rejoice, and their heart shall be glad in the Lord. These things too, in keeping with the sense above, they expound in two ways, so that either they say they have already been accomplished under the Maccabees, or they relate that they are to be accomplished under the Christ in the last age. And the sense is: when Judas has been made like a comely horse in battle, and has trodden down his adversaries like mire, and, with the Lord fighting beside him, has overcome, then all the cavalry of Greece will fall, and the house of Judah and the house of Israel — for he calls it the house of Joseph, that is, of the ten tribes — will be saved alike; and I will bring them back from the captivity in which they had been, and they shall be as they were at that time when I had not cast them off; for I am the Lord their God, who will hear them when they pray. And Ephraim, who are now held captive, shall afterwards be set free, and shall come to such joy that you would think them drenched with wine. Their sons also shall behold the triumphs of their fathers, and shall rejoice in the Lord, by whose gift they obtained the victory. Let us look for the history: when did Judah and Israel fight together against the Greeks, or at what time did Ephraim return from the Assyrian captivity, when, according to Ezekiel, the two staffs, that is, Judah and Ephraim, were joined to each other and coupled into one rod?

And they shall tread down, he says, their adversaries, crowned in martyrdom, and they shall say: The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life, of whom shall I be afraid? While the wicked drew near against me to eat my flesh, my enemies who trouble me, they themselves were weakened and fell. Though camps should stand together against me, my heart shall not fear; though battle should rise up against me, in this will I hope. Then shall that saying be fulfilled: One of you shall pursue a thousand, and two shall put many thousands to flight.

This can be explained according to tropology thus. When the Lord Almighty visits his flock, the house of Judah, then the riders on horses shall be confounded, of whom it is written: Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea. Of whom it is also sung in the voice of the psalmist: At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, they who mounted horses have slumbered. And the choir of the saints redoubles it: Some in chariots, and some on horses, but we will call upon the name of our God; they have been bound and have fallen, but we have risen and stand upright. In this cavalry the king of Egypt trusted; and, hurled headlong into the sea, he sank like lead into the depths, and learned by his own example that what is written is true: A horse is a deceitful thing for safety. These chariots and four-horse teams we interpreted above as the four passions, which, unless they are governed by the reins of a good charioteer, are carried over the precipice. But there is another charioteer, of whom Elisha speaks: Father, father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer.

Then God says that he strengthens the house of Judah and the house of Joseph, so that those who were divided while Jeroboam reigned may be united while Christ rules, and there may be one shepherd and one flock. For both Judah and Joseph, under different names, are brought together into the one understanding of the Savior, because Joseph lavished grain on the peoples hungering in Egypt, and the Lord satisfied the hunger of the world with his presence. And he will bring them back, and will have mercy on them, and so they shall be one, as they were before he cast them off. Take all these things of the persecutions, when, all hope being lost, the Lord heard his servants.

And they shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim, who, at first weak and infirm, shall afterwards be mighty and worthy of their name. For Ephraim is interpreted fruitfulness. And their heart shall rejoice when they have drunk the wine that was pressed from the vine of Sorek. Their sons also, to whom the apostle Paul speaks: My little sons, with whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you. And Peter, the prince of the apostles: As sons, he says, of obedience, not conformed according to your former manner of life. And in the psalm we read: Come, sons, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. These sons, therefore, shall exult and rejoice, and their heart shall be glad in the Lord.

I will whistle for them, and I will gather them, because I have redeemed them, and I will multiply them as they had been multiplied before. And I will sow them among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me, and they shall live with their sons, and shall return. And I will bring them back from the land of Egypt, and from the Assyrians I will gather them, and I will lead them to the land of Gilead and of Lebanon, and room shall not be found for them. LXX: I will signal to them, and I will receive them, because I will redeem them, and they shall be multiplied as they were very many, and I will sow them among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me. They shall nourish their sons and shall turn back, and I will bring them back from the land of Egypt, and from the Assyrians I will receive them, and into Galaaditis and into Lebanon I will bring them, and none of them shall be lacking. As the sign of their gathering, whether under the Macedonians or at the consummation of the world, as we said before, they shall have my whistle, he says, so that by my whistle I may gather them and show myself to be the shepherd. For I have redeemed them and freed them from captivity with an outstretched arm; and I will multiply them, I who had multiplied them before, so that the dispersion among the peoples may be seen to be not a division but the work of sowing, and, with the harvest of children and grandchildren multiplied, they may live with their sons; and they may return not only from the land of Egypt, but also from the Assyrians, and come back from both parts of the world to Judea, and to the land of Gilead and of Lebanon, which the ten tribes, called the house of Joseph and Ephraim, had possessed before; and so great shall be the number of those brought back that the land will not hold the multitude.

According to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy), the Lord signals and whistles to those who had before been captives to sins, and speaks to them: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and you shall find rest for your souls. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden is light. What is more merciful than this signal and whistle, by which the scattered people is gathered? And they are gathered because the Lord has redeemed them, not with corruptible silver and gold, from their vain manner of life, but with the precious blood, as of a spotless lamb, the Lord Jesus. Hence he speaks in the psalm: My exultation, deliver me from those who surround me, and again: You have redeemed me, O Lord God of truth. And he will multiply them as they had been multiplied before, so that what was promised to Abraham might be fulfilled: I will multiply him and I will bless him, and he shall be blessed, so that he may become the father of many nations. But we ought not to take as sons of Abraham those to whom the Lord says: If you were sons of Abraham, you would do the works of your father, but those of whom the Apostle says: As many as are of faith, they are the sons of Abraham. Of this multiplication Isaiah too testifies in mystical speech, saying: He who is little shall become thousands, and he who is small, a great nation. But let us not take the multiplication and blessing of children carnally: otherwise Elijah and Elisha and Jeremiah and John the Baptist, than whom there was none greater among those born of women, lacked this blessing; rather, let us take it of that blessing by which multitudes of the nations are called to the faith.

Of them in sooth He said by the voice of Isaiah, "I will make signs unto them, and receive them, because I will ransom them, and they shall be multiplied, as they were many: and I will sow them among the nations, and they who are afar off shall remember Me." For very many were they that were astray, but were called through Christ: and again they are many as they were before; for they have been received and ransomed, having obtained as the token of peace from God the Father, the adoption into His family and the grace that is by faith in Jesus Christ. And the divine disciples were sown widely among the nations: and what is the consequence? Those who in disposition were far from God, have been made near. To whom also the divine Paul sends an epistle, saying, "Now ye who some time were afar off have been made near in the blood of Christ."
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

In short, there follows: I will sow them among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me. They who heard the word of the Lord were sown among the peoples: Go, teach all nations, and in another place: You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and I have appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and your fruit should remain forever. And when the apostles have been sown among the peoples, the nations and peoples set far off shall remember me, that prophetic word agreeing with this saying: All the ends of the earth shall remember and shall turn to the Lord. And all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight. For the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations. And what is said: From afar they shall remember me, is like this: You who are far off, remember the Lord, and let Jerusalem come up upon your heart. The whole multitude of the nations was far off, but it remembered God, because we are all begotten of one parent. And when, the apostles having been sown among all the nations, the nations set far off have remembered God, they shall live with their sons, so that those who before were dead through unbelief may begin to live by faith. These are the sons whom Paul nourished in the gospel, writing to the Corinthians: I gave you milk to drink. And Peter writes to the faithful in the dispersion, who had been reborn: Not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, through the word of the living and abiding God, like newborn little children, that they might long for the rational milk and grow by it to salvation. To these sons John the evangelist too was writing: Little sons, keep yourselves from idols.

And I will bring them back, he says, from the land of Egypt, and from the Assyrians I will gather them. From the land of Egypt, in which King Pharaoh ruled, who once said boastfully: The rivers are mine, and I made them. And from the land of Asshur, which the king of Assyria held, the great mind, who himself also said: Above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High. And when the Lord has gathered the nations from the darkness of Egypt, and from the tribulation of the world, and from the power of the Assyrian, who is interpreted 'reproving and convicting', for he is the enemy and the avenger, he will lead them into the land of Gilead and of Lebanon. Gilead, turned into our language, is 'the testimony of migration', when we pass over from carnal things to spiritual, come from the part to the whole, leave earthly things behind and migrate to the heavenly. And Lebanon is interpreted λευκασμὸς, that is, whitening. So we are led out of the darkness of Egypt so that, after we have passed over and migrated out of the world, we may be made white in the Lord, and it may be said of us: Who is this who comes up made white? Others, following an ambiguity of the Greek tongue, by which both the mountain of Phoenicia and frankincense are called Libanus, here interpret Lebanon as frankincense, and think that God is signified by the frankincense, so that, after we have passed over from earth to heaven, the Savior's prayer may be fulfilled in us: Father, grant them that they may be one in us, as I and you are one. Hence the bride too says to the bridegroom in the Song: The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon. And when he has led us into the land of Gilead and of Lebanon, room shall not be found for us, so that we shall in no way be confined by the narrow bounds of the earth, but shall enjoy the breadth of the heavens.

And he shall pass through the strait of the sea, and shall strike the waves in the sea; and all the depths of the river shall be confounded, and the pride of Asshur shall be humbled, and the scepter of Egypt shall depart. I will strengthen them in the Lord, and in his name they shall walk, says the Lord. LXX: And they shall pass through in the narrow sea, and they shall strike the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the rivers shall be dried up; and all the injury of the Assyrians shall be taken away, and the scepter of Egypt shall be removed. And I will strengthen them in the Lord their God, and in his name they shall glory, says the Lord. The Hebrews relate that the captive people of the Jews was carried off by the Assyrians and Chaldeans not only to the Medes and Persians, but also to the Bosporus and the northern region, and that afterwards they were in part called back, as the mercy of God turned them to himself, and that this is what is now said: They shall pass through in the narrow sea: the narrows of the Propontis, which divide Chalcedon and what was once Byzantium by a short strait. And the Lord, he says, going before his people, shall strike the waves of the sea, and all the depths of the rivers shall be confounded, as was done of old when the Jordan was dried up and the people crossed the Red Sea in the desert. And when it has been freed from the depth of captivity, from the bitterness of evils, Asshur shall be humbled, and the dominion of Egypt shall depart from them. And they shall be strengthened in the Lord, and in his name they shall walk in the land of Israel, says the Lord. These things, as they were handed down to us by the Hebrews, we have set out for the men of our own tongue, referring the trustworthiness of what is said to those by whom it was said.

And when they have passed through the strait of the sea, and have trodden its waves under their foot, all the depths of the river shall be confounded, of which it is written: He who turns the sea into dry land; they shall pass through the river on foot; so that the pride, or the injury, of Asshur may be humbled, and the dominion of Egypt may depart from the saints and believers, and those who have been freed may be strengthened in the Lord and say: My strength and my praise is the Lord, and again: I will love you, O Lord, my strength, and with Jeremiah: My strength and my help and my refuge, O Lord my God.

For the rest, we who are reckoned by the name of Christ leave behind the letter that kills and follow the spirit that gives life, or rather, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, we look not for the Bosporus, and the drying of the sea once more, and the dry streams of the Jordan, which are like fables, but for the worthy mercy of God toward his servants, by which, as he goes before and opens the way for us, we pass through the strait of the sea, or the narrow sea, which for sinners is very broad: For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, strait and narrow the way that leads to life. Of this sea we also read in the psalms: They who go down to the sea in ships, doing business in many waters, they have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep. Into this sea of the world, in which the number of the saints is hemmed in and set in tribulation, the apostles went down, and first of all the Lord, that he might free us from the bitter waves. Into this sea is cast the dragnet of the gospel, which is woven of the testimonies of the Scriptures, so that it may draw out into the free air many fish overwhelmed by the whirlpools of this world, that they may be able to sing praises to God. These are they who have gone down to the sea, and in the ships of the churches do many works, and behold the wonders of God in the depth of the riches of his wisdom and knowledge, and in the Holy Spirit, who searches even the deep things of God; to whom the Lord says: Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men. Of these fishers, who go down to the sea and are in ships, Isaiah too prophesies: They shall fly in the ships of foreigners, and together they shall plunder the sea. For in the churches gathered from the number of the nations the apostles flew through the whole world, to plunder the sea and to carry off the spoils of the dragon who reigned in the sea, and of whom it is written: This sea, great and spacious in its arms; there are creeping things without number, small creatures with great. There the ships shall pass through; this dragon whom you formed to mock him. The sea is broad and spacious for the small and great living creatures that dwell with the dragon, and whose number is beyond count. But they who are upon the sea, and fly upon the sea itself in ships, shall hear, together with the Savior: You rule the power of the sea; you calm the motion of its waves.

Hence the Apostle too, in whom Christ was speaking, said: I can do all things in him who strengthens me; and not only shall they be strengthened in the Lord, but they shall also glory in him and say: But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world, and: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord, and in another place: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: to understand and know the Lord, and to do mercy and judgment in the midst of the earth. But since in the Hebrew it is written: And in his name they shall walk, it is to be understood thus: that Christians walk in the name of Christ, and a new name is written on their pebbles, and under the dignity of so great a name they walk with the Lord, as Enoch walked, and pleased God, and was translated.
11:
And when did Jerusalem after its siege by the Babylonians undergo a second burning, and have its Temple thrown to the ground?

And the figure used by the prophet is also exceedingly strange when he says, "O Libanus, open thy gates, and let fire devour thy cedars." For he calls the Temple here, as was not unusual, by the name of Libanus (it is so called in other prophecies). To this the Jews themselves now assent, since Isaiah, too, has a similar prophecy to the one before us, namely:

"Behold, the Lord of Sabaoth shall disturb the noble with might, and the lofty shall be crushed in their pride." And Libanus shall fall with its lofty ones, and there shall come forth a rod from the stem of Jesse, and a flower shall spring up from his roots, and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him."

To which he adds:

"And there shall be a root of Jesse, and he that shall rise to rule the Gentiles, in him shall the Gentiles trust."

Here, too, the destruction of Libanus and the call of the Gentiles is connected with the birth of Christ, of the seed of Jesse and David. And Ezekiel actually calls Jerusalem Libanus when he says, "The great eagle, with great wings, that hath the dominion, cometh to Libanus, and tore off the tender boughs of the cedar." And he goes on to explain this himself, as happening when Nebuchadnezzar shall come to Jerusalem and take her rulers, and that which follows. But Ezekiel's prophecy is about the first siege, and Zechariah's about the second. When, then, after the time of Zechariah in the time of the Macedonian Empire was the Temple burnt? There was no such time. For after its burning by the Babylonians, it was not burned again till in the time of Titus and Vespasian, the Roman Emperors, it was utterly destroyed by fire, and it is in relation to this that the prophet summons the ancient rulers of the nation in a figure to mourn and weep, when he says: "Let the pine weep because the cedar is fallen, because the great ones are in great misery. Let the oaks of Bashan weep, because the wood that is planted is torn down: a voice of shepherds that lament, because their greatness is in misery."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 4

Some, not understanding this place, refer Lebanon and the fir trees and pines and the oaks of Bashan, and the wooded or fortified forest, to the opposing powers, of which it is also said in Ezekiel, under the name of Asshur and of Pharaoh: Behold, Asshur was a cypress on Lebanon, fair in its branches, and thick with shade, and lofty in its height, and its top was among the clouds; water nourished it, the abyss raised it on high, and the rest, which are said both of Asshur and of Pharaoh, and they think these are said either of the opposing powers, or of all the proud and the princes, of whom we also read in the psalm: The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars, and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and in another place: The day of the Lord Sabaoth upon everyone who is insolent and proud, and upon everyone who is lofty and exalted, and a little after: And upon every cedar of Lebanon that is lofty, and upon every oak tree of Bashan. And of this Lebanon, they assert, it is prophesied: Lebanon shall fall with its lofty ones. But let us follow the former interpretation, especially since what follows also agrees with this sense.

Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Howl, O fir tree, for the cedar has fallen, because the magnificent have been laid waste. Howl, O oaks of Bashan, because the fortified forest has been cut down. LXX: Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Let the pine howl, for the cedar has fallen, for the nobles have been crushed. Howl, O oaks of Bashanitis, because the wooded forest has been brought down. Plainly Lebanon, to which the prophetic word turns, saying: Open your gates, O Lebanon, is understood as the temple of the Jews, which, restored, or rather built, by Zerubbabel, is sung as destined to be overthrown again by Vespasian and Titus. And because he had called the temple Lebanon μεταφορικῶς (metaphorically), he keeps the figure in the rest as well, so that by the cedars and fir trees and oaks of Bashan and the wooded forest he signifies the princes and priests and people of the Jews. And Lebanon opens its gates so that the Roman army may enter, and fire devours its cedars, so that either all things are laid waste by burning, or the leaders and princes are consumed by the onslaught of the enemy.

The fir trees howl because the cedar has fallen, the princes and priests mourning one another in their own devastation. And what he said obscurely before, he now sets out more plainly: Because the magnificent have been laid waste. I want to know what are the cedars of Lebanon that were burned, what are the fir trees to which howling is enjoined, what is the pine that has fallen; the magnificent, he says, have been laid waste. Howl, O oaks of Bashan, that is, of confusion and ignominy, because the most fortified forest, which in Hebrew is called besor, and was translated by the LXX as wooded, has been cut down; because the temple, which had grown up in impregnable strength, and had been built by various kings and princes, and afterwards by Herod, was destroyed when the Roman attacked it.

The voice of the howling of the shepherds, because their magnificence is laid waste; the voice of the roaring of lions, because the pride of the Jordan is laid waste. LXX: The voice of shepherds mourning, since their magnificence has been made wretched. The voice of lions roaring, because the roaring of the Jordan is afflicted. Part of the preceding passage is contained in these little verses too. Those whom he had called cedars, firs, pines and oaks of Bashan — and, explaining what these trees were, he had added, saying: Since the magnificent are laid waste — he now, by another μεταφορὰν (metaphor), says are shepherds, that is, princes and teachers; and those who were first among the people, he says, ought to weep and mourn, because their magnificence and beauty and glory has been laid waste and consumed, namely the temple, in which they gloried. And the voice, he says, of the roaring of lions: those whom he calls lofty trees, and again shepherds, the same he now calls lions. And because he had said lions, he keeps the metaphor, so as to add: Since the pride of the Jordan is laid waste, or the roaring and sound of the water running down, which in Hebrew is called gaon. And just as, according to the lie of the land of Judea, he compared the height of the temple to the height of Lebanon — for nothing in the land of promise is loftier than Lebanon, nor more wooded and dense —, so to the river Jordan, which is the greatest in Judea, and near which lions dwell, he joined the roaring of lions, on account of the burning of their thirst; and on account of the nearness of the desert and the breadth of the vast wilderness, and the reed-beds and sedge-beds. Hence it is also said through the prophet: The lion has come up from the Jordan, meaning to show that Nebuchadnezzar went out from his seat, like a lion from its lair, against Jerusalem. Another way: The voice of the roaring of lions, since the pride of the Jordan is laid waste. The voice, he says, of the nobles, because the temple has been destroyed, from which they always hoped for help, and which once nourished just, warlike and mighty lions.

And, as if already, so to speak, they had fallen into ruin and destruction, and were wailing and weeping on this account, the prophet hoard, he says, "the voice of shepherds wailing, because their might was brought low: the voice of lions roaring, because the pride of Jordan was spoiled." He calls the lions the pride of Jordan, by whom wore figured the chiefs of the Jewish synagogue: who, in just requital of their wickedness against Christ, wailed with their fathers and children, being consumed as with fire and sword, while the temple at Jerusalem was also burnt, and the cities throughout all Judaea abandoned to utter desolation.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

Thus says the Lord my God: Feed the cattle of slaughter, which those who had possessed them were killing, and were not grieving; and they were selling them, saying: Blessed be the Lord, we have become rich; and their shepherds were not sparing them. LXX: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Feed the sheep of slaughter, which those who possessed them were killing, and they did not repent; and those who were selling them were saying: Blessed be the Lord, and we have become rich; and their shepherds suffered nothing over them. Where the prophecy is most manifest, and through the metaphor the true order of the history is narrated, the interpretation of tropology is superfluous: that we should say that some shepherds are good and others bad, and refer this as much to the old people as to the new, that is, as much to the priests and princes of the Jews as to the bishops and presbyters of the Christians; and that whatever shepherds have been negligent and have scandalized one of the least, they are the ones who feed the cattle of slaughter, and suffer nothing over them, nor grieve, nor can say with the Apostle: Who is scandalized, and I do not burn? And that they sell the peoples entrusted to them, of whom it is written: Who devour my people as a meal of bread; and gain riches from the deaths of others, praising those who take plunder from the wretched, and blessing the wicked. Let others interpret these things as they will: let us keep the order of explanation which we once took up. Since Lebanon has been opened, and its cedars and firs have been consumed by burning flame, and the howling of the shepherds has been heard, and the roaring of the lions, because all the beauty and pride of the Jordan has been laid waste and consumed, therefore the Lord my God said these things to me: O prophet Zechariah, this word is addressed to you: Feed the flock of slaughter, that is, let it be nourished meanwhile for now and grow, which afterwards is to be slaughtered by enemies; which sheep and cattle the princes of the Romans, who possessed them and held them by right of victory, were killing and not pitying, or else were sacrificing; and they did not feel grief, that is, they suffered no harm for so great a cruelty; and they were selling those whom they kept not out of clemency but for the price. Let us read the old histories, and the traditions of the lamenting Jews, how at the Tent of Abraham — where now a most crowded market is held every year —, after the last overthrow, which they suffered under Hadrian, many thousands of men were sold; and those who could not be sold were carried over into Egypt, cut down as much by shipwreck and famine as by the slaughter of the nations. These victors, then, and avengers of the Lord, who were killing and not grieving, and were selling the cattle and saying: Blessed be the Lord, we have become rich, held this opinion: The Jews offended because of their sins, therefore we have crushed them, and from their price we have become rich. And no wonder, he says, if the enemies by the right of victors were killing the cattle and not grieving, were selling them and glorying in their crime; since their own shepherds and teachers did not spare them, and by their fault the flock was handed over to wolves.

Whenever I remember Zechariah, I shudder at the reaping hook and likewise at his testimony against the priests, his hints in reference to the celebrated Joshua, the high priest, whom he represents as stripped of filthy garments and then clothed in rich priestly apparel. As for words and charges to Joshua which he puts into the angel's mouth, let them be treated with silent respect, as referring perhaps to a greater and higher object than those who are many priests. But even at his right hand stood the devil, to resist him, a fact, in my eyes, of no slight significance and demanding no slight fear and watchfulness. Who is so bold and adamant of soul as not to tremble and be abashed at the charges and reproaches deliberately urged against the rest of the shepherds? A voice, he says, of the howling of the shepherds. A voice of the roaring lions, for this has befallen them. Does he not all but hear the wailing as if close at hand, and himself wail with the afflicted. A little further is a more striking and impassioned strain. Feed, he says, the flock of slaughter, whose possessors slay them without repentance. They sell them saying, "Blessed be the Lord, for we are rich," yet their own shepherds are without feeling for them. Therefore I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord almighty. And again: "Awake, O sword, against the shepherds, and smite the shepherds, and scatter the sheep, and I will turn my hand upon the shepherds"; and, "My anger is kindled against the shepherds, and I will visit the lambs," adding to the threat those who rule over the people. So industriously does he apply himself to his task that he cannot easily free himself from denunciations, and I am afraid that if I referred to the whole series, I should exhaust your patience. This must then suffice for Zechariah.
IN DEFENSE OF HIS FLIGHT TO PONTUS, ORATION 2:62-64

Because, then, their shepherds were not sparing them, and they themselves were the first to devour my people, therefore I too will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land of Judea, says the Lord. For he speaks of this land, of which his discourse was, and not of the whole world, as the Jews, interpreting badly, wish to twist God's sentence away from themselves in another direction. For after the overthrow of the temple — which befell them for this reason, that for forty-two years after the Lord suffered, though granted a space of time, they would not repent —, I will let loose, he says, each one against his neighbor; and they will cut one another down in mutual slaughter, or else in the very siege of the temple, when the Roman army shall surround Jerusalem; for there will be such wars and discords among the Jews themselves that the people will be divided into three parts. Let us read Josephus and the seven books of the Jewish Captivity, and we shall see by the truth of history that this prophecy has been fulfilled. And they shall cut down, he says, the land: there is no doubt that the Romans destroyed all the land and all the cities of the Jews. And I will not rescue them from their hand. Hear, O Jew, you who promise yourself the vainest hopes, and do not hear the Lord saying and affirming: I will not rescue from their hands, that your captivity among the Romans is to be eternal.

But if the price of Him that was valued, there cast down rendered the House profane, it is natural for Him to proceed to say, "And I cast the second rod, the Rope, to break the covenant between Judah and Israel."

For from that day the multitude of the nation was cut away from God's ancient providential guardianship. And I suppose the second rod to mean the whole Jewish nation. It is therefore called a Rope in the words, "The one I called Beauty, and the other I called a Rope." And he proceeds to speak clearly of the second: "And I cast away the second rod, the Rope, to break my covenant between Judah and Israel." For they were the Rope and the second rod. But the first rod, called Beauty, was Jerusalem itself, and the Mosaic Worship, and the whole of the old covenant. This is shewn by the prophecy, saying, "And I will take my rod of beauty, and I will cast it away, to break my covenant." You sec that it says that the first rod was the Covenant, and the second rod the Rope, but He threatens to cast them both away, first saying, "And I will take for myself two rods, the one I called Beauty, and the other I called a Rope"; or with Symmachus, "The one I called glory, and the other I called a Rope." For thus he rightly styled the glory and beauty of the whole nation the divine Law, and the Covenant, which it included. For the solemnities of Jerusalem, and the high-priestly ritual, and all the ancient observances of the divine Law and old Covenant, were a fair glory to them that lived under their order. And the multitude of the nation is called a Rope by Moses, when he says: "The portion of the Lord is His people Jacob, and Israel is the Rope of His inheritance."

But here it is prophesied that there will be a complete change of the two rods at the time named, so that the ancient Covenant that was therein of old, and its ancient beauty being destroyed, and the Rope and the whole nation broken through, when they had valued for thirty pieces of silver Him that was valued, they should bear the fit dishonour for their impiety. It therefore says, "And I will take my rod of Beauty, and cast it away, and break my covenant." And also, "And I cast away the second rod, the Rope." And when the prophecy goes on to say, "And I will take away three shepherds in one month," I think that it refers to the three divisions of the ancient leaders of the people of God—the King, the Prophet, and the High-Priest—for by those three shepherds all the affairs of the ancients were managed. But since those three offices were destroyed together in our Saviour's time—(for their king reigned not in accordance with the Law, being a foreigner and not a member of the Jewish race; their high-priest was appointed to his office by the Romans, and did not attain his rank by the order of succession of the tribe, nor according to lawful custom; and their prophets that had ceased until John arose were no longer active among them, but they had instead a wicked false prophet who led the people astray)— He rightly threatens that He will take away at one time the three offices of grace, that had of old adorned the whole nation with wondrous glory, and says, "And I will take away three shepherds in one month, and my heart shall be sorrowful for them." For which Aquila renders, "And my soul was torn asunder for them," Symmachus, "And my soul perished for them," and Theodotion, "And my soul perished about them." And he gives the reason of the perishing of his soul, saying, "For their souls were hardened to me." Instead of this Aquila has, "For their soul was strong in me"; and Symmachus, "And their soul reached its height in me." And a similar expression to the words, "Their souls are hardened to me," of the Septuagint, is found in Jeremiah as spoken by the Lord, namely:

"I have left my home, I have forsaken my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hand of its enemies. My inheritance has become to me as a lion in a forest, it has opened on me its voice. Is not my beloved now to me as a hyaena's cave? "

And then He naturally goes on to say:

"I will not shepherd you, that which is dying may die, that which is failing may fail, and let the remnant eat each one the flesh of his neighbour."

And after this He says, "I will take my rod of beauty and cast it away." For which Aquila renders: "And I took my rod, the Glory, and cut it off," meaning the Mosaic Worship. Thus the first rod mentioned in the beginning of the passage is said to be the first to be broken and cast away. But when the price of Him that was valued and the money paid for Him to the traitor was cast into the House of the Lord as into a furnace, then we see what is prophesied will happen to the second rod, that is to say to the whole nation in the words, "And I cast away the second rod, the Rope, to break my covenant between Judah and Israel."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 4
