And I took for myself two staffs: one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cords; and I fed the flock.

And I cut off three shepherds in one month, and my soul was straitened over them, since their soul also varied against me. And I said: I will not feed you; what dies, let it die, and what is cut off, let it be cut off, and let the rest devour each one the flesh of his neighbor. LXX: And I will take for myself two staffs: one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord; and I will feed the sheep. And I will take away three shepherds in one month, and my soul will grow heavy upon them, since their souls also were roaring against me. And I said: I will not feed them; what dies, let it die, and what fails, let it fail, and let the rest devour each one the flesh of his neighbor. Above he had said: For this, O poor of the flock; and, a break being made by ἀποσιωπήσει (by aposiopesis), there was understood: Give heed, because the gates of Lebanon are opened, and the oaks of Bashan, the firs and the cedars are cut down; and he had added, threatening: I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord. And he seemed to say this of the Jewish people alone, because, having killed the prophets, they had also laid hands on the Son of God, and with rash voice had cried out: His blood be upon us, and upon our children. Now the Creator and Lord of the universe sets forth the mysteries of his world, and says that he had two staffs, one of which he called Beauty, the other Cords, and that with the two staffs he fed the flock bound together; and also that he cut off three shepherds in one month, and that his soul was straitened, or indignant, or — as the Seventy translated —, my soul will grow heavy upon them; there is no doubt that he means the shepherds whom he cut off in one month. And he gives the reason why he was so indignant with the shepherds as to cut them off in one month: Since their soul also, he says, varied against me. And the sense is: They did not love me with a full heart, nor did the hireling shepherds love the true shepherd: For the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep. Wherefore I too, in indignation, pronounced sentence, and to those very shepherds whom I had cut off in my indignation, or else, the shepherds being cut off, to the flock left behind, I said: I will not feed you; but what has chosen death, let it die by its own will, and let them devour one another and tear one another apart in mutual slaughter. We have said this παραφραστικῶς (by paraphrase), to pave the path for the explanation to come.

And I will no longer spare those who dwell on the land, says the Lord. Behold, I will deliver men, each one into the hand of his neighbor, and into the hand of his king; and they shall cut down the land, and I will not rescue from their hand; and I will feed the cattle of slaughter for this, O poor of the flock. LXX: Therefore I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord. And behold, I will deliver men, each one into the hands of his neighbor, and into the hand of his kings; and they shall cut down the land, and I will not rescue from their hand, and I will feed the sheep of slaughter in Canaanitis. What the LXX translated at the end of the passage: And I will feed the sheep of slaughter in the land of Canaan, is not in the Hebrew, and is translated by none of the other translators.

And I will feed the cattle of slaughter, so that the Jews may always be nourished for death; because this is the sentence of God: O you who are the poor of the flock, that is, the just of Israel, who have believed in the Lord Jesus and received the Son of God, hear what is said, and learn the mysteries of the following passage. But what we read according to the Seventy: And I will feed the sheep of slaughter in the land of Canaan, we can understand thus: that the Lord feeds the people of the Jews, which is destined for death and scattered through the whole world — that is, in the land of Canaan and of the Gentiles —, and nourishes it for sacrifice.

The Creator and shepherd, whose sheep know his voice and follow him, took for himself two staffs, or two σκυτάλας, that is, sticks, which in Hebrew are called macaloth, to show the bearing of a shepherd. One staff he called Beauty: that is, under Noah he protected the whole human race with his blessing, when, the world being restored, sins had not yet made it foul. And therefore the calling of all the nations is called beautiful and fair, because nothing is more just than that the parent of the universe should call all equally, whom he begot in equal condition. And the other he called Cords; for when the Most High was dividing the nations and scattering the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of the Lord. And his people Jacob became the portion of the Lord; Israel the cord of his inheritance. And I fed, he says, the flock: either Israel itself, or, together with Israel, the whole human race.

Some have understood the two callings as those of the Jews and of the Gentiles: by the first name Israel, and by the last the Christians. But how the Christian calling was cast away first, and the Jews remained and were fed by God, they did not sufficiently consider.

And when the prophecy goes on to say, "And I will take away three shepherds in one month," I think that it refers to the three divisions of the ancient leaders of the people of God—the King, the Prophet, and the High-Priest—for by those three shepherds all the affairs of the ancients were managed. But since those three offices were destroyed together in our Saviour's time—(for their king reigned not in accordance with the Law, being a foreigner and not a member of the Jewish race; their high-priest was appointed to his office by the Romans, and did not attain his rank by the order of succession of the tribe, nor according to lawful custom; and their prophets that had ceased until John arose were no longer active among them, but they had instead a wicked false prophet who led the people astray)— He rightly threatens that He will take away at one time the three offices of grace, that had of old adorned the whole nation with wondrous glory, and says, "And I will take away three shepherds in one month, and my heart shall be sorrowful for them." For which Aquila renders, "And my soul was torn asunder for them," Symmachus, "And my soul perished for them," and Theodotion, "And my soul perished about them." And he gives the reason of the perishing of his soul, saying, "For their souls were hardened to me." Instead of this Aquila has, "For their soul was strong in me"; and Symmachus, "And their soul reached its height in me." And a similar expression to the words, "Their souls are hardened to me," of the Septuagint, is found in Jeremiah as spoken by the Lord, namely:

"I have left my home, I have forsaken my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hand of its enemies. My inheritance has become to me as a lion in a forest, it has opened on me its voice. Is not my beloved now to me as a hyaena's cave? "
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 4

And I cut off, he says, three shepherds in one month. I have read in the commentaries of a certain writer that the shepherds cut off by the Lord's indignation are to be understood as the priests and false prophets and kings of the Jews; because after the passion of Christ all were cut off at one time, those of whom Jeremiah speaks: The priests did not say: Where is the Lord? Those who held my law did not know me. And the shepherds transgressed against me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal, and followed idols. Not content with this explanation, he wants the three shepherds cut off in one month to be taken as those who have sinned against the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; for all heretics sin either against one, or against two, or against three persons at once. Let him have said what he wished, for one must not detract from another's sense. To us the three shepherds who were cut off in one month seem to be Moses, and Aaron, and Miriam; of whom Miriam died in the first month, which is called Nisan, in the desert of Zin, and in the same place, on account of the water of contradiction, and in the same month, Moses and Aaron were condemned not to enter the land of promise. And so it came about that of the three shepherds, one was cut off by present death, the others by the sentence of a death to come. And my soul, he says, was straitened over them, namely over the three shepherds whom I had set over my flock. Because their soul also varied against me; for they did not glorify me at the water of contradiction. But if we refer it to the people, that the soul of the people varied against God, it must be explained thus: I was indignant with them for this reason, that they too, wavering between me and idols, fought against me in various ways.

Let us understand this according to the letter of Moses and Aaron. Moses indeed was led out, and Aaron, but not led into the land of promise. Jesus succeeded him. See what is written. Moses died in the desert, Aaron died, Miriam died; and this is what is written in the prophet: "And I will strike," it says, "three shepherds in one month." They died: for they could not enter into the land of promise. They only saw over against the land of promise, and could not enter.

O shepherds, disciples of the Lord, feed the flock and lead (it) well! Strengthen the sick, support the weak, bind up the broken, make whole the lame, and take heed to the fattened ones for the Lord of the flock. Be not likened unto an unskilled and foolish shepherd, who in his foolishness is not able to feed the flock, and whose arm is dried up, and whose eye has been blinded, because he said: "dying, let it die; and perishing, let it perish, and the flesh that is left shall be eaten by its companions ". And when the Chief of the shepherds comes He will condemn the unskilled and foolish shepherd who has not cared well for his fellow servants. And he who has shepherded the flock and led (it) well shall be called "a good and skillful servant" (cf. S. Mt. 25: 21), who has presented the flock to the Shepherd while it was intact.

O stupid and foolish pastor, to whose right hand and to whose right eye I committed my sheep. Because thou didst say concerning the sheep, let that which dieth, die, and let that which perisheth perish, and whatever is left, let them devour the flesh of one another; therefore, behold I will make blind thy right eye and I will wither up thy right arm. Thy eye which regarded a bribe shall be blinded, and thy hand which did not rule in righteousness shall waste away.

Wherefore in indignation I said to Moses: I will not feed you; let me alone and I will destroy them. But when, in anger, he says, let me alone, he invites entreaty, and shows that he can be held back by him. What dies, he says, let it die, and what is cut off, let it be cut off; let the bodies of all fall in the wilderness, and, turned to sedition, let them be torn by one another's bites like beasts, and let none enter the land of promise.

We find the God of the universe often giving rein to humanity because of the excess of its wickedness, and he allows the human race to be borne where it will. Of this he has warned us speaking through his prophet to Israel: "And I said, 'I will not tend you. That which dies, let it die, and that which perishes, let it perish; and for the rest let each devour the flesh of his neighbor.' " When wicked rulers are in control, and cruel, harsh masters rule households, then we should implore the one who directs the universe and, by conversion of life and a change in our ways, make supplication, rousing him to help us, fervently begging him to give us better times.

And I took my staff which was called Beauty, and I cut it off, to make void my covenant which I had struck with all peoples. And it was made void on that day, and thus the poor of the flock who keep watch for me knew that it is the word of the Lord. LXX: And I will take my fair staff, and I will cast it away, to scatter my testament which I disposed toward all peoples; and it shall be scattered on that day, and the Canaanites shall know, the sheep that are kept for me, that it is the word of the Lord. After the calling of Israel, and the taking up of the second staff, which was called Cord, the Lord took the first staff, the nations of the whole world, which were called beautiful, and cut them off from his worship, because they venerated idols, and all have turned aside, together they have become useless. And setting out more plainly what this staff was, he added: To make void my covenant which I had struck with all peoples. For as soon as Israel was taken up, the crowd of the nations was cast away; and as soon as the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was born — who later in the Gospel, when she was twelve years old, is related to have fallen sick and died —, the αἱμοῤῥοῦσα (the woman with a flow of blood) began to flow with blood and to be tormented by a perpetual infirmity.

And as the oracle intended clearly their destruction by this, it naturally goes on to say that they shall no longer recognize the power of things prophesied, but the Canaanites will, when He says, "And the Canaanites shall know, my sheep kept for me, because it is the Word of the Lord." Who are meant by the Canaanites but ourselves, who once were foreigners, and sheep kept for Christ from all the old heathen and sinful nations? We that have been converted by His grace, and understanding the things prophesied, have received the true knowledge of the word of the Lord; yea, we Canaanites know and understand what was meant; but they that boasted of Israel, and gloried in being of the seed of Abraham, neither knew nor understood.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 4

And it was made void, he says, my covenant which I had entered into with all the nations. And the poor of the flock understood, that is, the people Israel which keeps my commands, that it is the word of the Lord, that is, that it is the Lord's will to cast off the nations that deny, and in Abraham to take up Israel that confesses. For what we have translated: And thus the poor of the flock knew, the Seventy translated: And the Canaanites shall know, the sheep that are kept for me, which some expound thus: The people of the Jews shall know, to whom it was said: Seed of Canaan, and not of Judah, which is now kept by my ceremonies; or else, because Canaanites is interpreted 'ready for humiliation', those shall know who were once made ready to be humbled by the Lord and to be abandoned. But why, for what we have translated: Thus the poor, they said: Canaanites, the cause is manifest; for among the Hebrews 'thus' is called chen, 'poor' anie; they, joining the two words into one, for what is: Thus the poor, that is, chen anie, translated the name of the Canaanite nation.

Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,  Saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. And they said, What is that to us? see thou to that.  And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.  And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.  And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in.  Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day.  Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value;  And gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me. [Zechariah 11:12]

But since what the evangelist says after these things (then was fulfilled that which had been spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, saying the things which are written) — this is not found to have been prophesied by Jeremiah anywhere in his books, whether those which are read in the churches or those which are recited among the Jews — but if anyone can know, let him show where it is written. I suspect, however, that either it is an error of the Scripture and Jeremiah is put for Zechariah, or that there is some secret writing of Jeremiah in which it is written. Now such is the text in Zechariah the prophet: "and I will say to them: if it is good in your sight, give me my wages, or refuse them; and they appointed my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: put them down into the furnace, and see if it is genuine, even as I was proved for their sake. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and put them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace". But if anyone saying this supposes that he stumbles, let him see whether this may be prophesied somewhere in the secret writings of Jeremiah, knowing that the Apostle too brings forward certain writings of the secret books, as he says somewhere: "what eye has not seen nor ear heard"; for in no canonical book is this found set down, except in the secret writings of Elijah the prophet.

[Passage quoted, Zech. xi. 7b-14.]

THIS was fulfilled when, according to Luke:

"Judas went away, and spoke with the chief priests and scribes and captains of the Temple, that he might betray him unto them. And they were glad, and covenanted to give him money;"

or, according to Mark when, "he went to the chief priests to betray him; and they were glad and promised to give him money." In each case it is simply money that is named. But in Matthew the amount is recorded, and it agrees with the quotation from Zechariah. For Matthew says:

"Then went one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, to the chief priests, and said to them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? and they weighed unto him thirty staters."

And this agrees with, "And they weighed my price thirty pieces of silver," spoken by the Lord in the prophecy.

And there is added to this, "And the Lord said to me, Drop them into the furnace, and see if it is good metal, as I was tested by them." For which Aquila renders: "And the Lord said to me, Drop them into the furnace, cast them to the potter: very great is the price, at which I was valued by them."

And notice how the Lord Himself confesses that a sum of thirty pieces of silver was given for Him. The meaning of His words implies something like this: I the Lord from the very first day ceased not to give to you Jews proofs of My kindness, and in countless ways I did you good, not only through the earliest prophets, but also by My presence in moral teaching and spiritual education, in signs and wonders, and other miracles, and in cures and attentions: now you that were privileged to receive such benefits, give My price or refuse it, demanding of them, it would seem, the fruits of holiness, and the proof of their faith in Him. But they, as the preceding quotation tells, instead of loving Me spoke evil of Me, and laid evil on Me instead of good, and hatred instead of My love, weighing out thirty pieces of silver, as if they valued at that price Him that was sold. But since the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is, He rightly bids them cast it into the furnace, adding, "As I was tested by them." Perhaps the House of God is here called a Furnace. For the Lord says, according to the Septuagint, "Cast them into the Furnace," and adds, "And they cast them into the Furnace, the House of God"; while according to Aquila the Lord says, "Cast it, that is the money, to the potter," and adds, "And I cast it in the House of the Lord to the potter." According to Symmachus, the Lord says, "Cast it into the furnace," and adds, "I cast it into the House of the Lord, into the Furnace." And was not this fulfilled when Judas—

"3. that betrayed the Lord, seeing that he was condemned, repented and returned the money to the chief priests and elders, saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood? 4. And they said to him, What is that to us? see thou to that. 5. And he cast down the money in the Temple and went and hanged himself. 6. And the chief priests took the money and said, It is not lawful to put them in the treasury, for it is the price of blood. 7. And they took counsel, and bought with them the potters' field to bury strangers in: 8. Wherefore that field is called the field of blood unto this day. 9. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value, 10. and gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me."

But as this passage is not found in the prophecy of Jeremiah, you must consider whether it is to be supposed that they have been removed through any evil intention, or whether there has been an error in copying, through the mistake of some careless transcriber of the Holy Gospels, who wrote Jeremiah instead of Zechariah, where he ought to have copied, "Then was fulfilled that which was written by Zechariah the prophet," and instead of, "And they cast them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace," wrote in error, "And they bought with them the field of the potter." For the prophecy explicitly states that the money was cast into the Temple of the Lord, so does the Gospel: for, "Judas," it says, "cast the money into the Temple, and departed." And perhaps it was through this money that the Temple was rendered profane, and the words, "Behold, your house is left unto you desolate," were fulfilled. And you may well ask whether the House of God was called a Furnace, because it is there that the souls of men are fashioned as in a crucible by the fire of divine teaching, or convicted of impurity, as if they were fired and tried in a furnace. Hence Aquila says, "I cast the money in the house of the Lord to the potter," clearly teaching that the Divine Word dwells like a potter in the House of the Lord, and moulds and renews the souls of them that enter.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 4

Hear now in regard to thirty pieces of silver: "And I will say to them, 'If it seems good to you, give me my wages, or refuse.' " One recompense is due me for curing the blind and the lame, and I receive another; instead of thanksgiving, dishonor, and instead of worship, insult. Do you see how Scripture foresaw all this? "And they counted out my wages, thirty pieces of silver." O prophetic accuracy! A great and unerring wisdom of the Holy Spirit! For he did not say ten or twenty but thirty, exactly the right amount. Tell also what happened to this payment, O prophet! Does he who received it keep it, or does he give it back? And after its return what becomes of it? The prophet says, "So I took thirty pieces of silver, and I cast them into the house of the Lord, into the foundry." Compare with the prophecy of the Gospel, which says, "Judas repented and flung the pieces of silver into the temple and withdrew."

You observe that he was appraised by the traitor's covetousness at thirty pieces of silver. Of this also the prophet speaks, "And I said to them, If you think good, give me my price, or if not, forbear"; and "presently, I received from them," he says, "thirty pieces of silver, and I cast them into the house of the Lord, into the foundry." Is not this what is written in the Gospels, that Judas, "repenting of what he had done, brought back the money, and threw it down in the temple and departed"? Well did he call it his price, as though blaming and upbraiding. For he had done so many good works among them, he had given sight to the blind, feet to the lame, the power of walking to the palsied, life also to the dead; for all these good works they paid him death as his price, appraised at thirty pieces of silver. It is related also in the Gospels that he was bound. This also the word of prophecy had foretold by Isaiah, saying, "Woe to their soul, who have devised a most evil device against themselves, saying, 'Let us bind the just one, seeing that he is unprofitable to us.' "

The Jews, interpreting this place maliciously, relate the thirty pieces of silver to thirty commands of the law which they are ordered to do in the law, and again thirty-six others which are forbidden in the law; and they say that they are told to return the silver of the Lord's commands to their modeller and moulder, God, and that because they would not do it, they were cast away. I wished to indicate briefly what they think; otherwise it is wearisome to unroll their most long-winded explanation, so that we may pass on to the rest.

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one valued, whom they valued from the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed for me. This testimony is not found in Jeremiah; but in Zechariah, who is almost the last of the twelve prophets, a certain likeness is reported, and although the sense does not differ much, yet both the order and the words are different. I read recently, in a certain Hebrew volume which a Hebrew of the Nazarene sect brought to me, an apocryphal Jeremiah, in which I found these things written word for word. But still it seems to me that the testimony is rather taken from Zechariah, in the common manner of the evangelists and apostles, who, passing over the order of the words, bring forward only the sense from the Old Testament as an example.

And I said to them: If it is good in your eyes, bring my wage, and if not, be still; and they weighed out my wage, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: Cast them to the statuary, the fine price at which I was priced by them; and I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them into the house of the Lord to the statuary. LXX: And I will say to them: If it is good in your sight, give, setting my wage, or refuse. And they set my wage, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: Put them down into the furnace, and consider whether it is tested, as I was tested for them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and put them into the house of the Lord into the furnace. Since the poor of the Israelite flock, who keep my commands, knew that what I spoke was the word of the Lord, and that what I said was true — what I said, that is, to the poor of the flock: If it pleases you; for you are men, and once for all I created you with free will, you to whom I also spoke in the desert: If you hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land; in return for this taking up, by which I cast off the whole human race and chose you for myself as a flock of my own, and, the Creator of all, willed to have a small cord, give me back my wage, that is, keep my precepts. But if you do not wish to pay the wage, and it does not please you in your eyes to be reckoned by my name, refuse openly, and do what you will. And they then indeed answered Moses: All things whatsoever the Lord says, we will do. But at the end of the times, in return for my having chosen them from the midst of the nations, and freed them from the iron furnace of Egypt, they weighed out my wage, thirty pieces of silver, giving them to Judas the traitor for my blood.

And thus it is that Matthew here relates what took place between Pilate and the Lord.

First, however, he makes a digression with the purpose of telling the story of Judas' end, which is related only by him. His account is in these terms: "Then Judas, which had betrayed Him, when he saw that He was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, I have sinned, in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. And they said, What is that to us? See thou to that. And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself. And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in. Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of Him that was valued, whom the children of Israel did value, and gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me."

Now, if any one finds a difficulty in the circumstance that this passage is not found in the writings of the prophet Jeremiah, and thinks that damage is thus done to the veracity of the evangelist, let him first take notice of the fact that this ascription of the passage to Jeremiah is not contained in all the codices of the Gospels, and that some of them state simply that it was spoken "by the prophet." It is possible, therefore, to affirm that those codices deserve rather to be followed which do not contain the name of Jeremiah. For these words were certainly spoken by a prophet, only that prophet was Zechariah. In this way the supposition is, that those codices are faulty which contain the name of Jeremiah, because they ought either to have given the name of Zechariah or to have mentioned no name at all, as is the case with a certain copy, merely stating that it was spoken "by the prophet, saying," which prophet would assuredly be understood to be Zechariah. However, let others adopt this method of defence, if they are so minded. For my part, I am not satisfied with it; and the reason is, that a majority of codices contain the name of Jeremiah, and that those critics who have studied the Gospel with more than usual care in the Greek copies, report that they have found it stand so in the more ancient Greek exemplars. I look also to this further consideration, namely, that there was no reason why this name should have been added [subsequently to the true text], and a corruption thus created; whereas there was certainly an intelligible reason for erasing the name from so many of the codices. For venturesome inexperience might readily have done that, when perplexed with the problem presented by the fact that this passage could not be found in Jeremiah.

How, then, is the matter to be explained, but by supposing that this has been done in accordance with the more secret counsel of that providence of God by which the minds of the evangelists were governed? For it may have been the case, that when Matthew was engaged in composing his Gospel, the word Jeremiah occurred to his mind, in accordance with a familiar experience, instead of Zechariah. Such an inaccuracy, however, he would most undoubtedly have corrected (having his attention called to it, as surely would have been the case, by some who might have read it while he was still alive in the flesh), had he not reflected that [perhaps] it was not without a purpose that the name of the one prophet had been suggested instead of the other in the process of recalling the circumstances (which process of recollection was also directed by the Holy Spirit), and that this might not have occurred to him had it not been the Lord's purpose to have it so written. If it is asked, however, why the Lord should have so determined it, there is this first and most serviceable reason, which deserves our most immediate consideration, namely, that some idea was thus conveyed of the marvellous manner in which all the holy prophets, speaking in one spirit, continued in perfect unison with each other in their utterances,—a circumstance certainly much more calculated to impress the mind than would have been the case had all the words of all these prophets been spoken by the mouth of a single individual. The same consideration might also fitly suggest the duty of accepting unhesitatingly whatever the Holy Spirit has given expression to through the agency of these prophets, and of looking upon their individual communications as also those of the whole body, and on their collective communications as also those of each separately. If, then, it is the case that words spoken by Jeremiah are really as much Zechariah's as Jeremiah's, and, on the other hand, that words spoken by Zechariah are really as much Jeremiah's as they are Zechariah's, what necessity was there for Matthew to correct his text when he read over what he had written, and found that the one name had occurred to him instead of the other? Was it not rather the proper course for him to bow to the authority of the Holy Spirit, under whose guidance he certainly felt his mind to be placed in a more decided sense than is the case with us, and consequently to leave untouched what he had thus written, in accordance with the Lord's counsel and appointment, with the intent to give us to understand that the prophets maintain so complete a harmony with each other in the matter of their utterances that it becomes nothing absurd, but, in fact, a most consistent thing for us to credit Jeremiah with a sentence originally spoken by Zechariah? For if, in these days of ours, a person, desiring to bring under our notice the words of a certain individual, happens to mention the name of another by whom the words were not actually uttered, but who at the same time is the most intimate friend and associate of the man by whom they were really spoken; and if forthwith recollecting that he has given the one name instead of the other, he recovers himself and corrects the mistake, but does it nevertheless in some such way as this, "After all, what I said was not amiss;" what would we take to be meant by this, but just that there subsists so perfect a unison of sentiment between the two parties—that is to say, the man whose words the individual in question intended to repeat, and the second person whose name occurred to him at the time instead of that of the other—that it comes much to the same thing to represent the words to have been spoken by the former as to say that they were uttered by the latter? How much more, then, is this a usage which might well be understood and most particularly commended to our attention in the case of the holy prophets, so that we might accept the books composed by the whole series of them, as if they formed but a single book written by one author, in which no discrepancy with regard to the subjects dealt with should be supposed to exist, as none would be found, and in which there would be a more remarkable example of consistency and veracity than would have been the case had a single individual, even the most learned, been the enunciator of all these sayings? Therefore, while there are those, whether unbelievers or merely ignorant men, who endeavour to find an argument here to help them in demonstrating a want of harmony between the holy evangelists, men of faith and learning, on the other hand, ought rather to bring this into the service of proving the unity which characterizes the holy prophets.

I have also another reason (the fuller discussion of which must be reserved, I think, for another opportunity, in order to prevent the present discourse from extending to larger limits than may be allowed by the necessity which rests upon us to bring this work to a conclusion) to offer in explanation of the fact that the name of Jeremiah has been permitted, or rather directed, by the authority of the Holy Spirit, to stand in this passage instead of that of Zechariah. It is stated in Jeremiah that he bought a field from the son of his brother, and paid him money for it. That sum of money is not given, indeed, under the name of the particular price which is found in Zechariah, namely, thirty pieces of silver; but, on the other hand, there is no mention of the buying of the field in Zechariah. Now, it is evident that the evangelist has interpreted the prophecy which speaks of the thirty pieces of silver as something which has received its fulfilment only in the Lord's case, so that it is made to stand for the price set upon Him. But again, that the words which were uttered by Jeremiah on the subject of the purchase of the field have also a bearing upon the same matter, may have been mystically signified by the selection thus made in introducing [into the evangelical narrative] the name of Jeremiah, who spoke of the purchase of the field, instead of that of Zechariah, to whom we are indebted for the notice of the thirty pieces of silver. In this way, on perusing first the Gospel, and finding the name of Jeremiah there, and then, again, on perusing Jeremiah, and failing there to discover the passage about the thirty pieces of silver, but seeing at the same time the section about the purchase of the field, the reader would be taught to compare the two paragraphs together, and get at the real meaning of the prophecy, and learn how it also stands in relation to this fulfilment of prophecy which was exhibited in the instance of our Lord. For [it is also to be remarked that] Matthew makes the following addition to the passage cited, namely, "Whom the children of Israel did value; and gave them the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me." Now, these words are not to be found either in Zechariah or in Jeremiah. Hence we must rather take them to have been inserted with a nice and mystical meaning by the evangelist, on his own responsibility,—the Lord having given him to understand, by revelation, that a prophecy of the said tenor had a real reference to this occurrence, which took place in connection with the price set upon Christ. Moreover, in Jeremiah, the evidence of the purchase of the field is ordered to be cast into an earthen vessel. In like manner, we find in the Gospel that the money paid for the Lord was used for the purchase of a potter's field, which field also was to be employed as a burying-place for strangers. And it may be that all this was significant of the permanence of the repose of those who sojourn like strangers in this present world, and are buried with Christ by baptism. For the Lord also declared to Jeremiah, that the said purchase of the field was expressive of the fact that in that land [of Judæa] there would be a remnant of the people delivered from their captivity. I judged it proper to give some sort of sketch of these things, as I was calling attention to the kind of significance which a really careful and painstaking study should look for in these testimonies of the prophets, when they are reduced to a unity and compared with the evangelical narrative. These, then, are the statements which Matthew has introduced with reference to the traitor Judas.
The Harmony of the Gospels, Book 3, Chapter 7

And the Lord said to me, says the prophet, or else the Savior himself, whose are the preceding words, bearing witness that the Father spoke to him: Cast it to the statuary, for which in the Hebrew is read ioser, that is, τὸν πλάστην, whom we can call moulder and potter. And the sense is: Cast my price to the potter, who is the Creator and moulder of all. Nor did he say, put it down, but cast it, so that the wage of the Lord might be weighed by the judgment of the moulder and modeller. And εἰρονικῶς (ironically), seeing his price, that is, the price of the divine majesty, in thirty pieces of silver, and himself betrayed for so cheap a wage: A fine price, he says, at which I was priced by them; and this must be read with more emphasis, with the mockery and derision of the speaker: At so much did my people, once the poor of the flock and chosen by me as sons, judge that I should be bought and sold! And I took, says the Lord through the prophet, as I had been commanded by the Lord, the thirty pieces of silver, and I did not put them down, but cast them into the house of the Lord to the moulder; in the house of the Lord I caused them to be returned by the traitor to the priests and Pharisees, the very man who sold me confessing: I have sinned, betraying just blood. But they, since it was the price of blood, would not put it into the corbona, that is, into the treasury; but with it they bought the potter's field for the burial of strangers. For all of us who were strangers and sojourners from the law, redeemed by his most precious blood, are buried and rest in the house of the potter and Creator of all. For πλάστῃ and moulder I once translated statuary, compelled by the ambiguity of the word, because it signifies statuary and moulder by a single term.

And I cut off my second staff, which was called Cord, so that I might dissolve the brotherhood between Judah and Israel. LXX: And I cast away the second staff, which was called Cord, so that I might scatter the covenant that was between Judah and Israel. In this place too I know that I have read a long explanation by a certain writer, or rather inextricable tangles, who brings forward from the book of Ezekiel the two staffs joined into one fellowship, and fits to this passage everything that is to be understood spiritually about the concord of Judah and Ephraim. But let us follow the order we have begun. After the Lord was crucified by the Jews and valued at thirty pieces of silver, and the price of his blood availed for the burial of the Gentiles, who were strangers to the law and the commandments of God, at once the Lord, no longer putting off his sentence, says: I cut off my second staff, which was properly mine, which clung to me in such a way that in Jeremiah it was called a loincloth and a girdle and a waistband, or, to use the everyday word, a hip-band; this second staff, once called Cord and my portion, was therefore cast away by me, so that I might dissolve the pact and the brotherhood and the concord that had been between Judah and Israel, and separate the brothers from one another. So that, in the number of the apostles and of those who repented, the name Judah should again be given, as to one who also confesses his God; while those should be called Israel and Ephraim and Joseph who, persisting in hardness of heart, said: We have no king but Caesar. Hence he did not add: So that I might make void the pact, or covenant, which I had with Judah and Israel — for to this day he stretches out his hand to the repentant —, but also that he might divide from one another, out of the one people, some who believe and others who do not believe, saying: Do not think that I came to send peace on the earth; I did not come to send peace, but a sword. For I came to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man's enemies are those of his own household.

O shepherds, disciples of the Lord, feed the flock and lead (it) well! Strengthen the sick, support the weak, bind up the broken, make whole the lame, and take heed to the fattened ones for the Lord of the flock. Be not likened unto an unskilled and foolish shepherd, who in his foolishness is not able to feed the flock, and whose arm is dried up, and whose eye has been blinded, because he said: "dying, let it die; and perishing, let it perish, and the flesh that is left shall be eaten by its companions ". And when the Chief of the shepherds comes He will condemn the unskilled and foolish shepherd who has not cared well for his fellow servants. And he who has shepherded the flock and led (it) well shall be called "a good and skillful servant" (cf. S. Mt. 25: 21), who has presented the flock to the Shepherd while it was intact.

O stupid and foolish pastor, to whose right hand and to whose right eye I committed my sheep. Because thou didst say concerning the sheep, let that which dieth, die, and let that which perisheth perish, and whatever is left, let them devour the flesh of one another; therefore, behold I will make blind thy right eye and I will wither up thy right arm. Thy eye which regarded a bribe shall be blinded, and thy hand which did not rule in righteousness shall waste away.

Such is my defense; its reasonableness I have set forth. And may the God of peace, who made both one and has restored us to each other, who sets kings upon thrones and raises up the poor out of the dust and lifts up the beggar from the dunghill, who chose David his servant and took him away from the sheepfolds, though he was the least and youngest of the sons of Jesse, who gave the word to those who preach the gospel with great power for the perfection of the gospel—may he himself hold me by my right hand. [May he] guide me with his counsel and receive me with glory, who is a Shepherd to shepherds and Guide to guides. [May he guide us] that we may feed his flock with knowledge, not with the instruments of a foolish shepherd, according to the blessing, and not according to the curse pronounced against the men of former days. May he give strength and power to his people and himself present to himself  his flock resplendent and spotless and worthy of the fold on high, in the habitation of them that rejoice, in the splendor of the saints, so that in his temple everyone, both flock and shepherds together may say, Glory in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be all glory forever and ever. Amen.
IN DEFENSE OF HIS FLIGHT TO PONTUS, ORATION 2:117

And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself yet again the instruments of a foolish shepherd. For behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, who will not visit what is forsaken, will not seek what is scattered, and will not heal what is broken, and will not nourish what stands, and he will eat the flesh of the fat ones and break apart their hooves. O shepherd and idol, forsaking the flock, a sword upon his arm and upon his right eye; his arm shall be dried up with withering, and his right eye, growing dark, shall be darkened. LXX: And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself yet again the shepherd's instruments of an unskilled shepherd. For behold, I will raise up a shepherd upon the land, who shall not visit what is forsaken and shall not seek out what is scattered, and shall not heal what is broken, and shall not guide what is whole, and shall devour the flesh of the choice ones, and twist their ankles. O you who pasture vain things, and who have forsaken the sheep, a sword upon his arm, and upon his right eye; his arm shall be dried up with withering, and his right eye shall be darkened with blindness. When he says: Take for yourself yet again the instruments of a foolish shepherd, he means this: that above he had taken to himself two staffs, one Beauty and the other Cord. And because through their own vice and sin he cast them away, and, the brotherhood between Judah and Israel being dissolved, we have been grafted into the root of the good olive, and blindness has come in part upon the house of Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, now the prophet is told to take up the most grievous prophecy of the foolish, or unskilled, shepherd. The foolish and unskilled shepherd is without any doubt the Antichrist, who is said to be coming at the consummation of the world, and what sort he will be is indicated. By the instruments of the shepherd we ought to understand his insignia and his garb: the wallet, the staff, the pipe and the whistle. And just as Isaiah, to show the captivity of the people, walks about naked, and Jeremiah goes to the potter's house, so that from the shattering of the vessel which was turning on the wheel and being shaped by the craftsman's hand he might show both the destruction of Israel and the power of God, and Ezekiel, to show the overthrow of Jerusalem and the flight of Zedekiah and the burdens of the captives not only by his voice but also by his garb, digs through the wall and is carried out upon his shoulders, so Zechariah takes on the garb of a foolish and unskilled shepherd, to announce him who is to come.

This shepherd will rise up in Israel for this reason, because the true shepherd had said: I will no longer feed you. Under another name, both in the prophet Daniel and in the Gospel and in Paul's epistle to the Thessalonians, he is prophesied as the abomination of desolation, who is to sit in the temple of the Lord and make himself out to be God; and through Isaiah too he is called the great mind. And he comes for this, not to heal but to destroy the flock of Israel. For the good shepherd visits the sick animals, seeks out the scattered, brings back those left behind, supports the weary. On the contrary, the bad shepherd does everything the opposite way, and having devoured the flesh of the fat ones, he breaks apart and twists the hooves of the rams and the sheep, so that they may not walk with a straight foot. This shepherd the Jews received, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the spirit of his mouth and will bring to nothing by the brightness of his coming, so that those who did not believe the truth, lest they should be saved, may believe a lie and be judged, because they consented to iniquity.

Having described the worst shepherd, foolish and unskilled, the prophetic discourse turns to the shepherd himself: O shepherd and idol. So wicked is the shepherd that he is called not a worshiper of idols but himself an idol, since he calls himself God and wishes to be adored by all. He forsook the flock to be devoured by beasts, the flock which the Lord had guarded for so long a time. A sword upon his arm, and his strength, and upon his right eye, by which he boasted that he keenly discerned the mysteries of God and saw more than all the prophets before him had seen, so much so that he called himself the Son of God. And that sword is the one of which we both learn above and shall now speak in part, the one of which Isaiah too speaks: My sword has been made drunk in heaven. And it is for this reason that the sword of the Lord will be upon his arm and upon his right eye, that his strength and all the boasting of his might may be dried up with withering, and the knowledge which he promised himself under a false name may be darkened with eternal darkness.
12: There are many statements of spirit in general in the sacred Scriptures, and a person could easily become confused from ignorance, if he did not know to what sort of spirit the particular text refers; therefore we must be sure of the nature of the Holy Spirit according to Scripture. For example, Aaron is called Christ (anointed), and David also, and Saul and others are called christs, yet there is only one true Christ; similarly, since the name of spirit has been given to many things, we must determine what in particular is called the Holy Spirit. Many things are called spirits; our soul is called spirit; this wind, which is blowing, is called spirit; great valor is called spirit; impure action is called spirit; and a hostile devil is called spirit. Take care, therefore, when you hear such things, not to mistake one for another because of the similarity of the name. Scripture says of the soul, "When his spirit departs, he returns to the earth"; and again of the soul: "Who forms the spirit of man within him."

Therefore he referred the thunders to the words of the Lord, the sound of which went out into all the earth. And we understand the word spirit in this place of the soul, which he took endowed with potential reason and perfection. For the Scripture often designates the soul of humankind by the word spirit, as you read: "Who creates the spirit of man within him." So too the Lord signified his soul by the word spirit, when he said, "Into your hands I commend my spirit."

The burden of the word of the Lord upon Israel. The Lord said, stretching out the heaven and founding the earth and forming the spirit of man within him: Behold, I will make Jerusalem a lintel of drunkenness for all the peoples round about; but Judah too shall be in the siege against Jerusalem. And it shall be: on that day: I will make Jerusalem a stone of burden for all the peoples; all who have lifted it shall be torn with gashing, and all the nations of the earth shall be gathered against her. LXX: The taking up of the word of the Lord upon Israel. The Lord says, stretching out the heaven and founding the earth, and forming the spirit of man within him: Behold, I will make Jerusalem like lintels that are shaken for all the peoples round about, and in Judea. And there shall be a siege around Jerusalem, and it shall be on that day, I will make Jerusalem a stone that is trodden down by all the nations; everyone who treads her down, mocking shall mock, and I will gather against her all the nations of the earth. There is a threefold interpretation from the place in which we read: Behold, I will make Jerusalem a lintel of drunkenness for all the peoples round about, as far as the place where it is written: Sword, awake against my shepherd, and against the man who is my companion, says the Lord of hosts. Strike the shepherd and the sheep shall be scattered. For some of the Jews think that these things have already been partly fulfilled, from Zerubbabel down to Gaius Pompey, who was the first of the Romans to take Judea and the temple, a history which Josephus writes. Others, however, think that they are to be fulfilled at the end of the world, when Jerusalem shall have been restored, which the wretched Jewish nation promises itself with its ἠλειμμένῳ (anointed one), whom we read of above as the foolish shepherd. But others, that is, we who are reckoned by the name of Christ, declare that they are daily being fulfilled, and are to be fulfilled, in the Church until the end of the world. And so as not to stretch the measure of the volume by going through every point, setting it out thus: Those men say this, others suppose so, we think thus, we have set down three opinions, so that from the variety of interpretation the prudent reader may understand what is to be fitted to what. The Lord, then, who stretched out the heaven like a skin, and made the earth firm with a lofty mass, and formed the spirit of man within him, is likewise the Creator of all souls, so that out of the two substances of soul and body he might put together one living being. For spirit is frequently taken for soul, as there: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit, and: You will take away their spirit and they will fail, and they will return to their dust.

I do not want anyone to tell me that this view [that God condemns innocent souls] should be supported by the passage "who formed the spirit of man in him" and "who made the heart of every one of them." Something supremely strong and invincible is needed to force me to believe that God condemns any souls without any guilt of theirs. It is either as great a thing, or it is, perhaps greater, to create as to form, yet it is written, "Create a clean heart in me, O God." This is no argument for thinking that the soul in this passage prays to be made before it had any being. As, therefore, while now existing, it is created by renewal of its justice, so, while now existing, it is formed by the shaping force of doctrine.

Hence we ought to understand this passage so that we do not take the words "he breathed into him the breath of life, and he became a living soul" to mean that a part, as it were, of the nature of God was turned into the soul of man. Thus we are not forced to say that the nature of God is mutable. It is especially in this error that the truth weighs down upon these Manichaeans. For as pride is the mother of all the heretics, they dared to say that the soul is the nature of God. And thus they are under pressure from us when we say to them, "Then the nature of God errs and is unhappy and is corrupted by the stain of vices and sins, or is, as you say, soiled by the filth of the opposing nature," and other such things that it is wicked to believe about the nature of God. For in another passage Scripture clearly says that the soul was made by almighty God and that it is therefore not a part of God or the nature of God. There the prophet says, "He who formed the spirit for all men made all things," and in another place it says, "He who formed the spirit of man is in him." These testimonies clearly prove that the spirit of man was made. In Scripture the rational part of man's soul by which he differs from the beasts and rules over them by the law of nature is called the spirit of man. On this the apostle says, "No one knows what pertains to man except the spirit of man which is within him." If these testimonies were not clear proof that the soul of man was made, there would be no lack of those who would say that the spirit of man was not made and who would think that it is the nature of God and say that part of God was changed into it, when there took place that breathing forth by God. Healthy doctrine likewise rejects this, because the spirit of man itself is at times in error and at times thinks wisely; thus it proclaims that it is mutable, and it is in no way permissible to believe this of the nature of God. But there cannot be a greater sign of pride than that the human soul says that it is what God is, while it still groans under such great burdens of vice and unhappiness.

When, then, after the time of Zechariah in the time of the Macedonian Empire was the Temple burnt? There was no such time. For after its burning by the Babylonians, it was not burned again till in the time of Titus and Vespasian, the Roman Emperors, it was utterly destroyed by fire, and it is in relation to this that the prophet summons the ancient rulers of the nation in a figure to mourn and weep, when he says: "Let the pine weep because the cedar is fallen, because the great ones are in great misery. Let the oaks of Bashan weep, because the wood that is planted is torn down: a voice of shepherds that lament, because their greatness is in misery." Then truly Jerusalem was as a portico shaken by all nations around it, and there was a force encircling Judaea, and their venerated Temple and its Holy Place is even to-day a stone trodden under the feet of all nations, and all that mock are mocked according to the prophecy.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 4

Concerning the Church it can be interpreted thus: that all the persecutors who have fought against the house of the Lord are made drunk with that cup which Jeremiah gives to all the nations to drink, so that they drink and are drunk, and fall, and vomit, and go mad. I know that in the time of persecution many of our own were compelled to fight against the Church; but whoever wishes to lift this weight will indeed lift it, and will bear it up in his hands for the wrath of the Lord by which he chastises sinners; yet he himself will not go unpunished, since the sword of God fights against him. For the stone of burden, which we have rendered as best we could, the Seventy translated: A stone trodden down by all the nations. Everyone who treads it down — or her, that is, Jerusalem —, mocking shall mock. Its sense is plain: that in both ways Jerusalem is to be trodden down both by hostile nations and by persecutors, and is to be mocked at the pleasure of those who mock. But the former sense is better and truer. We expound each point briefly, so that we may at last come to the end, lest, if we write at greater length, the reader's mind be confused both by the obscurity of the matters and by the length of the discourse.

This Creator, then, and Lord of the universe testifies that he will make Jerusalem a lintel of drunkenness for all the peoples round about, so that whoever touches its threshold may be made drunk and fall, or else the lintel itself may fall upon the one by whom it is touched. But Judah too, when Jerusalem is besieged, is captured by the nations, and passing into their fellowship he will be compelled to besiege his own mother city.

And not only will the Lord make Jerusalem like a lintel of drunkenness for all the peoples; he will also make her like a stone of burden for all the peoples, and whoever tries to lift it will be torn with gashing. For all the kingdoms of the earth will be gathered against Jerusalem. It is the custom in the cities of Palestine, and to this day the old practice is kept throughout all Judea, that in villages, towns and forts round stones of very great weight are set, on which young men are accustomed to exercise themselves; and they lift them according to the variety of their strength, some up to the knees, some up to the navel, others to the shoulders and the head, some above the crown of the head, with arms held straight and hands joined, raising the weight and showing the greatness of their strength. On the citadel of the Athenians, beside the statue of Minerva, I saw a bronze sphere of very great weight, which I, because of the weakness of my poor body, could scarcely move. And when I asked what it meant, the answer was given by the inhabitants of that city that the strength of athletes was proved by that mass, and that no one went down to a contest until it was known, from his lifting of the weight, with whom he ought to be matched. So the sense is this: I will make Jerusalem for all the nations like a very heavy stone to be lifted. They will indeed lift her, and lay her waste according to the variety of their strength; but it must be that, while she is being lifted, in the very straining and raising of the weight, the very heavy stone leaves some gash or scrape on the bodies of those who lift it.

On that day, says the Lord, I will strike every horse with astonishment, and its rider with madness; and upon the house of Judah I will open my eyes, and every horse of the peoples I will strike with blindness. LXX: On that day, says the Lord Almighty, I will strike every horse with astonishment, and its rider with madness; but upon the house of Judah I will open my eyes, and all the horses of the peoples I will strike with blindness. At that time — for this is what 'day' signifies —, when Jerusalem shall have been besieged, so that Judah too is compelled to besiege her, the Lord will strike, both carnally and spiritually, all the horses of the adversaries with astonishment, so that all who see that they have been struck are astonished, and their riders, under the pressure of the greatness of their ills, will be turned to madness; and upon the house of Judah, who were being compelled to do something against their mother city, the Lord will open his eyes, to have mercy on them, and to make them worthy of his gaze, and to illumine them with the light of his eyes; but all the horses of the peoples he will strike with eternal blindness. What horses are to be understood spiritually we have said above: A horse is deceptive for safety, and: These in chariots, and those in horses, and other things like these. Their riders too we said were either demons or false teachers, who will all be turned to astonishment and madness, so that they are convicted of knowing nothing, but darkness that can be felt overwhelms them, such as there was when the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck. But upon the house of Judah, that is, the people that confesses God and that, broken by the straits of persecution and terrified by fear, seems to be in the number of the persecutors, the Lord will open his eyes, so as to look back upon many who say to him: Look upon me, and have mercy on me; and they may deserve to hear: And the Lord shall be to you an everlasting light. This is the tearing by the very heavy stone, which the Lord threatens against his adversaries, who tried to lift and harass Jerusalem.

And the chiefs of Judah shall say in their heart: Let the inhabitants of Jerusalem be strengthened for me in the Lord of hosts, their God. LXX: And the tribunes — that is, οἱ χιλίαρχοι —, of Judah shall say in their hearts: We shall find for ourselves those who dwell in Jerusalem in the Lord Almighty, their God. When the Lord has opened his eyes upon Judah, and has struck all the horses of the nations with blindness, the chiefs of Judah, of whom it was said above: But Judah too shall be in the siege against Jerusalem, will make vows in their hearts, since they will not dare to speak freely, that Jerusalem may conquer, and that Judah, conquered along with the enemies, may conquer along with his fellow citizens. Where we said: Let them be strengthened for me, and the LXX translated εὑρήσομεν ἑαυτοῖς, that is: we shall find for ourselves, in the Hebrew is written emsa li, which Aquila translated καρτέρησόν μοι, that is, strengthen for me, so that the sense is: The chiliarchs and tribunes, and the chiefs of Judah, will wish, and will make vows in the hidden secret place of their minds, that God may strengthen the inhabitants of Jerusalem in the Lord their God, and that they may conquer their adversaries. According to tropology, the chiefs and tribunes are the apostles, and all apostolic men and teachers who have been set over the army of Christ, who would wish to find for themselves no others but those who dwell in Jerusalem, the vision of peace, and who dwell in the Lord Almighty, their God. Of these chiefs was Paul the apostle, who found Titus and Timothy, Luke and Silvanus; Peter too, who instructed Mark, the writer of the Gospel; and the rest of the apostles, who filled the whole world with their teaching and learning, so as to have as disciples inhabitants of Jerusalem.

All, then, who are on the right way, to whom it is said: Do not be overly just, and on the left, who hear: The ways that are on the left are perverse, the devouring flame shall consume; and when the adversaries have been destroyed and removed, Jerusalem, that is, the Church, will again receive her former glory; and she will be in her own state, and the tents of Judah will be saved, the gatherings of Christians scattered throughout the whole world, from which, as from tents and tabernacles, we long to go to the house that is not made with hands, and to the heavenly Jerusalem. And it is for this reason that the tents of the common people, and of all who are reckoned by the Christian name and are counted among the crowd, receive peace first, while the princes of the churches are besieged and put to flight, so that the masters and teachers may in no way think that peace was restored to the Churches by their own teaching and wisdom, but by the help of the Lord.

On that day I will make the chiefs of Judah like a furnace of fire among wood, and like a torch of fire in hay; and they shall devour to the right and to the left all the peoples round about; and Jerusalem shall be inhabited again in her own place, in Jerusalem. And the Lord shall save the tents of Judah, as in the beginning, so that the house of David may not glory magnificently, and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem against Judah. LXX: On that day I will make the tribunes of Judah like a firebrand among wood, and like hay of fire in stubble; and they shall devour on the right and on the left all the peoples of the Lord round about, and Jerusalem shall be inhabited still in herself; and the Lord shall save the tents of Judah, as from the beginning, so that the glory of the house of David may not be magnified, and the exaltation of the inhabitants of Jerusalem over Judah. When the chiefs of Judah have said in their hearts: Strengthen for me, O Lord, the besieged of Jerusalem, so that those who have been conquered through their own weakness may prevail by your help, then I, the Lord Almighty, their God, will make the princes of Judah like a furnace of fire among wood, and like a torch in stubble, so that they may devour the adversaries to whom they were joined in feigned friendship. And let them devour on the right and on the left, and slay all the peoples round about, so that Jerusalem may again be inhabited in her own place and may in no way fear hostile assaults.

Let us say that, in the time of the Church's persecution, the chiefs and tribunes of the Christian name, of whom we spoke above, when the Lord has restored peace to Jerusalem and has slain the adversary with the spirit of his mouth, will be like a furnace of fire among wood, to devour the unfruitful trees, and like torches in stubble, so that whatever has no grain, and is carried about by every wind of doctrine, may be given over to burning. And the chiefs of Judah and the tribunes, he says, shall devour to the right and to the left those who were unwilling to walk in the middle of the road, who do not know that ὑπερβολὰς (excesses) belong to κακίας (vice); whence the people of God promises: we will turn aside neither to the right nor to the left, we will walk in the straight way. The right way is stinginess, which the Greeks call φειδολίαν; the left, extravagance; the middle and straight way, frugality.

And of the holy apostles and evangelists Christ somewhere spoke by one of the prophets: "And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will make the heads of the thousands of Judaea like a firebrand among wood, and like a fiery lamp among reeds; and they shall devour on the right hand and on the left all the nations round about." For, so to speak, like fire they ate up all the nations, and fed upon the whole earth, kindling all its inhabitants, who as I said were cold, and had suffered the death of ignorance and sin.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

Let them restore too the cities and towns, and the farms and villages of the tribe of Judah, which had been plundered and laid waste, as they had been before they were laid waste; and let the royal house, and the renowned and magnificent men of the tribe of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem in no way glory against the tribe of Judah, that it is ruled by their command and governed by their counsel; but let them know that the victory on both sides is the Lord's. Whether these things according to the history have been done or are yet to come, we leave the truth of the matter to the judgment of the Lord, and to his saints, who have received from him the spirit of wisdom and truth.

On that day the Lord shall shield the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and he who has stumbled among them on that day shall be as David. And the house of David as God, as the angel of the Lord in their sight. LXX: And it shall be on that day, the Lord shall shield the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and he who is weak among them on that day shall be as the house of David; and the house of David as the house of God, and the angel of the Lord in their sight. When Judah obtains the victory, and the Lord restores its tents as they had been from the beginning, so that the royal house may in no way glory against the people, on that day and at that time the Lord — by whose help Judah shall devour its adversaries on the right and on the left — shall shield also the besieged of Jerusalem, and all things shall be changed into such great happiness and blessedness that he who was thought the most worthless shall be as the royal house; and he who was of the royal house shall be as of the house of God, that is, as a messenger of the Lord and of angelic dignity in the sight of those who shall have been saved again at that time. According to anagogy: the Lord shall shield the inhabitants of the Church, when the peace of the churches has been restored after a most grievous persecution, when she shall also be adorned by the interpretation of her own name. For Jerusalem is rendered as vision of peace. And those who have fought as soldiers for the Church and have confessed the Lord in persecution shall be so blessed that he who was least, and who, as a man, has stumbled in some sin and word, shall be placed in the rank of the teachers; and the teachers who have kept their own station shall be as the house of God and as the angel of the Lord, because this is what we labor for with all zeal, set on earth and sweating in varied toil: that we may be transformed into angelic glory.

Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be moved. And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven, and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn (24, 29—30ᵃ). Since we consider that greater themes here come under discussion than lie within the grasp of human understanding — even of those who have advanced in wisdom far beyond others — let us come and examine the passage: first inquiring into those things which can readily be admitted for an exposition of the Gospel text, as though the Lord Himself were prophesying in it; and afterward we shall look for what the truth of these words may be according to those who judge that there is something deeper and more subtle in the words, keeping to the sequence of the moral traditions in these matters as well, in the same manner as above.

Someone, then, will say: just as when great fires begin to be kindled a darkness seems to be raised up out of the abundant smoke, so at the consummation of the world, by the fire which is to be set alight, even the "great lights" shall be darkened, so that, the sun being darkened, and in consequence of the darkening of the sun, the moon too, hindered by the sun from receiving light, is not permitted even to give its own light. And thus of necessity a great darkness must first take hold of the nature of the world. And so, when the light of the stars has thus withered away, the remaining body of them, having become grosser, since it cannot be borne aloft as at first when it was lifted up carried by the light itself, will fall from heaven. And when these things happen, it follows that the rational powers of the heavens, suffering amazement, undergo a certain commotion and are troubled, being, that is, removed from their former functions. So he who understands these things to be thus will add that the sign of the Son of man, in whom "the things that were in the heavens and the things that were on earth" were made heavenly, shall then appear: namely, the power which the Son of man wrought when He was hung upon the tree; and in heaven above all shall His sign shine forth. And men out of all the tribes, who formerly did not believe in the Christianity that was proclaimed but even spoke evil of it, then, recognizing it through that sign made manifest, shall mourn and lament because of their ignorance and their sins, in that they did not receive the word of the Lord.

But another will judge otherwise concerning these words, holding that (as these words themselves show) the destruction of the world will not come about by fire, but by its own failing. And he will make use of such an illustration: that just as, when the light of a lamp fails, the light is little by little diminished, so, when the nourishment of the heavenly lights fails, the sun shall be darkened, no longer having the breaths that come to it from them coming upon it. And when the greater light suffers this, all the more will the moon too be unable to display that fiery splendor which appears according to its own phases. When, therefore, these things befall the sun, the light of the stars too will fail, so that what has remained in them, being as it were earthy, falls from heaven, and, these things happening, all the powers of the heavens shall be moved. For just as, in the dispensation of the cross, "when the sun failed, darkness came over all the earth", so also, when the sign of the Son of man appears in heaven, the light of the sun and of the moon shall fail, and yet more that of the stars, as though consumed by the great power of that sign; and when it appears, the tribes that shall then have remained on the earth shall mourn.

For these things he will use the illustration of the prophet Isaiah, who speaks in this manner: "For behold, the incurable day of the Lord comes, of wrath and fury, to make the circle of the earth a desert and to destroy sinners out of it. For the stars of heaven and Orion and all the ornaments of heaven shall not give their light, and the sun shall be darkened in the east, and the moon shall not give her brightness. And I will command evils upon the circle of the earth, and their sins upon the ungodly." Likewise also such things from Joel: "Before His face the earth shall be confounded and the heaven shall be moved, the sun and the moon shall be darkened, and the stars shall not give their light. And the Lord shall utter His voice before the face of His power, for exceeding strong is His camp, since mighty are the works of His words." Likewise: "And I will give portents in the heaven above, and on the earth blood and fire and vapor; the sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and illustrious day of the Lord comes."

And many things like these you will find in the Scriptures, if you are willing to look at nothing else in the Gospel passages beyond the plain words. For according to this too, that it says, then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, as though needing no interpretation, you will receive from the prophet Zechariah such words as these: "And it shall be in that day that I will seek to take away all the nations that shall come against Jerusalem, and I will pour out upon the house of David and upon all the inhabitants in Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of compassion; and they shall look upon me because they danced, and they shall mourn over themselves with a mourning as over a beloved one, and they shall grieve with grief as over a firstborn. In that day the mourning shall be magnified over Jerusalem like the mourning of a pomegranate cut down in the plain, and the land shall mourn by tribes: the tribe of the house of David apart and their women apart, the tribe of the house of Nathan apart and their women apart, the tribe of the house of Levi apart and their women apart, the tribe of the house of Shimei apart and their women apart, all the tribes that are left remaining apart and their women apart." It will seem, then, to some that one ought to carry the interpretation this far and to examine nothing beyond the text.

Nevertheless, when these things have thus been done, there shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven, and then the tribes of the earth shall mourn. For these things it is not absurd to use the examples of the prophet Zechariah, which run thus: "and it shall be in that day that I will seek to take away all the nations that come against Jerusalem, and I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants in Jerusalem a spirit of grace and of compassion; and they shall look upon me because they danced, and they shall mourn over themselves a mourning as over a beloved one, and they shall grieve with grief as over a firstborn. And in that day the mourning shall be magnified in Jerusalem like the mourning of a pomegranate cut down in the field, and the earth shall mourn by tribes: the tribe of the house of David apart by itself and their women apart by themselves; the tribe of the house of Nathan apart by itself and their women apart by themselves; the tribe of the house of Levi apart by itself and their women apart by themselves; the tribe of the house of Shimei apart by itself and their women apart by themselves; and all the remaining tribes apart by themselves and their women apart by themselves". Therefore every earthly company, since it is a tribe of the earth — which rank they attributed to themselves — will mourn together with those like itself, especially if in some category of sinners it must mourn more abundantly.

But I think that through these things there are shown the differences of those who seem to have been in the faith and in their own company, yet did not please God. There is, therefore, a house of David that mourns — those who, set up from among the people, did deeds worthy of mourning, or [those drawn] from among kings and magnates.
