But those from among the teachers who lived badly are the tribe of Nathan that mourns, since Nathan was a prophet; and to teach is to prophesy. So those who are sinners from among those who were set over the Church and had the priesthood enjoined upon them and did not administer their office well, are the tribe of the house of Levi that mourns. And to speak the truth, whether concerning those tribes which we have mentioned or concerning the tribe of Shimei, belongs to God alone. But we, for the present, think that all who were catechized and instructed in the divine mystery, and were not ordained in any of the tribes which we mentioned above, and committed grave sins (such as are very many of the laity), are the tribe of Shimei; while the remaining men are those he called the 'remaining' tribes, which he did not name specifically. But it is no trifling task to speak also concerning the women of the individual tribes, who mourn apart by themselves. And see whether you can, in each and every class, call those who were more bodily and more worldly the 'women', but say that those who by comparison with them were better were the 'men'.

And it shall be on that day: I will seek to crush all the nations that come against Jerusalem. And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of prayers. LXX: And it shall be on that day: I will seek to take away all the nations that come against Jerusalem; and I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of mercy. On that day when the Lord shall shield the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the Lord will seek to crush all the nations that come against Jerusalem. But he will crush them not unto perdition but unto amendment, so that they may cease to wage war against Jerusalem and begin to be of Jerusalem. For if he created all things out of nothing, he did not make them in order to destroy what he had created, but so that the things that were created might be saved by his mercy. Hence also in the Wisdom that bears the name of Solomon — if, however, anyone is pleased to accept the book — we find it written: He created all things that they might be, and the generations of the world are healthful; and there shall be no deadly poison in them. For just as the Lord came to seek what had perished, and saved the human race, so too he destroyed the nations in this respect, that they were hostile nations.

The Jews therefore, because it was the preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath day, (for that sabbath day was an high day,) besought Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away.  Then came the soldiers, and brake the legs of the first, and of the other which was crucified with him.  But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs:  But one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water.  And he that saw it bare record, and his record is true: and he knoweth that he saith true, that ye might believe.  For these things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken.  And again another scripture saith, They shall look on him whom they pierced. [Zechariah 12:10]

And in what kind of sensation and punishment the wicked are to be, hear from what was said in like manner with reference to this; it is as follows: "Their worm shall not rest, and their fire shall not be quenched;" and then shall they repent, when it profits them not. And what the people of the Jews shall say and do, when they see Him coming in glory, has been thus predicted by Zechariah the prophet: "I will command the four winds to gather the scattered children; I will command the north wind to bring them, and the south wind, that it keep not back. And then in Jerusalem there shall be great lamentation, not the lamentation of mouths or of lips, but the lamentation of the heart; and they shall rend not their garments, but their hearts. Tribe by tribe they shall mourn, and then they shall look on Him whom they have pierced; and they shall say, Why, O Lord, hast Thou made us to err from Thy way? The glory which our fathers blessed, has for us been turned into shame."

We must after all this turn our attention to those scriptures also which forbid our belief in such a resurrection as is held by your Animalists (for I will not call them Spiritualists), that it is either to be assumed as taking place now, as soon as men come to the knowledge of the truth, or else that it is accomplished immediately after their departure from this life... Who has yet beheld Jesus descending from heaven in like manner as the apostles saw Him ascend, according to the appointment of the two angels? [Acts 1:11] Up to the present moment they have not, tribe by tribe, smitten their breasts, looking on Him whom they pierced. [John 19:37; Zechariah 12:10] No one has as yet fallen in with Elias; [Malachi 4:5] no one has as yet escaped from Antichrist; [1 John 4:3] no one has as yet had to bewail the downfall of Babylon. [Revelation 18:2] And is there now anybody who has risen again, except the heretic? He, of course, has already quitted the grave of his own corpse — although he is even now liable to fevers and ulcers; he, too, has already trodden down his enemies — although he has even now to struggle with the powers of the world. And as a matter of course, he is already a king — although he even now owes to Cæsar the things which are Cæsar's. [Matthew 22:21]
On the Resurrection of the Flesh, Chapter 22

Then shall the son of perdition be brought forward as the accuser, with his demons and with his servants, by angels stern and inexorable. And they shall be given over to the fire that is never quenched, and to the worm that never sleeps, and to the outer darkness. For the crucifiers shall see him in human form, as he appeared to them "when he came" by the holy virgin in the flesh and as they crucified him. And he will show them the "prints of the" nails in his hands and feet, and his side pierced with the spear, and his head crowned with thorns, and his honorable cross. And once for all shall the people of the Hebrews see all these things, and they shall mourn and weep, as the prophet exclaims, "They shall look on him whom they have pierced."
ON THE END OF THE WORLD 40

Yea, in return for their insults to the Lord who thus prophesied, there has not failed for them lamentation, mourning and wailing. And it was only after our Saviour came, and even until our own time, that all the families of the Jewish nation have suffered pain worthy of wailing and lamentation because God's hand has struck them, delivering their mother-city over to strange nations, laying their Temple low, and driving them from their country, to serve their enemies in a hostile land; wherefore even now every house and every soul is a prey to lamentation. And so the prophecy says, "And family shall mourn by family, the family of the house of David by itself, and their wives by themselves, and all that follows this."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 4

In short, there follows: I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of mercy. Of this grace the apostle Paul also writes: The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. And in the above-mentioned volume it is contained: The things that are in heaven, who has searched out? Except that you gave wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from on high; and so the paths of those who dwell on earth were corrected; and men were taught the things that please you. And in Isaiah the Lord says: I have given my spirit upon you. And again Scripture records of the same: I have given my Spirit upon him. But the word of pouring out shows the sense of largess, as is plain in what we have said: The charity of God has been poured out in your hearts. And in another place, in the person of God: I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh. And what the spirit of grace is, the same Apostle tells the Hebrews: How much worse punishments do you think he deserves who has trampled upon the Son of God, and has counted polluted the blood of the covenant in which he was sanctified, and has done outrage to the spirit of grace. Hence also the graces of the Holy Spirit are said to be diverse. And the greeting of the Apostle: Grace, he says, and peace be multiplied to you, so that after he has forgiven us our sins, then peace may follow through mercy. The Jews record these things as already done in part, and to come more fully at the consummation of the world. But we understand and prove that they are fulfilled daily since the coming of Christ.

And they shall look upon me whom they pierced; and they shall mourn him with a mourning as over an only-begotten, and they shall grieve over him, as one is wont to grieve at the death of a firstborn. LXX: And they shall look upon me, because they mocked; and they shall mourn over him a mourning, as over one most dear. And they shall grieve with grief, as over a firstborn. The Hebrew letters daleth and res, that is, d and r, are alike and are distinguished only by a small stroke. From this it comes about that those who read the same word differently translate it now one way, now another. For the sake of understanding let us give one example: And Samuel, it says, was clothed in an ephod bad, that is, in a linen garment; for linen is called bad; hence also linens are called baddim. In place of this Hebrew and Latin expression some wrongly read ephod bar; for bar means either a son, or a sheaf of grain, or chosen, or οὖλος, that is, curly. What happened there by an error of interpretation we detect has happened here too. For if dacaru is read, it is taken as ἐξεκέντησαν, that is, they pricked or they pierced; but if, in the reverse order, with the letters exchanged, racadu, it is understood as ὠρχήσαντο, that is, they danced. And the error was born from the likeness of the letters. But John the evangelist, who drew wisdom from the breast of the Lord, a Hebrew of the Hebrews whom the Savior loved most, did not greatly care what the Greek letters contained, but rendered word from word, as he had read it in the Hebrew, and said that it was fulfilled at the time of the Lord's passion. But if anyone does not accept this, let him bring evidence from what passage of the holy Scriptures John brought forth these words, and when he has not found it, he will be forced against his will to accept the truth. And the Jews shall mourn as over an only-begotten and a firstborn, the same thing being signified in the Lord Savior, both only-begotten and firstborn. He is called Only-begotten on account of the property of his nature; Firstborn, according to the Apostle, of those who rise from the dead. For only-begotten the Seventy translated most dear, of whom we read in the Gospel: This is my most dear Son, in whom I am well pleased. Then they shall grieve that he was crucified by them, when they see him reigning in glory. The word κατωρχήσαντο (they danced over), among the Greeks, is compounded not from mockery but from dancing, namely because they danced against the Lord as if in sport, when, mocking and laughing, they said: Vah, you who destroy the temple and in three days build it, save yourself, coming down from the cross. These and other things they spoke as they mocked, dancing in a kind of frenzied leaping.

And perhaps it is then that the words "all flesh" will become more perfectly fulfilled. Now I mean to say, flesh has seen him, but not all flesh. Then, however, at the judgment, as he comes with his angels to judge the living and the dead, "when all who are in tombs hear his voice and come forth, some to the resurrection of life, others to the resurrection of judgment," it is not only the just but also the wicked, those on the right, these on the left, who will see that form which he pleased to take on for us. Even those who killed him "will look on the one whom they have pierced." So "all flesh shall see the salvation of God." Body will be seen by body, because he will come to judge him in his real body. But to those placed on the right and sent on into the kingdom of heaven, he is going to show himself in the same way as he could already be seen in the body; and yet he had said, "Whoever loves me shall be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and manifest myself to him."

He commanded them, among other things, to pray as follows: "And forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors." Or [it may be that] he calls his disciples "evil" because in comparison with the divine goodness, every creature is judged to be evil, as the Lord says, "No one is good except God alone." It is only by participation in the divine goodness that a rational creature is recognized as being capable of becoming good. Hence the Lord also bears witness by a benevolent promise that your heavenly Father will "give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him." This is to the point that those who of themselves are evil can become good through receiving the gift of the Spirit. He pledged that his good Spirit would be given by the Father to those asking for him, because whether we desire to secure faith, hope and charity, or any other heavenly goods at all, they are not bestowed upon us otherwise than by the gift of the Holy Spirit. So it is that the same spirit, in Isaiah, is named the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord; and in another place, the spirit of love and peace, [and] the spirit of grace and prayer. Undoubtedly whatever good we truly have, whatever we do well, this we receive from the lavishness of the same Spirit. When a prophet who understood this was seeking purity of heart, saying, "Create a pure heart in me, O Lord," he immediately added, "Renew an upright spirit in my inmost parts." If the upright spirit of the Lord does not fill our innermost being, we have no pure heart where he may abide. When in his eager longing for and advance in good for his work he had said, "Lord, I have had recourse to you, teach me to do your will," he at once showed in what way he had to secure this when he went on, "Let your good spirit lead me into the right way."

On that day there shall be a great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Adadremmon in the plain of Megiddo. And the land shall mourn, families and families apart; the families of the house of David apart, and the women — or wives —, of them apart — for the Hebrew word nese, that is, γυναῖκες, signifies both —, the families of the house of Nathan apart, and their women apart, the families of the house of Levi apart and their women apart, the families of Shimei apart and their women apart. All the remaining families, families and families apart and their women apart. LXX: On that day there shall be a great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning for the pomegranate that is cut down in the plain, and the land shall mourn by tribes and tribes; the tribe of David apart and their women apart, the tribe of the house of Judah apart and their women apart, the tribe of the house of Nathan apart and their women apart, the tribe of the house of Levi apart and their women apart, the tribe of Simeon apart and their women apart; all the remaining tribes apart and their women apart. Adadremmon, for which the LXX translated ῥοῶνος (of the pomegranate grove), is a city near Jezreel which was once called by this name, and today is called Maximianopolis, in the plain of Megiddo, in which Josiah, the just king, was wounded by the Pharaoh surnamed Necho; over him Jeremiah wrote Lamentations, which are read in the Church, and that he wrote them the book of Chronicles testifies. Just as, therefore, at that time, after the sinful kings, all the hope of the people was in Josiah, and when he was slain a great mourning was stirred up in the city, as we read in the Hebrew: The spirit of our mouth, Christ the Lord, was taken in our sins, to whom we said: In your shadow we shall live among the nations. Although others, according to the spiritual understanding, refer this to the Lord Jesus; so, when the Savior has been crucified, the mourning shall be renewed in Jerusalem, as once it was in the city of Adadremmon, in the plain of Megiddo.

Let us say also that according to the LXX it is called ῥοῶν, not a single tree of pomegranates, that is, of the Punic apple, but a place planted with these trees, of which, according to the spiritual understanding, the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: I went down to see in the produce of the torrent whether the vine had flowered, whether the pomegranates had flowered. For the Savior went down to the torrent of this world and its turbid waters, from which Elijah too, in a type of him, is described as having drunk, so that after the flowers of the vine and of the pomegranate he might receive the fruit of both, and, making his Church drunk, might hear from her: You shall give me to drink of the perfumer's wine, of the wine of my pomegranates. A drink of this kind not only drives away the heats of the stomach, but is also said to heal a corrupted belly and to benefit the other inner organs. For nothing is more beautiful than this fruit; in its redness it signifies the modesty of the Church, in the order of its seeds the ranks and members of the whole body distributed through their several offices. When the Savior has not found fruit in a vine and pomegranates of this kind, he will say: Every branch that does not bear fruit the Father will take away; and every one that bears fruit he will prune, that it may bring more fruit. And in another place John the Baptist cries out: Already the axe is laid to the roots of the trees. Every tree that does not make good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire. At the cutting down of the vines or of the pomegranates, when on the day of judgment all titles of dignity shall be laid down and that which is written shall have been fulfilled: Behold the man and his works; and when the chaff has been separated from the wheat, there shall be a great mourning not in another place but in Jerusalem. For the blow and the judgment shall begin from the saints, and kings and priests and prophets and teachers shall beat their breasts with their hands when they see that the most beautiful pomegranates have been cut down, and him whom they had pierced reigning in the majesty of the Father and his own.

And as they kept silence, I went on: "[The Scripture], speaking by David about this Christ, my friends, said no longer that 'in His seed' the nations should be blessed, but 'in Him.' So it is here: 'His name shall rise up for ever above the sun; and in Him shall all nations be blessed.' But if all nations are blessed in Christ, and we of all nations believe in Him, then He is indeed the Christ, and we are those blessed by Him. God formerly gave the sun as an object of worship, as it is written, but no one ever was seen to endure death on account of his faith in the sun; but for the name of Jesus you may see men of every nation who have endured and do endure all sufferings, rather than deny Him. For the word of His truth and wisdom is more ardent and more light-giving than the rays of the sun, and sinks down into the depths of heart and mind. Hence also the Scripture said, 'His name shall rise up above the sun.' And again, Zechariah says, 'His name is the East.' And speaking of the same, he says that 'each tribe shall mourn.'"

Josiah also was persecuted as Jesus was persecuted. Josiah was persecuted, and Pharaoh the Lame slew Him; and Jesus was persecuted, and the people that were made lame by their sins slew Him. Josiah cleansed the land of Israel from uncleanness; and Jesus cleansed and caused to pass away uncleanness from all the earth. Josiah hallowed and glorified the name of his God; and Jesus said:—I have glorified and will glorify (His Name). Josiah because of the iniquity of Israel rent his clothes; and Jesus because of the iniquity of the people rent the vail of the Holy Temple. Josiah said:—Great is the wrath that shall come upon this people; and Jesus said:—There shall come wrath upon this people, and they shall fall by the edge of the sword. Josiah cast out uncleanness from the Holy Temple; and Jesus cast out the unclean traders from His Father’s house. For Josiah the daughters of Israel mourned and wailed, as Jeremiah said:—O daughters of Israel, weep for Josiah; and over Jesus did the daughters of Israel weep and mourn, as Zechariah said:—The land shall mourn, families over families.

And what follows: The families and families shall mourn, or tribes and tribes, apart: the families of the house of David apart, and the wives or the women of them apart; this signifies that in a time of tribulation and grief we ought not to be given over to marriage and the work of wedlock. Hence also in Joel, when the captivity was near, it is said to the Jews: Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room. And when the flood was impending, Noah is commanded: Enter into the ark, you and your sons, and your wife, and the wives of your sons. And afterwards, when the flood was over, it is said to him: Go out, you and your wife, and your sons, and their wives, so that those who had been separated in the ark while the peril hung over them, once restored to the world, might devote themselves to begetting and to children. And this is done not only in a time of distress but also in a time of prayer, when we wish to entreat the Lord, as the Apostle says to the Corinthians: Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by consent for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer. Therefore now too the tribe of the house of David, and the tribe of the house of Nathan, and the tribe of the house of Levi, and the tribe of the house of Shimei are separated from their wives, so that they may mourn the only-begotten and firstborn Lord Jesus, of whom it had been said: His blood be upon us and upon our children. In David the royal tribe is understood, that is, Judah. In Nathan the prophetic order is described. Levi refers to the priests, from whom the priesthood arose. In Shimei the teachers are understood, for from this tribe the hosts of the masters sprang up.

He was silent about the remaining tribes, which have no privilege of dignity. But in saying: All the remaining tribes, tribes and tribes apart, and their wives apart, he includes them all without a name.
13: On that day there shall be a fountain open to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman. LXX: On that day every place shall be opened in the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, both for transformation and for sprinkling. Of this fountain, which goes forth from the house of David, it is written also in the prophet Ezekiel that a fountain bursts forth in the house of the Lord and grows into a river, which is called the water of remission and pardon, and goes on to the wilderness and to the sea which is now called the Dead Sea, and gives life to all the fish, and on either bank of the river trees of various kinds rise up, always abounding with new fruits month by month. And so that we may know that the house, that is, the temple of God, is itself the house of David, which in Ezekiel is called the house of God and in Zechariah the house of David, this fountain going forth from the house of God is referred to the Church and to the knowledge of the Scriptures, so that we may all be reborn in Christ and our sins may be forgiven us in the water of baptism. Nothing is more unclean than a menstruous woman, who makes unclean whatever she touches, and yet her filth shall be washed away by the baptism of Christ. For the washing of sins and of the menstruous woman the LXX translated transformation and sprinkling, because we pass over from the law to the Gospel, from the letter to the spirit, from the shadow to the truth, and things future and eternal succeed in place of things brief and present. And the sprinkling signifies the blood of the Lord, of which the apostle Peter also speaks: Grace to you, and peace be multiplied, unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, and again: Knowing that you were redeemed not with corruptible things, silver and gold, but with the precious blood as of a lamb unspotted and most pure; whoever has been sprinkled and redeemed with it will be able to say with the prophet: You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.

Let us see, then, the necessity of literary erudition; let us reflect that partly it cannot be admitted, partly cannot be avoided. Learning literature is allowable for believers, rather than teaching; for the principle of learning and teaching is different. If a believer teaches literature, while he teaches doubtless he commends, while he delivers he affirms, while he recalls he bears testimony to, the praise of idols interspersed therein. He seals the gods themselves with this name [of gods], whereas the law, as we have said, prohibits "the names of gods to be pronounced" and this name [of God] to be conferred on vanity. Hence the devil gets people's early faith built up from the beginnings of erudition. Inquire whether he who catechizes about idols commits idolatry. But when a believer learns these things, if he is already capable of understanding what idolatry is, he neither receives nor allows them; much more if he is not yet capable. Or, when he begins to understand, it behooves him first to understand what he has previously learned, that is, touching God and the faith. Therefore he will reject those things and will not receive them; and [the believer] will be as safe as one who knows it not, who knowingly accepts poison but does not drink it. To him necessity is attributed as an excuse, because he has no other way to learn. Moreover, the not teaching literature is as much easier than the not learning, as it is easier too for the pupil not to attend than for the master not to frequent the rest of the defilements incident to the schools from public and scholastic solemnities.

And it shall be on that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will destroy the names of the idols from the land, and they shall be remembered no more; and the prophets and the unclean spirit I will take away from the land. LXX: And it shall be on that day, says the Lord Sabaoth, I will destroy the names of the idols from the land, and there shall be no more remembrance of them; and the false prophets and the unclean spirit I will take away from the land. On that day, which he mentions so often, all idols shall be taken away from the land: whether those idols of which the psalmist says: The images of the nations are silver and gold, the works of men's hands, so that there may be no other religion but only that of the Christian name, and of which it is written in the prophet: Howl, you carved images in Jerusalem and in Samaria. For as I have done to Samaria and to her carved images, so will I do to Jerusalem and to her idols; or those idols of which the Apostle speaks: But the Spirit says manifestly that in the last times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons, in the hypocrisy of liars who have their conscience cauterized. For just as idols are made by the hand of a craftsman, so the perverse doctrine of the heretics turns into an idol whatever it has feigned, and causes the antichrist to be worshipped in place of Christ. For false prophets, in the Hebrew prophets is read absolutely, that is, nebim, who themselves also signify false prophets; but besides, the priests of the idols are also called prophets by the heathen.

Hermes Trismegistus lamented these vain, deceptive, pernicious, sacrilegious things because he foresaw that the time was coming when they would be abolished. He was impudent in his grief as imprudent in his prophecy, since the Holy Spirit had made no revelation to him as to the holy prophets, who exultantly proclaimed their inspired visions: "Shall a man make gods to himself, and they are no gods?" and again, "And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord of hosts, that I will destroy the names of the idols out of the earth, and they shall be remembered no more." It is relevant to recall that holy Isaiah uttered a particular prophecy concerning Egypt: "And the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst thereof," and the rest.

And it shall be, when anyone prophesies any more, his father and his mother, who begot him, shall say to him: You shall not live, because you have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord; and his father and his mother, who begot him, shall pierce him when he prophesies. LXX: And it shall be, if a man prophesies any more, his father and his mother, who begot him, shall say to him: You shall not live, because you have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord; and his father and his mother who begot him shall fetter him when he prophesies. When the names of the idols have been taken away from the land, and the false prophets, and the unclean spirit that spoke in them, if anyone wishes to try any more and to prophesy something in the person of the Lord, at once his father and mother will forget that they are parents, so as to hold fast to the service of God, and they will pronounce the sentence of death against their son; and the minds of all will be so devout toward God that no public judgment will be awaited, but those who are such will perish by the sentence of their kinsfolk. For what we have rendered, they shall pierce him, there is in the Hebrew the same word as above, dacaru. By what reasoning, then, did the LXX translators choose to translate there κατωρχήσαντο, that is, they insulted, or they mocked, and, to render word for word, they danced against him, and here συμποδιοῦσιν, that is, they shall fetter, when Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion rendered alike both there and here: they pierced? And rightly is he who has prophesied falsehoods called a man, as the Apostle says: For since there are among you rivalries and contentions, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man? And in the psalms: But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes. And those unworthy of the Spirit of God deserve to hear: My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.

And it shall be on that day, the prophets shall be confounded, each one by his vision when he has prophesied, nor shall they be covered with a cloak of sackcloth in order to lie. But he shall say: I am not a prophet, I am a man, a tiller of the ground, for Adam has been my example from my youth. And it shall be said to him: What are these wounds in the middle of your hands? And he shall say: With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me. LXX: And it shall be on that day, the prophets shall be confounded, each one by his vision when he has prophesied, and they shall put on a skin of haircloth because they have lied; and he shall say: I am not a prophet, for a man begot me from my youth. And I will say to him: What are these wounds in the middle of your hands? And he shall say: Those with which I was struck in the house of the one who loved me. Whoever has attempted to prophesy, and has been condemned by the judgment of his parents, and whose prophecy has been proved false by the contrary outcome of events, shall be confounded by his vision, and shall no longer be covered with haircloth in order to lie. For this was the habit of the prophets: that when they were calling the people to repentance, they put on haircloth. Hence Isaiah too is commanded to take the sackcloth from his loins and to walk naked; for it was by no means a time of repentance, but of impending captivity.

What is written, Nor shall they be covered with a cloak of sackcloth in order to lie, the Hebrews expound thus: and they shall not be filled with the demonic spirit, those whom we read of in Isaiah as τριχιῶντας, that is, hairy ones, lest on this occasion of a feigned habit they belie the utterances of God within them, or deny God. For Chaesu can be interpreted both 'they shall lie' and 'they shall deny'.

Therefore this false prophet too will by no means take up the prophetic habit, lest under another's clothing and covering he deceive all the simple, but rather he will cleave the earth with the ploughshare and, given over to farming, will prove himself a man, and subject to the sentence of God, who spoke to Adam: Cursed is the ground in your work; in toil you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth; and in the sweat of your face you shall eat bread.

Again, in Zechariah thirteen it is said: I am a husbandman, for Adam has been my example from my youth; Gloss: "That I may eat my bread in the sweat of my face, while he showed himself born for this, that in the sweat of his face he might eat bread"; but this most befits one who needs bread and can bear labor and sweat; and such is the able-bodied poor person: therefore he is bound to labor bodily.
Disputed Questions on Evangelical Perfection, Question 2

And when he has shown that he was born for this, to eat his bread in the sweat of his face, another will question him and say: What do these wounds mean, and these gashes that are in the middle of your hands? And the sense is: Why do you cling to the gibbet? Why are your hands pierced with nails? What have you committed, that you should be subjected to this penalty and torment? And he will answer and say: These gashes and these wounds I received, condemned by the judgment of my parents and of those who did not hate me but loved me. And truth will prevail so far, once falsehood has been put to flight, that even he who has been punished for his own fault confesses that he has suffered justly.
And I will say unto him, What are these wounds between thine hands? And he shall say, wounds which I received in the house beloved by me.

And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives.  And Jesus saith unto them, All ye shall be offended because of me this night: for it is written, I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered. [Zechariah 13:7] But after that I am risen, I will go before you into Galilee.

And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives.  Then saith Jesus unto them, All ye shall be offended because of me this night: for it is written, I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered abroad. [Zechariah 13:7] But after I am risen again, I will go before you into Galilee.

Moreover, the prophet Zechariah foretold that this same Christ would be smitten, and His disciples scattered: which also took place. For after His crucifixion, the disciples that accompanied Him were dispersed, until He rose from the dead, and persuaded them that so it had been prophesied concerning Him, that He would suffer; and being thus persuaded, they went into all the world, and taught these truths. Hence also we are strong in His faith and doctrine, since we have [this our] persuasion both from the prophets, and from those who throughout the world are seen to be worshippers of God in the name of that crucified One. The following is said, too, by Zechariah: "O sword, rise up against My Shepherd, and against the man of My people, saith the Lord of hosts. Smite the Shepherd, and His flock shall be scattered."

Besides, Christ himself has confirmed this prefigurement of himself when he said that a shepherd who flees when he sees the wolf and leaves the flock to be devoured is wicked. Such a shepherd will be banished from the farm; his separation pay will be kept from him as compensation for his damage; in fact, he will have to pay back something from his former wages to indemnify the losses of the master. "For to him who has shall be given and from him who does not have even that which he seems to have shall be taken away." Thus Zechariah threatens, "Arise, O sword, against the shepherds, and pluck out the sheep, and I will turn my hand against the shepherds." And against them Ezekiel and Jeremiah thunder with similar recriminations, in that they have not merely battened upon their sheep and fattened themselves but they have themselves dispersed the flock and, without a leader to guide them, left them as prey to all the beasts of the field. For this is what happens when the church is deserted by the clergy in time of persecution.
ON FLIGHT IN TIME OF PERSECUTION 11:2

If there is anyone who, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the law which is written according to the letter displeases him, because in many things it does not seem to preserve consistency, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, and leads him to it, that he may drink from there and refresh his thirst. But this rock, unless it be struck, will not give waters; but when struck it brings forth fountains. For Christ, when struck and driven to the cross, brought forth the fountains of the New Testament; and therefore it was said of Him that "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered". It was necessary, then, that He be struck; for unless He had been struck and "water and blood had come forth from His side", we should all suffer "a thirst for the word of God". This, then, is what the Apostle also interpreted, that "they all ate the same spiritual food, and they all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed; and the rock was Christ". Observe, however, what God said in this place to Moses: "go before the people, and take with you the elders, that is, the presbyters of the people". Not Moses alone leads the people to the waters of the rock, but also the elders of the people with him. For not the law alone announces Christ, but also the prophets and the patriarchs and all the "elders".

Christ spoke of the betrayer; he foretold that all would run away; he predicted his own death. "I shall smite the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered." He foretold who was going to deny him, when he would do so, and how many times it would happen. He predicted everything accurately. After he had foretold all these things as a sufficient proof that he possessed knowledge of what was going to happen, he went to a certain place to pray. The heretics say that the prayer is the prayer of the divinity; we say it is the prayer of the plan of redemption.

O sword, be roused against my shepherd and against the man who cleaves to me, says the Lord of hosts. Strike the shepherd and the sheep shall be scattered, and I will turn my hand to the little ones. And there shall be in all the land, says the Lord: two parts in it shall be destroyed and shall fail, and the third part shall be left in it. And I will lead the third part through fire, and I will burn them as silver is burned, and I will test them as gold is tested. He shall call on my name and I will hear him; I will say: You are my people; and he shall say: The Lord is my God. LXX: O sword, arise against my shepherd and against the man his fellow citizen, says the Lord Almighty. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered, and I will bring my hand upon the shepherds. And it shall be on that day, says the Lord, two parts shall perish and shall fail, and the third part shall be left in it; and I will lead the third part across through fire, and I will burn them as silver is burned and I will test them as gold is tested. He shall invoke my name, and I will hear him and will say: This is my people; and he shall say: You are the Lord my God. For sword (framea), which the LXX translated ῥομφαίαν, we find in the Hebrew areb, and in Aquila and Symmachus μάχαιραν, that is, sword or point. And for what we have rendered, Against the man who cleaves to me, that is, προσκεκολλημένον μοι, Aquila translated: Against the man of my tribe, that is, σύμφυλόν μοι. Symmachus: Against the man of my people, which in Hebrew is said amithi. The LXX: Against the man his fellow citizen. Theodotion: Against the man his neighbor; they read vav at the end of the word instead of yod, letters which differ from each other only in size; and if yod is read it means 'my', if vav, 'his'. But I am amazed that some wish to thin out with allegorical interpretations this prophecy — which the evangelist Matthew referred to the Lord and Savior after the disciples fled at his passion, and says that it was then fulfilled —, and, while they want to seem to know more than the rest, do not hold to the rule of truth. For the evangelist Matthew relates: Then Jesus says to them: You will all take offense at me this night. For it is written: I will strike the shepherd and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered. And again: But all this was done that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples, leaving him, fled. Nor should it be thought that the testimony was taken from another place because in the Gospel God says that the shepherd was struck by himself, while in the present place we read that the sword and the point are commanded: Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered. This is the sword, and this is the broadsword and the sword (framea), of which the Lord also speaks to the Father in Psalm 21 (22): Deliver my soul from the sword and my only one from the hand of the dog. Of this broadsword it is also written in Amos the prophet: All the sinners of the earth shall die by the sword. This cannot stand at all according to the letter, for many sinners perish by shipwreck, others by poison; these are choked by water, those a fire consumes. But by this sword and this broadsword all sinners perish, and the Ethiopians of black color too, of whom Zephaniah testifies with his sacred mouth, saying: But you also, Ethiopians, shall be slain by my sword. After the good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep, who spoke to the Father: Him whom you struck they have persecuted, and they have added to the pain of my wounds, was struck by the Father's will, and the man who cleaves to God, who says: I am in the Father, and the Father in me, hung on the gibbet and said: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit, at once the sheep were scattered, the whole multitude of believers in Christ. And the Lord turned his hand, as is read in the LXX, to the shepherds, whom many wrongly interpret as the princes of the Jews. But as it is written in the Hebrew, to the little ones, to whom the Lord had said in the Gospel: Fear not, little flock, and in Isaiah: Behold I and the children, or the little ones whom the Lord has given me.

For it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered. This is written in other words in Zechariah the prophet, and, unless I am mistaken, it is said in the person of the prophet to God: Strike the shepherd, and let the sheep be scattered, Psalm 68 (69) also, which is sung throughout in the Lord's person, agreeing with this sense: For they have persecuted him whom you have struck. And the good shepherd is struck so that he may lay down his life for his sheep, and that out of many flocks of errors there may be made one flock and one shepherd. Of this testimony more has been said in the little book which we wrote on the best kind of translating.

There was, therefore, a great and excellent faith in that thief. Clearly it is great and admirable faith which believed that the crucified Christ was being glorified more than punished. For this is the shape that all salvation takes—that the Savior should be recognized as the Lord of majesty when he is seen to be crucified and subject to humiliation. Hence the apostle says, "If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty." This, I say, is an excellent faith, to believe that Christ on the cross is God and not a wrongdoer. Therefore that thief was justified while the Jews insulted the Savior on the gibbet and said to him as if he were a criminal, "Free yourself if you are able." But [the thief], certain of Christ's divinity and sure of his good will, asks instead to be freed himself. There was a great faith in that thief, I say, and one which was comparable to that of the holy apostles; indeed, it preceded theirs. For he who preceded with respect to devotion preceded with respect to the prize, for the thief came to paradise before the apostles did. Peter follows the Lord, and this man accompanies him. But the Lord gives him a reward according to faith and merit, for, as we read, all the disciples were afraid during the Savior's suffering, and all left him just when he was betrayed. It happened as it was written: "I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered."

I will smite the shepherd and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered. Of this passage also the Lord made mention at the time of his Passion, applying it to himself when he was on the point of being betrayed.

And two parts were made in all the land, of the Jews and of the Gentiles, who perished alike and failed. For at his passion the voice of the psalmist was fulfilled, saying: Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed, and: All have turned aside, together they have become useless; there is none who does good, there is not even one. As the Gentiles and the Jews were perishing, a third part in the world, that is, the third people, of Christians, suddenly sprang up. And he says beautifully: The third part shall be left in it, that is, in the land, because of the Jews and the Gentiles those alone who confessed the Lord were kept for life and for dwelling in the land.

These cases occur in persecutions more than at other times (for it is then that we are approved or condemned, humbled or corrected). Their general occurrence is permitted or commanded by him at whose will they happen even partially; by him, I mean, who says, "I am he who makes peace and creates evil"—that is, war, for that is the antithesis of peace. But what other war has our peace than persecution? If in its issues persecution emphatically brings either life or death, either wounds or healing, you have the author too of this. "I will smite and heal, I will make alive and put to death." "I will burn them," he says, "as gold is burned; and I will try them," he says, "as silver is tried," for when the flame of persecution is consuming us, then the steadfastness of our faith is proved. These will be the fiery darts of the devil, by which faith gets a ministry of burning and kindling; yet by the will of God. As to this I do not know who can doubt, unless it be persons with frivolous and frigid faith, which seizes upon those who with trembling assemble together in the church. For you say, seeing we assemble without order, and assemble at the same time, and flock in large numbers to the church, the heathen are led to make inquiry about us, and we are alarmed lest we awaken their anxieties. Do you not know that God is Lord of all? And if it is God's will, then you shall suffer persecution; but if it is not, the heathen will be still. Believe it most surely, if indeed you believe in that God without whose will not even the sparrow, which a penny can buy, falls to the ground. But we, I think, are better than many sparrows.
ON FLIGHT IN TIME OF PERSECUTION 3

And that this third part too might not be soft, and its confession careless, it is led through fire and tested like silver and gold, the fire which the Lord too longs to blaze in believers and Paul desires to be fervent. Hence the apostles too, baptized in the Spirit and in the fire of the Lord, speak in the psalm: For you have tested us, O God; you have tried us with fire as silver is tried. And a little after: We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment. And in another place it is said to the believer: If you pass through fire, the flame shall not burn you, because I am with you. And the reason the fire does not consume and the flame does not devour is this: For the voice of the Lord cuts through the flame of fire. When the little ones, over whom the Lord turned his hand, have been tested in this way, and through their calling the whole throng of the nations has believed, then the people of believers will call Christ by his name, and when he says: You are my people, the people will answer: You are the Lord my God. The Jews refer these things to Christ and contend that they will come to pass in the last time, but the difference between us and them is this: we say that they have already been fulfilled, they speak of them as yet to be fulfilled.
14:
[Passage quoted, Zech. xiv. 1, 2.]

The fulfilment of this also agrees with the passages quoted on the destruction of the whole Jewish race, which came upon them after the coming of Christ. For Zechariah writes this prophecy after the return from Babylon, foretelling the final siege of the people by the Romans, through which the whole Jewish race was to become subject to their enemies : he says that only the remnant of the people shall be saved, exactly describing the apostles of our Saviour.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

[Passage quoted, Zech. xiv. 1-10.]

AFTER the first siege of Jerusalem, and its total destruction and desolation by the Babylonians, and after the Return of the Jews from their enemies' land to their own, which came to pass in the time of Cyrus king of Persia, when Jerusalem has just been restored, and the Temple and its Altar renewed by Darius the Persian, the present prophecy foretells a second siege of Jerusalem which is to take place afterwards, which it suffered from the Romans, after its inhabitants had carried through their outrage on our Saviour Jesus Christ. Thus the coming of our Saviour and the events connected therewith are very clearly shewn in this passage—I mean what was done at the time of His Passion, and the siege that came on the Hebrew race directly after, the taking of Jerusalem, the call of the Gentiles also, and the knowledge attained by all nations of the one and only God. But the inspired prophet pathetically bewails the woes of the Jews as those of his own people, and begins his prophecy with a cry against them. He means by "days of the Lord," here as well as in other places, the time of our Lord's presence among men. And he clearly shews how the Lord Himself, as being the true Light, will become some day the maker of His own days, and will shine on all men in the world, all the nations receiving Him and the rays of His light, when all nations are enlightened, according to the words, "I have set Thee for a light to the Gentiles, for a covenant of my race," and the Jewish nation through their unbelief will fall into great trouble.

For such is the meaning of "Behold the days of the Lord come, and thy spoils shall be divided within thee, and I will gather all the Gentiles to Jerusalem to war. And the city shall be taken, the houses plundered, and the women ravished, and half of the city shall go into captivity."

And after the siege of Jerusalem, and the captivity of the Jews which succeeds it, he next adds a prophecy of good things for all: "And the Lord shall be King over all the earth." And again: "There shall be one Lord, and his name one, encircling all the earth and the wilderness."

But who would not be surprised at the fulfilment of a prophecy which revealed that the Jewish people would undergo these sufferings in the days of the Lord? For as soon as Jesus our Lord and Saviour had come and the Jews had outraged Him, everything that had been predicted was fulfilled against them without exception 500 years after the prediction: from the time of Pontius Pilate to the sieges under Nero, Titus and Vespasian they were never free from all kinds of successive calamities, as you may gather from the history of Flavius Josephus. It is probable that half the city at that time perished in the siege, as the prophecy says. And not long after, in the reign of Hadrian, there was another Jewish revolution, and the remaining half of the city was again besieged and driven out, so that from that day to this the whole place has not been trodden by them.

Now if any one supposes that this was fulfilled in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, let him inquire if the rest of the prophecy can be referred to the times of Antiochus —I mean the captivity undergone by the people, the standing of the Lord's feet on the Mount of Olives, and whether the Lord became King of all the earth in that day, and whether the name of the Lord encircled the whole earth and the desert during the reign of Antiochus. And how can the fulfilment of the remainder of the prophecy in the days of Antiochus be asserted? But, according to my interpretation, they are fulfilled both literally and also in another sense. For after the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ, their city, Jerusalem itself, and the whole system and institutions of the Mosaic worship were destroyed; and at once they underwent captivity in mind as well as body, in refusing to accept the Saviour and Ransomer of the souls of men, Him Who came to preach release to those enslaved by evil daemons, and giving of sight to those blind in mind. And while they suffered through their unbelief, those of them who recognized their Ransomer became His own disciples, apostles and evangelists, and many others of the Jews believed on Him, of whom the apostle says, "So also now there is a remnant according to the election of grace." And "If the Lord of Sabaoth had not left unto us a seed we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorra." They were preserved safe from the metaphorical siege, and also from the siege literally understood. For the apostles and disciples of our Saviour, and all the Jews that believed on Him, being far from the land of Judaea, and scattered among the other nations, were enabled at that time to escape the ruin of the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And the prophecy anticipated and foretold this where it said, "And the remnant of my people shall not be utterly destroyed." To which it adds afterwards, "And the Lord shall go forth, and shall fight for those nations, as a day of his battle in the day of war." For which nations will the Lord fight, but for those that shall besiege Jerusalem? The passage shews that the Lord Himself will fight for the besiegers, being among them and drawn up with them, like their general and commander warring against Jerusalem. For it does not say that the Lord will fight against the nations. With whom and against whom, then, will He fight? Surely against Jerusalem and her inhabitants, concerning whom it is spoken.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 18

And which were the days after the age of Zechariah, when the spoils of Jerusalem were divided, and all nations were gathered against them in battle, and the city was taken, their houses looted, their women defiled, and they themselves led into captivity, while the Lord was at the same time aiding the nations warring against Jerusalem and drawn up against them? Or when did His feet stand on the Mount of Olives? Or when was the Lord King of all the earth, when was there one Lord over all men, when did His Name encircle the whole earth and the wilderness? It is impossible to argue that this was fulfilled previously to the period of the Romans, in whose time the Jewish Temple was burnt for the second time after its destruction by the Babylonians, and their city from then till now has been inhabited by foreign nations.

And it was when our Lord Jesus, the Christ of God, had visited the olive-grove over against Jerusalem, since the words of the prophecy were fulfilled which said, "His feet shall stand upon the Mount of Olives opposite to Jerusalem," that is, the life of holiness having been established throughout all the world, that all the nations, according to the prophecy, kept the Feast of Tabernacles together in every place to the God of the prophets, and the Egyptians from that time recognizing God erected tents in every town and country place, which mean the local Christian Churches. For the power of our Saviour Jesus Christ has pegged them far better than Moses' tents through the whole world, so that every race of men and all the Gentiles may keep their Feast of Tabernacles to Almighty God.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 4

Behold, the days of the Lord shall come, and your spoils shall be divided in the midst of you. And I will gather all the nations to Jerusalem for battle, and the city shall be taken, and the houses shall be laid waste, and the women shall be violated, and half of the city shall go forth into captivity, and the rest of the people shall not be taken away from the city. LXX: Behold, the days of the Lord come, and your spoils shall be divided in you, and I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem, to make war; and the city shall be taken, and the houses shall be plundered and the women shall be defiled, and half of the city shall go forth into captivity; but the rest of my people shall not perish from the city. The days which the Lord threatens shall come, so that the spoils of Jerusalem are divided in the midst of it, and the other things that the prophetic word includes, are those of which we also read in Isaiah: The day of the Lord shall come, incurable, of fury and of wrath, to lay the whole world waste, and to take away the sinners from it. But how great will the distress be, that its spoils are divided in the midst of it? It often happens that what has been plundered in a city by a sudden assault is divided outside, in the field or in the wilderness, lest perhaps an enemy come upon them. But here so great a weight of evils will press down that what has been plundered is divided in the middle of the city, so secure is the victory.

And not only shall Jerusalem be taken, when all the nations have been roused against it in battle, but also the houses of those who dwell in Jerusalem shall be laid waste, and the women shall be violated, to the grief of their masters and husbands, who will be able to prevent neither the pillaging of their houses nor the rape of their wives by the enemy, according to what we read elsewhere: Those who are gathered in the midst of you shall fall by the sword, and they shall dash your sons to pieces in your sight, and they shall plunder your houses, and they shall have your wives; nothing crueller and nothing more wretched than this can be found, that from fear of their own death they dare to defend neither the safety of their sons nor the chastity of their wives. Amos the prophet too says this very thing, threatening Amaziah the impious priest: Your wife shall play the harlot in the city, and your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword, and your ground shall be measured with a line. And all these things shall befall the people of the Jews: For the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things. The kings of the earth stood by and the princes came together as one against the Lord and against his Christ. And he laughed at them and derided them, and troubled them in his fury, so much so that the Apostle too, seeing that the years which had been given them for repentance were now completed, and that those who killed the Lord and persecuted the prophets and the apostles nevertheless persisted in denial, said: Wrath has come upon them to the end. Josephus, who wrote the Jewish history, relates most fully that they endured all these things, and things much greater than we read in the prophets; so too Cornelius Tacitus, who set down in thirty volumes the lives of the Caesars after Augustus up to the death of Domitian. But how half of the city was taken and the rest of the people remained in the city is proved both at that time and at others: the northern and lower part of the city was taken, but the mountain of the temple, and Zion, on which the citadel was, remained intact. The Jews say that these things are to be fulfilled under Gog, others that they were in part accomplished in the times of the Macedonians and the Egyptians and of various nations. We, leaving the variety of the times to the judgment of the Lord, let us explain what is written.

And the Lord shall go forth, and shall fight against those nations, as he fought on the day of conflict. And his feet shall stand on that day upon the Mount of Olives, which is opposite Jerusalem to the east; and the Mount of Olives shall be split from the middle of itself to the east and to the west, with a very great chasm. LXX: And the Lord shall go forth, and shall fight against those nations, as on the day of engagement, and on the day of battle. And his feet shall stand on that day upon the Mount of Olives, which is opposite Jerusalem on the eastern side. And the Mount of Olives shall be split, half of it to the east, and half of it to the sea, with an exceedingly great abyss. That God goes forth, and fights against the nations, and that his feet stand upon the Mount of Olives, and the other things that are said ἀνθρωποπάθως (in human fashion) in the holy scriptures and are contained there in a fleshly way, we ought to take in a manner worthy of God. Otherwise, since the Apostle says: Who is the image of the invisible God, and again: To the King of the ages, incorruptible, invisible, God, and it is written in the Gospel: No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known, and again: Not that anyone has seen God, except him who is from the Father; just as we take his wrath and repentance and soul and hands, and feet and belly, and eyes and the other members of the body according to the variety of the occasions and of the senses of interpretation, so too what is written, The Lord shall go forth, and shall fight, is to be taken according to what we read in Habakkuk: You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ, and in Micah: For behold, the Lord shall go forth from his place, and shall come down and tread upon the high places of the earth, and the mountains shall be consumed beneath him, and the valleys shall be split, and in Isaiah too: The Lord of powers shall go forth and crush the war, and shall stir up zeal and shall cry out over his enemies with strength. God therefore goes forth from his place when he is compelled to break off his quiet and gentleness and clemency for the correction of those who sin; though he is sweet by nature, by our fault he παραπικραίνεται, that is, is made bitter, not to himself, but to those who suffer, to whom the torments are bitter. He who elsewhere says through the prophet: I am God, and I do not change, and to whom it is said: But you are the same, and you endure, and in the epistle of James: With whom there is no change, now goes forth and fights as on the day of conflict, when he drowned Pharaoh in the Red Sea and fought for the people of Israel.

And the words, "And his feet shall stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem to the eastward," what else can they mean than that the Lord God, that is to say the Word of God Himself, will stand, and stand firm, upon His Church, which is here metaphorically called the Mount of Olives? For as "My Beloved had a vineyard," and "There was a vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth," are used in a figurative sense of "the house of Israel and the plant of Judah His beloved vine," so also we may say in the same sense that the Church of the Gentiles has become an olive-garden to the Master, which of old He planted with wild olives, and grafted them on the apostolic roots of the good olive after cutting away the old branches, as the apostle teaches. And the Lord planted it for Himself, saying as much in the prophecy: "The Lord hath called thy name a beautiful and shady olive." For when the first vineyard should have brought forth grapes it brought forth thorns, and not justice but a cry, God rightly withdrew from it as unfruitful, its mound and its wall, and gave it to its enemies, "to rob and to tread down," according to the prophecy of Isaiah, but established another field for Himself, here named "the olive-garden," as that which had obtained God's mercy, and been planted by Christ with ever-flourishing plants, that is with souls that are holy and nourish the light, which can say, "I am like a fruitful olive-tree in the house of God."

And this Mount of Olives is said to be over against Jerusalem, because it was established by God after the fall of Jerusalem, instead of the old earthly Jerusalem and its worship. For as Scripture said above with reference to Jerusalem: "The city shall be taken, and the nations that are her enemies and foes shall be gathered together against her, and her spoils shall be divided," it could not say that the feet of the Lord should stand upon Jerusalem. How could that be, once it were destroyed? But it says that they will stand with them that depart from it to the mount opposite the city called the Mount of Olives. And this, too, the prophet Ezekiel anticipates by the Holy Spirit and foretells. For he says:

"22. And the Cherubim lifted their wings, and the wheels beside them, 23. and the glory of the God of Israel was on them above them, and he stood on the mount which was opposite to the city."

Which it is possible for us to see literally fulfilled in another way even to-day, since believers in Christ all congregate from all parts of the world, not as of old time because of the glory of Jerusalem, nor that they may worship in the ancient Temple at Jerusalem, but they rest there that they may learn both about the city being taken and devastated as the prophets foretold, and that they may worship at the Mount of Olives opposite to the city, whither the glory of the Lord migrated when it left the former city. There stood in truth according to the common and received account the feet of our Lord and Saviour, Himself the Word of God, through that tabernacle of humanity He had borne up the Mount of Olives to the cave that is shewn there; there He prayed and delivered to His disciples on the summit of the Mount of Olives the mysteries of His end, and thence He made His Ascension into heaven, as Luke tells us in the Acts of the Apostles, saying that while the apostles were with Him on the Mount of Olives:

"While they beheld he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight. And as they gazed steadfastly into heaven while he went up, behold two men stood by them in white apparel, who also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing into heaven? This same Jesus that is taken up from you into heaven shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven."

To which he adds: "Then they returned from the mount called the Mount of Olives, which is opposite to Jerusalem." The Mount of Olives is therefore literally opposite to Jerusalem and to the east of it, but also the Holy Church of God, and the mount upon which it is founded, of which the Saviour teaches: "A city set on a hill cannot be hid," raised up in place of Jerusalem that is fallen never to rise again, and thought worthy of the feet of the Lord, is figuratively not only opposite to Jerusalem, but east of it as well, receiving the rays of the divine light, and become much before Jerusalem, and near to the Sun of Righteousness Himself, of Whom it is said: "And on them that fear me shall the sun of righteousness arise."

And if it says next: "That the Mount of Olives shall be divided, half of it to the east and towards the sea, a very great chasm, and half of it shall lean towards the north, and half of it towards the south," it possibly shews the expansion of the Church throughout the whole inhabited world, for it has filled the east, and the western and eastern nations; it stretches to the western sea, and the isles therein; yea, it has reached to west and south, and to north and north-east. On all sides and everywhere the Church figuratively called the Olive of the Lord is planted. And it is possible that by its division is figuratively meant the schisms and heresies and moral declensions in everyday life that have taken place in the Church of Christ, and are even now taking place; for it says, the mountain shall be divided, half of it towards the east and the sea, a very great chasm, and half of it shall lean towards the north, and half of it towards the south, as being divided into four parts, two of which are worthier and better, and two the reverse. And note in this passage how the part to the east and the part to the south may refer to two sections of those who have made progress in the things of God, the first those who are perfected in knowledge and reason and the other graces of the Holy Spirit; and the second, those who live a good life but pass their time in ways self-chosen. And the other two parts separated from the first, one to the sea and one towards the north, both signify tendency to evil. For "from the face of the north," he says, "shall be burned the evil of all the inhabitants of the earth," while the Dragon is said to have his home in the sea. So that, probably, two kinds of character in those that fall away from the Church, the morally sinful, and the one who slips away from healthy and orthodox knowledge, are here figuratively represented by the prophecy as divisions in the Mount of Olives.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 18

But it might happen that he should sit upon a foal; give us rather a sign where the king who enters will stand. Give us a sign not far from the city, that it may not be unknown to us; give us a sign nearby and clearly visible, that being in the city we may behold the place. Again the prophet answers, saying, "That day his feet shall rest upon the Mount of Olives, which is opposite Jerusalem to the east." Is it possible for anyone standing within the city not to behold the place?

Let us speak παραφραστικῶς (by paraphrase), so that what is written may become clear: When the Mount of Olivet has been broken open by a great abyss, so that one part of the abyss faces east, the other west, suddenly in that very abyss, sheer and lofty on either side, another abyss will break open, one toward the north, another toward the south, and the chasm will become four-cornered, so that the abyss stretches in four directions, to the four quarters of east and west, of north and south. And you shall flee, he says, to the valley that is between the temple and Zion. For these two mountains, of the temple and of Zion, are called the mountains of God; because that valley of the Mount of Olivet, which is girded on this side and that by sheer mountains, will draw its abyss as far as the mountain of the temple, which is holy. But the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah is said to belong to that time when Uzziah, who is called by another name Azariah, trying to claim for himself a priesthood not lawful for him, was struck with leprosy on his forehead; of this earthquake we also read at the beginning of Amos: The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake. In short, after this wicked king died, at whose impiety the whole earth was shaken, Isaiah saw the great vision which he wove into his book. Let us pass to the spiritual understanding. After the Mount of Olives has been separated toward the east and the west by the calling of the nations and the casting off of the Jews, there will again be another cleft, of north and south. The north will be joined to the west, the south to the eastern quarter; on the left will stand the circumcision, on the right the Christian people. Of these two winds the Church speaks: Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind, so that, as the north wind, a most cold wind, which is interpreted as the devil, withdraws, the south wind, a warm wind, may come; seeking him, the bride says: Where do you pasture, where do you lie down, at noon? Of him Habakkuk too speaks mystically: God will come from Teman; for which it is written in the Hebrew: God from the south, that is, from the fullest light. Of this light the psalmist elsewhere cries out: You give light wonderfully from the everlasting mountains. But when the division of the two peoples in the whole world has become so great that some are separated toward the east and the south, that is, to the right, others toward the north and the west, that is to say, to the left, then whoever is holy will flee to the valley of the mountains of God, of which we spoke above, of the temple and of Zion, that is to say, the two testaments, for that abyss which had formerly belonged to each mountain will stretch as far as Asael, that is, as far as the house of God, which is near to paradise, and to the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the holy mountain on which the temple is set. And as at that time when, under King Uzziah the leper, a most violent earthquake terrified the hearts of mortals and scattered them, terrified, this way and that. So the separation of the two peoples, and again the fellowship of believers in one faith, will rest between the two mountains in a peaceful seat, for the old and the new instrument will both be joined to each other. But what is said, As far as Asael, that is, as far as the nearest, means this: that the two instruments, of the law and of the Gospel, are indeed joined to each other, but joined in such a way that they are neighbors rather than one; for we have let go many things of the old law, and have taken up many of the new grace. And when this has been accomplished in this manner, then, he says, the Lord my God shall come, and all the saints with him. But if, for what we have said, you shall flee, we wish to follow what the other translators translated, The valley of their mountains shall be stopped up, or shall be filled, we shall say this: that the coming of the Lord and Savior, when the two peoples have been separated from each other, stops up and fills that abyss which divided the two peoples, so that they may walk toward each other on a level road.

And his feet shall stand for those on whom he has had mercy, and shall by no means be moved in such a way that it could again be said of him: And the Lord shall sound the trumpet, and shall walk in the threat of his wrath. Nor shall he walk when the sun is already declining and the darkness is near, after midday, as we read that he did over Adam. And when he has stood, he will not stand in a valley and in low places but on a mountain, one that has no fruitless trees and barren forest, but where olive groves grow, by which the eternal light is fed, and infirmities are loosed, and rest is given to the weary. And this Mount of Olives, on which the feet of the Lord stand, is opposite Jerusalem and to the east, whence the sun of justice rises, and it is planted with those olive trees of which it is said: Your sons like young olive plants, round about your table. Half of it shall be split toward the east, the half in which are the trees planted from the nations, one of which says: But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped. And the other half shall be split toward the west and the sea, with a very great chasm: this is the people of the circumcision, to whom God speaks through the prophet: Why has my beloved done abomination in my house? Shall vows and holy flesh take away your wickedness from you, or will you escape by these? This beloved did abomination in the house of God, so that she crucified the Son of God and heard: The Lord called your name a shady olive tree and a wooded beauty; and your branches became useless, which were broken off from the good root, so that we might be grafted in their place. And note the mysteries of the scriptures, how the half that slopes toward the west, and is beaten by salt and bitter waves, is said to be not simply in the sea, but in the sheer abyss of the sea, an exceedingly great one, of which Micah too speaks: I will drag down its stones into the valley — Jerusalem's, no doubt —, and I will lay bare its foundations. These things we have said, as in very difficult and very obscure places, according to the slenderness of our powers. But the Jews, following the letter that kills, try to show that God stands upon the Mount of Olivet, and that the mountain itself is divided into two parts, so that the cleft has its beginning in one part toward the east, and the other part stretches its end toward the west, and in the middle, very steep, one part is divided toward the north, the other toward the south.

After this the prophecy recurring to the Coming of the Lord announces it more clearly, saying: "And the Lord my God shall come, and all His holy ones with Him," referring either to His apostles and disciples as holy ones, or certain invisible powers and ministering spirits, of whom it was said: "And angels came and ministered to him." And then of the Coming of the Lord, he says: "It shall be day, and it shall not be light, and cold and frost shall I be for one day." Instead of which Symmachus translated:

"And in that day there shall be no light, but frost and cold shall be for one day, which is known to the Lord, not day nor night, but at eventide it shall be light."

See how clearly this description of the day of our Saviour's Passion, a day in which "there shall be no light," was fulfilled, since "from the sixth hour to the ninth hour there was darkness over all the earth." And also the "frost and cold," since according to Luke:

"They led Jesus to the palace of the high priest. And Peter followed afar off. And while they kindled a fire in the midst of the hall, he sat down, according to Mark, with the others to warm himself. And John, too, especially mentions the cold, saying, The servants and the ministers stood, having made a fire of coals, for it was cold, and they warmed themselves.''

And this day, he says, was known to the Lord, and was not night. It was not day, because, as has been said already, "there shall be no light"; which was fulfilled, when "from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the earth until the ninth hour." Nor was it night, because "at eventide it shall be light" was added, which also was fulfilled when the day regained its natural light after the ninth hour. And this was fulfilled figuratively as well, generally in the Jewish race, darkness, cold, and frost coming on them after their outrage on the Christ, their understanding being darkened, so that the light of the Gospel should not shine in their hearts, and their love to God waxing cold, and then at eventide the light of the knowledge of the Christ arose, so that they who sat of old in darkness and the shadow of death saw a great light, in the words of the prophet Isaiah.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 18

To this he adds afterwards: "And the valley of my mountains shall be closed up, and the cleft of my mountains shall be joined unto Asael, and shall be closed up as it was blocked up in the days of the earthquake in the days of Ozias king of Judah."
